reads, with the argument for each member recorded at the member. The
completeness test now classifies against all three. A behaviour test
(`TestIdempotentMutationsAreRetried`) drives the real
`EnsureServiceIdentity` through a 429 and asserts two calls and the
agent address surviving the retry — so the decision is pinned by what
the code does, not only by list membership.

### gofmt — already clean

`gofmt -l .` prints nothing. `analyzer.go` and `edges.go` were
formatted at some point after the item was logged (2026-08-01); the
item is closed by verification, not by an edit.

### The stage table — already current

`docs/tako-agent-plan.md` §"Stages 5–9 (closed…)" carries the five-row
table. Brought current in Z2b as the resume brief says; verified, not
redone.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- Nothing new. The retry classification above was discovered work from
  Z2b and is closed here rather than logged forward.

## Z5 — DX proposal: the Cloud Tasks name-reuse wait (2026-08-04) — AWAITING APPROVAL

The last Z5 item is a user-facing error text, so it stops here for
wording approval like any other.

### The failure

Cloud Tasks blocks reusing a deleted queue's name for 7 days. Any
destroy-then-redeploy inside that window cannot converge: the deploy
dies creating a queue whose name it just released. Hit during the T3
walk (2026-08-01) and worked around with `--env u1` throughout.

Today `tasks.go` `Create` hands the failure to `Classify`, which has no
arm for it, so the user gets the fall-through:

```
create the tasks queue: <Google's message> (HTTP 400 from cloudtasks.googleapis.com)
```

Google's message says the queue existed too recently. It does not say
how long the wait is, does not say when the clock started, and does not
say that another environment sidesteps it — all three of which tako
knows and the user does not.

**One honesty note about the matcher.** The T3 log paraphrases Google's
text rather than quoting it (`a queue with this name existed too
recently`), and no verbatim transcript survives. The match is therefore
on the shortest fragment both the paraphrase and Google's documented
wording share, lowercased: `existed too recently`. If the live text has
drifted, the arm silently does not fire and the user gets today's
message — a miss, never a wrong answer.

### Proposed text

```
cannot recreate the tasks queue "u1-mailer-tako" — Cloud Tasks blocks reusing a
deleted queue's name for 7 days after the delete, and this name is still inside
that window. tako cannot work around it: either wait, or deploy under another
environment, whose queues get fresh names — tako deploy --env <name>
```

Deliberate choices in that wording:

- **"cannot recreate"**, not "cannot create". The user is redeploying
  something that existed; saying "create" invites them to look for a
  name collision with something live.
- **No countdown.** Google's error carries no delete timestamp, so tako
  cannot say "4 days left" without inventing it. It names the length of
  the wait and where the clock starts, which is everything it actually
  knows.
- **"tako cannot work around it"** pre-empts the next question. There is
  no force flag to look for; the block is Google's and there is no API
  to shorten it.
- **`--env <name>` and not a specific name.** The suggestion is a
  different environment, not a blessed scratch one.

### The call worth making, and my recommendation

**Should `tako destroy` warn before the delete, not just the redeploy
after it?** Recommended: **yes**. The error above arrives at the only
moment the information is useless — the queue is already gone and the
7 days already running. Destroy's preview already prints every object
and a `DATA — deleted with the app, gone forever` block, and the
confirmation prompt is still ahead of the user, so one line in that
preview is where the fact can still change a decision:

```
  NAME REUSE — Cloud Tasks blocks recreating these queue names for 7 days:
    u1-mailer-tako
```

Printed only when the observed set contains a tasks queue. If that is
out of scope for a housekeeping slice, say so and only the error text
ships — but the error alone closes the item as written while leaving the
avoidable version of the problem in place.

### Tests

- `TestClassifyTaxonomy`-style case pinning the new message on a 400
  carrying the fragment, asserting the three load-bearing parts:
  `cannot recreate the tasks queue`, `7 days`, `--env`.
- A negative case: an unrelated 400 from cloudtasks still falls through
  to today's message, so the arm cannot swallow other failures.
- If the destroy warning is approved, a preview test asserting the line
  appears with a tasks queue observed and is absent without one.

### Cloud errors & permissions

No new permissions and no new call — this reads a failure the deploy
already receives. No preflight is possible: name reuse is only knowable
by attempting the create, since Google exposes no "is this name
available" endpoint and no listing of recently-deleted names.

## Stage 10 — the open question answered, by rendering both halves (2026-08-04)

> Can every alert built in Z1–Z4 be written using plain tako alert
> constructs?

**No — but not for the reason the resume brief expected, and the real
reason is a better argument.** Answered by compiling each raw
alternative through `alertQuery` and putting it beside the preset's
line from `siren_queries.golden.txt`, rather than by reading
signatures. Two defects fell out of doing it that way, which is the
third time this stage that rendering the artifact found what reading
the code did not.

### The brief's headline claim is wrong

The brief says "there is no raw reader for tako's OWN per-endpoint
metrics… nothing in the SDK surface can name them." There is.
`PlatformMetric` takes any metric type and any raw matchers, and
`platformResource` already maps the `custom.googleapis.com/tako/`
prefix to `generic_task`. Rendered:

```
PlatformMetric("custom.googleapis.com/tako/requests",
    `job="gallery"`, `route="GET /api/photos"`, `status="5xx"`)
→ max(custom_googleapis_com:tako_requests{monitored_resource="generic_task",
    job="gallery",route="GET /api/photos",status="5xx"}) > 1
```

So naming is not the barrier. Two other things are, and both are
sharper.

**1. The `namespace` label cannot be written at declaration time.** It
is `App + "-" + Env` (`alerts.go` `takoRequests`), so the honest value
is `gallery-x1` — a string that only exists after a deploy and changes
per environment. A hand-written `PlatformMetric` over tako's own
metrics either omits it, and matches every environment including
previews, or hard-codes one and silently matches nothing everywhere
else. This is the identical argument `ServiceMetric`'s own doc comment
makes about `service_name`, applied to a label no constructor scopes.

**2. The raw Google-metric path has exactly ONE reduction: `max()`.**
`platformQuery` falls through to `"max(" + scopedSelector(...) + ")"`
for every unscoped and scoped-metric case; the only exception is
`ServicePercentile`. But `tako/requests` is a DELTA counter, and every
preset over it needs a reduction the raw path cannot produce:

| preset | reduction it needs |
|---|---|
| `RequestsErroring` | ratio of two `sum(rate(…))` |
| `RequestsSlow` | `histogram_quantile` over `_bucket` |
| `CronFailed` | `sum(increase(…))` |
| `CronMissed` | `absent_over_time(…)` |
| `JobFailed` | `sum(increase(…))` |

`max()` of a delta counter is neither a rate nor a count. So even with
every matcher written correctly by hand, none of those five is
reachable — the gap is REDUCTION, not naming, and it is not closed by
adding a constructor that names a metric.

### What IS expressible, rendered side by side

Verified by compiling both and comparing the strings, not by reasoning
about them:

| preset | raw equivalent | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `ServiceAtCapacity(Grind)` | `WhenAbove(ServiceInstances(Grind), max-0.5, w)` | **byte-identical** |
| `SingletonDown(Ticker)` | `WhenBelow(ServiceInstances(Ticker), 1, w)` | **byte-identical** |
| `QueueBacklogged(work, 50, w)` | `WhenAbove(QueueMetric(work, "…/num_undelivered_messages"), 50, w)` | **off by one** |
| `QueueStalled(work, 60s, w)` | `WhenAbove(QueueMetric(work, "…/oldest_unacked_message_age"), 60, w)` | **off by one** |

The two identical ones still cost the user something: `ServiceAtCapacity`
compiles `MaxInstances - 0.5`, so writing it raw means knowing the
half-unit idiom AND duplicating a number that already lives in the
service's footprint — a copy that goes stale silently when the
footprint changes.

The off-by-one is not a rounding quibble. Counting presets compile with
the `atleast` operator (`>= 50`); the raw vocabulary has only
`WhenAbove` (`> 50`). A user rewriting `QueueBacklogged(work, 50, w)`
by hand gets a condition needing 51, in the quiet direction — which is
exactly the defect `atleast` was introduced to fix, reappearing the
moment someone leaves the presets.

### Two defects found while rendering

Both are in shipped surface, both are the "well-formed query that
matches nothing" shape, and both are logged as discovered work rather
than fixed here.

**D1 — `WhenAbsent` on any Google-metric constructor compiles to its
inverse.** `alertQuery`'s `platform` case ignores the op and hands the
query to `comparison`, whose default arm is `> threshold`; an absent
condition carries threshold 0. So:

```
WhenAbsent(ServiceMetric(Svc, "run.googleapis.com/container/instance_count"), w)
→ max(run_googleapis_com:container_instance_count{…,service_name="x1-gallery"}) > 0
```

That fires when the metric IS present and goes quiet when it vanishes —
the precise opposite of what was asked. Nothing rejects it: the
analyzer accepts `WhenAbsent` with any `Metric`, and `absent_over_time`
is only ever reached from `customQuery` and `cron_missed`. Same family
as the `increase(x[26h]) == 0` lesson in §7, and the raw half is where
it survived.

**D2 — a user-written `subscription_id` matcher on `QueueMetric`
duplicates the label instead of overriding it.**

```
QueueMetric(work, "…/num_undelivered_messages", `subscription_id="x1-gallery-makethumb-dead"`)
→ max(…{monitored_resource="pubsub_subscription",
    subscription_id="x1-gallery-makethumb",subscription_id="x1-gallery-makethumb-dead"})
```

Two contradictory matchers on one label. This is the obvious thing to
try when reaching for the dead-letter subscription raw, and it is the
fourth instance of a matcher naming something no deploy has. tako
supplies `subscription_id` and `service_name` itself; a user matcher on
a label tako already writes should be refused at analysis time with the
constructor that does scope it named, not silently concatenated.

### So: are the presets sugar, or load-bearing?

**Load-bearing, for everything measured on tako's own metrics** — nine
of the twenty-four golden conditions. The presets are the only way to
reach a rate, an increase, a ratio, an absence or a quantile over
`tako/requests` and `tako/request_ms`, and the only thing that scopes
`namespace` to the deployed environment. For Google's own metrics they
are close to sugar: two compile byte-identically to a raw pair, and two
more differ only by the missing `atleast`.

**The follow-up is a design choice, not a backlog item, and the brief's
last option is the strongest one.** The metric names, the `namespace`
scheme and the `job`/`route` label spellings are tako's implementation
detail — three of them have already been changed once this stage, each
time because a query matched nothing. Exposing a `RouteMetric` or
`EndpointMetric` constructor freezes all of that as API, and the raw
path would also need a reduction vocabulary (`Rate`, `Increase`,
`Ratio`) it does not have, which is a much larger surface than the
question implies. The narrow reading — presets are deliberately the
only door to framework-internal metrics — costs nothing and is already
what the code does.

If anything is added, the argument is strongest for the two cases that
are about GOOGLE's metrics rather than tako's, where the vocabulary
already fits: a `DeadLetters(c)` selector so `QueueMetric` can name the
`-dead` subscription tako derives (which D2 shows users will otherwise
try to write by hand and get silently wrong), and an `atleast`-shaped
comparison so a hand-written counting condition is not off by one.
Neither exposes a tako metric name.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **D1: `WhenAbsent` over `ServiceMetric`/`QueueMetric`/`PlatformMetric`
  compiles to `> 0`,** the inverse of the request. Either compile it to
  `absent_over_time` like the custom-metric path, or refuse it — but not
  silently invert it.
- **D2: `QueueMetric`/`ServiceMetric` concatenate a user matcher onto a
  label tako already supplies,** producing a contradictory selector.
  Refuse at analysis time, naming the constructor that scopes it.
- Neither is in Z5's scope and neither is fixed here.

## D1/D2 — the two defects, fixed (2026-08-04)

Approved directly by the owner after the open-question analysis.
Together they are one commit: both are the same failure shape, both are
in the raw half of the alert surface, and neither has a gate because
neither adds surface.

### D1 — absence over Google's metrics compiled to its inverse

`alertQuery`'s `platform` case handed every op to `comparison`, whose
default arm is `> threshold`; an absent condition carries threshold 0.
So `WhenAbsent(ServiceMetric(Grind, …))` compiled to `max(…) > 0` —
firing while the metric was being written and going quiet the moment it
stopped. Fixed by giving the platform case an absence branch, the same
one `customQuery` has had since Y1.

Three things fell out of writing it that were not in the defect report:

**absent_over_time must not wrap a reduction.** `max()` of an empty
vector is empty, so `absent_over_time(max(…))` can never fire. The
absence branch takes the raw selector — which is why it is a separate
function rather than a wrapper around `platformQuery`.

**A distribution has no bare series to be missing.** `ServicePercentile`
absence asks about `_count`, the series that exists whenever anything
was recorded at all. Asking under the bare name would report "absent"
forever, on a metric being written every second — the exact trap Z3 was
built to close, in the one path Z3 did not touch.

**A Google metric has no schedule, and the lookback fallback did not
know that.** `cronPeriod` answers 24h for any handler it cannot find a
schedule on, so an ungated `lookback = 2 * cronPeriod(…)` gave every
platform absence a 48h window derived from a cron default that had
nothing to do with it. The derivation is now gated on
`Reading == "cron_missed"`, and everything else falls back to the
reduction period. **A wrong number that looks deliberate is worse than
the `[0s]` it replaced, because `[0s]` would have been refused.**

The notification sentence had the same defect: every platform reading
shared the threshold sentence, so an absence read "… is above 0" —
a sentence describing the query that used to be generated. Absences now
say what stopped, naming the deployed object:

```
siren/x1: service x1-siren-grind is reporting no instance count
```

### D2 — a matcher on a label tako owns is now refused

`{subscription_id="x1-siren-grind",subscription_id="x1-siren-grind-dead"}`
is what you got for trying to reach the dead-letter subscription by
hand: PromQL accepts both matchers and satisfies neither.

Refused rather than merged, and refused rather than overridden. Merging
is what produced the contradiction. Overriding would have been worse —
it would accept an env-prefixed physical name hand-written at
declaration time, which is the trap the scoped constructors exist to
close.

Which labels each constructor owns is a field on the `scopedMetrics`
table rather than a switch, so a new constructor cannot be added without
declaring them — the completeness habit the retry allowlist learned in
Z5 two commits ago.

The refusal names the thing that does answer the question, because a
refusal with no alternative just moves the dead end:

```
app.go:64:4: tako.QueueMetric already matches subscription_id for the consumer you
named — a second matcher on the same label matches nothing, and the deployed
subscription is env-prefixed so it cannot be written by hand; for the dead-letter
subscription use tako.QueueBacklogged or tako.QueueStalled with
tako.QueueWatch{DeadLetters: true} (tako/scoped-label)
```

### What demands it

`examples/siren` gains `Unreported` — `WhenAbsent(ServiceInstances(Grind))`
— so the fixed query is IN the golden rather than only in a unit test.
That is deliberate: this defect survived a live 22-policy walk and was
found by rendering the artifact, so the fix belongs in the artifact.

```
Unreported
  siren/x1: service x1-siren-grind is reporting no instance count
  absent_over_time(run_googleapis_com:container_instance_count{monitored_resource="cloud_run_revision",service_name="x1-siren-grind",state="active"}[600s])
```

### Tests

Four new provision tests and three new analyzer golden cases. The
provision ones assert the properties rather than the string: absence is
`absent_over_time`, contains no comparison operator, reduces nothing,
keeps its lookback, and — for distributions — names `_count`. Plus a
sentence test asserting no absence sentence contains "above" or "below".

`docs/reference/alerts.md` also carried a claim this falsifies: it said
`PlatformMetric` gives you "every matcher … including the one that says
which resource". `monitored_resource` is derived and now refused.
Corrected, with the new rule documented verbatim from the golden.

### Still open, from the same analysis and NOT done here

The owner's two directions, which are their own tasks:

1. **Stabilize the metric names and pin the generated PromQL.** The
   argument that names have changed three times is an argument for
   pinning them, not for hiding them.
2. **Let users write finer-grained alerts by starting from a preset** —
   read what it compiles to, then write their own version of it.

Proposal for both goes in separately. Neither is in D1/D2's scope.

## FA1–FA4 — DX proposal: stable metric names, and alerts you can fork (2026-08-04) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Owner, after D1/D2: metric names should be stabilized and the generated
PromQL pinned by unit tests, and a user should be able to start from a
preset, look at what it compiles to, and write their own finer-grained
version.

**Both are accepted as the right calls, and the second retires the
position I argued yesterday.** I claimed that because the label
spellings had been wrong three times, exposing them would freeze
mistakes as API. That reads the evidence backwards: three silent
breakages is an argument for pinning the names, not for keeping them
private. Nothing was protecting users from those bugs — the presets
carried them, and the presets are all anyone had.

Four slices. FA1 has no user-facing surface at all; FA2 is CLI only;
FA3 and FA4 are SDK API and are therefore their own tasks under the
normative-API rule.

### FA1 — one definition of every metric tako writes, locked

Today the writer (`pkg/runtime/http.go`) and the readers
(`pkg/provision/alerts.go`) agree about `tako/requests` by hand. Every
label defect this stage came out of that gap: `route` declared and empty
on all 88 series, `job` spelled three ways, `subscription_id` naming a
topic, `response_class="2xx"` where Pub/Sub writes `ack`. Each was
well-formed and matched nothing.

Proposed, no new user surface:

- **One exported table** in a single package naming each metric tako
  writes — type, kind (DELTA/GAUGE), value type, and every label with
  the values it takes. Writer and readers both derive from it, so they
  cannot disagree by editing.
- **A lock golden**, `testdata/metrics_lock.golden`, in the shape of the
  existing `sdk_lock.golden`. Changing a metric name or a label spelling
  fails a test that says so, which is the check that did not exist.
- **A writer/reader agreement test**: every label a query matches on must
  be one the runtime actually writes. This is the test that would have
  caught all four defects above, and none of them needed a cloud call to
  find — only something asserting the two halves name the same thing.
- **The names become documented API** in `docs/reference/alerts.md`, at
  which point FA3 can let users name them.

This is a prerequisite for FA3 and not merely adjacent: exposing a name
that is still free to change would hand users the same trap.

### FA2 — `tako alerts`, so a preset can be read before it is forked

"Look at the code" has no seam today. `tako deploy --plan` prints
`+ create alert policy Slowing` and never the query; the rendered
queries exist only as `siren_queries.golden.txt`, a test artifact inside
this repo. A user of tako cannot see what their own alert compiles to.

```
$ tako alerts

Slowing · GET /slow is slow
  when   p99 of request_ms over 60s exceeds 2000ms, sustained 5m
  query  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(custom_googleapis_com:tako_request_ms_bucket{
           monitored_resource="generic_task",namespace="shop-prod",job="shop",
           route="GET /slow"}[60s])) by (le)) > 2000
  notify ops@example.com
  preset tako.RequestsSlow(Slow, 2*time.Second, 0.99)
```

Everything printed is already computed by `alertQuery` and
`conditionSentence`, both pure functions of the graph and the config —
no cloud call, works offline, and `--env` picks which environment's
names to render. The `preset` line is what makes forking possible: it
says which call produced this, so the user knows what to replace.

`tako alerts --explain <Name>` prints one alert with the compiled query
broken into its parts. Worth having and cheap; it is the difference
between reading a query and understanding which piece to change.

### FA3 — the raw vocabulary reaches tako's own metrics

The gap measured yesterday: `PlatformMetric` can NAME
`custom.googleapis.com/tako/requests`, but the raw Google-metric path
has exactly one reduction — `max()` — while every preset over it needs
a rate, an increase, a ratio, an absence or a quantile. And `namespace`
is `App+"-"+Env`, so no hand-written matcher is correct at declaration
time. Naming was never the barrier; reduction and scoping were.

Proposed — tako's own metrics become HANDLES carrying the reading
methods that already exist, rather than a second parallel vocabulary:

```go
tako.Requests(Boom).Rate()                    // this route's request rate
tako.Requests(Boom).Status("5xx").Rate()      // just the failures
tako.RequestMs(Boom).Percentile(0.99)         // what RequestsSlow reads
tako.Requests(Sweep).Count()                  // a cron's runs, per window
```

The target supplies `namespace`, `job` and `route` exactly as the
presets do, so the env-prefixed half stays tako's. `.Status` is the one
label value users need, and its vocabulary (`2xx`/`4xx`/`5xx`) is
tako's own classification rather than a Google detail — stable once FA1
locks it.

`.Rate()`, `.Count()`, `.Percentile(q)` are the SAME methods a declared
Counter or Histogram carries. No new reading vocabulary, and the
analyzer's `readingMethods` table already resolves them.

Then every preset is expressible, which is the acceptance test:

```go
// tako.RequestsSlow(Slow, 2*time.Second, 0.99) written out
tako.WhenAbove(tako.RequestMs(Slow).Percentile(0.99), 2000, w)

// tako.CronMissed(Sweep) written out
tako.WhenAbsent(tako.Requests(Sweep), tako.Window{For: 30 * time.Minute})
```

**One call for the owner.** `RequestsErroring` is a RATIO of two rates,
and nothing in the vocabulary divides. Recommended: `tako.Ratio(a, b
Metric) Metric`, a combinator rather than a method, so it reads as what
it is:

```go
tako.WhenAbove(tako.Ratio(
    tako.Requests(Boom).Status("5xx").Rate(),
    tako.Requests(Boom).Rate()), 0.05, w)
```

Verbose next to `RequestsErroring(Boom, 0.05, w)` — deliberately. The
preset stays the way to say the common thing; this is the way to say a
different thing, and the two now differ by editing rather than by
giving up.

### FA4 — `WhenAtLeast`, so a fork is not off by one

Counting presets compile `>= n`; the raw vocabulary has only
`WhenAbove` (`> n`). A user rewriting `QueueBacklogged(work, 50, w)` by
hand today gets a condition that needs 51 — quietly under-reporting,
which is the direction nobody notices, and the exact off-by-one the
`atleast` operator was added to fix. It reappears the moment anyone
leaves the presets, which is what FA2 and FA3 invite them to do.

`WhenAtLeast(m, n, w)` compiles to `>= n`. One constructor, one arm in
`comparison`, one analyzer table entry.

### What demands them

`examples/siren` again: it already declares every preset, so it can
declare the hand-written twin of each one and a test can assert the two
compile to the SAME PromQL. That test IS the feature — "you can write
this yourself" is a claim, and a golden where preset and fork agree
character for character is its proof.

### Cloud errors & permissions

None new. FA1 and FA4 add no calls; FA2 reads no cloud at all; FA3 reads
metrics the deployer already lists. FA2's one failure mode is being run
outside a tako module, which every other command already answers.

### Size, and where this goes in the queue

Honestly: FA3 is the largest single SDK addition since alerting itself,
and FA1 is a refactor touching the runtime and the provisioner. This is
a stage, not a slice.

**Recommended ordering.** FA1 and FA2 can land now — FA1 adds no
surface and pays for itself the first time a label is renamed, FA2 is a
read-only command. FA3 and FA4 should follow FL1–FL4, because those are
the release gate and this is not. The alternative reading is that FA3 is
what makes alerting honest and should not wait behind four unrelated
slices; that is a real argument and the owner's call.

## Z5 — the Cloud Tasks name-reuse wait, shipped (2026-08-04)

Text approved as proposed; the destroy warning approved as recommended.
Z5 is now closed.

### Shipped

**The deploy error**, when a recreate is blocked:

```
cannot recreate the tasks queue "u1-mailer-tako" — Cloud Tasks blocks reusing a
deleted queue's name for 7 days after the delete, and this name is still inside
that window. tako cannot work around it: either wait, or deploy under another
environment, whose queues get fresh names — tako deploy --env <name>
```

**The destroy preview**, ahead of the confirmation prompt, printed only
when a tasks queue is actually going:

```
  NAME REUSE — Cloud Tasks blocks recreating these queue names for 7 days:
    u1-mailer-tako
    redeploying this app sooner needs a different --env
```

The warning earns its place by being the exception to the rule the rest
of the preview follows. Everything else `tako destroy` deletes converges
— a service comes back, a subscription comes back, the next deploy
re-derives it. A Cloud Tasks queue's NAME does not, for a week, and
that is Google's block with no API to shorten it. So this is the only
line in the preview describing something a redeploy cannot undo, which
is exactly why it belongs before the prompt rather than in the error a
week later.

`QueueNameReuseDays` is one constant read by both the CLI and the
provisioner, so the two cannot come apart on the number — the same
failure mode as a doc quoting a behaviour it does not share.

### Tests

Four, and two of them are about what must NOT happen:

- the message carries the queue name, the wait, "tako cannot work around
  it", and the `--env` remedy;
- it promises no countdown — asserted by banning "days left",
  "remaining" and "until", because the API carries no delete timestamp
  and an invented one is worse than none;
- a 403 on the same call still reports as a permission problem with its
  role remediation, so the new arm cannot swallow a different failure
  and send someone away to wait out a week for nothing;
- the destroy warning is silent with no tasks queue observed. A standing
  caveat in a preview trains people to skip the block it lives in.

### On the matcher, honestly

It fires on the lowercased fragment `existed too recently`. The only
transcript of this failure is the T3 walk's paraphrase, so a fuller
match risked never firing. If Google's wording has drifted, the arm is
silently skipped and the user gets the old generic message — a miss,
never a wrong answer. This is checkable the next time a destroy and a
redeploy happen inside the same week, and worth checking then.

### Docs

`docs/reference/queue.md` gains both texts under "Errors you'll meet",
verbatim from the tests. `docs/reference/cli.md`'s confirmation-ladder
section points at it — that section is about friction scaling with
irreversibility, and this is the least reversible thing a destroy does.

## FA1–FA4 — built (2026-08-04)

Approved by the owner, who also directed FA before FL. Landed as three
commits: FA1, FA2, then FA3+FA4 together (FA4 is one constructor and the
twin test needs it, so splitting them would have shipped a test that
could not pass).

### FA1 — the metric contract, and what it found on the way in

`internal/metrics` is now the single definition. Verified by mutation
rather than assumed: spelling `job` as `job_name` and `5xx` as `500`
both fail the agreement test. It reads the RENDERED golden rather than
the code that builds it, because the golden is what Cloud Monitoring
evaluates.

One drift found immediately: the descriptor documented `status` as
"2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx" while the runtime has always been able to emit
`1xx`. Harmless, and exactly the kind of thing that is invisible until
something depends on it.

Honest about reach: it covers tako's own metrics only. A wrong label on
a Google metric — which `response_class="2xx"` was — is still only
catchable live.

### FA2 — `tako alerts`

`AlertCondition` gains `Ctor`, so the command can say which call
produced a query. Derived in the analyzer rather than reconstructed
downstream from the reading: a second reading→constructor table would be
free to drift from the first, which is the failure FA1 was about.

`DescribeAlerts` is one renderer used by both the command and the siren
golden, so the artifact this repo reads and the output a user reads
cannot disagree.

### FA3 — one deviation from the approved proposal, and why

**The proposal said `tako.Ratio(a, b Metric) Metric`. What shipped is
`Requests(t).Status(c).Fraction()`.** Flagging it rather than burying
it: this is a smaller surface than was approved.

The reasons, in order of weight:

1. **No example demands the general form.** The standing rule is no
   feature without an example demanding it, and nothing in the five
   examples divides two unrelated metrics. `Fraction` is demanded by
   siren's `Rejecting`; a general `Ratio` would have shipped on an
   argument rather than a need.
2. **It delivers strictly more than the preset.** `RequestsErroring` is
   hard-wired to 5xx. `Status("4xx").Fraction()` is a question no preset
   can ask, which is the whole point of the slice.
3. **The general form needs a nested graph node.** `Ratio(x, y)` means
   `AlertCondition` carries two child conditions, and every consumer —
   query, sentence, preflight, `tako alerts` — grows a recursive case.
   That is a real cost for a shape nothing has asked for.

`Ratio` remains available later if a second example needs a ratio of
genuinely different metrics. Say so if you want it now instead.

### What the twin test found

`testdata/twins` declares each preset beside its hand-written
replacement and asserts identical PromQL. It caught a real gap on the
first run: `Requests(cron)` did not scope to the cron's synthetic route,
so the twin of `CronMissed` read the whole service — a query that looks
almost right and answers a different question. Fixed by deriving the
cron route the same way the presets do.

Six presets now restate character for character: RequestsErroring,
RequestsSlow, CronMissed, CronFailed, ServiceAtCapacity, QueueBacklogged.

A preset with no twin is REPORTED by that test rather than silently
skipped, so coverage cannot erode without someone seeing it.

### A defect fixed in passing

`trimZeros` trimmed significant zeros: a p50 rendered as **"p5"** and a
p90 as "p9". It has done that to every `ServicePercentile` sentence
since Z3 — a page naming the wrong quantile at 3am. Found because
siren's new `Sagging` is a p50; a p99 has no trailing zero to lose,
which is why nothing caught it before.

### API change

`testdata/sdk_lock.golden` gains 14 lines: `Requests`, `RequestMs`,
their handles and readings, and `WhenAtLeast`. This IS the API task, so
the lock was updated deliberately — the test asks for it to be called
out, and this is that.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **A `Count` reading with `Op == absent` is made to state an `Every`
  it never uses.** `WhenAbsent(x.Count(), Window{For: …})` is refused
  until a counting period is added, and the absent path uses `For` as
  the lookback and ignores it. Visible in `testdata/twins`, where the
  twin of `CronMissed` carries an `Every` for no reason. The rule should
  exempt absences.

## FL1 — `tako.RedirectPermanent` (2026-08-04)

Approved with FL2–FL4 in one go; ordering left to the suggested
FL1 → FL3 → FL4 → FL2.

### Shipped

`tako.RedirectPermanent(target)` — 301 on plain requests, and
deliberately IDENTICAL to `Redirect` under htmx: `HX-Redirect` + 200.
That last part is the design decision worth stating. Permanence is
something you say to crawlers and caches about a URL; a client-side
navigation is neither. A 301 htmx cannot follow would be a regression
dressed up as correctness.

`HTML` gains an unexported `status`, and `hooks.HTMLParts` widens to
carry it. Zero means 303, which is why `Redirect` needed no change and a
bare `HTML{}` is still not a redirect — the default is the old behaviour
rather than a value someone has to remember to set.

### What demands it

journal grows a rename. A post moved to a new slug leaves a `MovedURL`
record behind, and `read` serves 301 from it when the requested id is
gone. This is precisely what `SiteConfig.Redirects` cannot do: that map
is read at ANALYSIS time, and no analysis knows a slug a user will type
next week.

The write order in `rename` is the care of it: new post, then the
forwarding record, then delete the old. A crash anywhere leaves the post
reachable at one slug or both — never at neither.

`rename` itself answers 303, not 301. The redirect after a write is
about that write; the permanent one belongs in `read`, where the old
slug is actually requested. Getting that backwards would have made every
rename tell crawlers that `/write` had moved.

### Tests

Four, and two of them exist because a 301 and a 303 differ only in a
number — nothing else in the stack notices if they merge:

- a renamed post answers 301 at its old slug, with the right Location,
  and the new slug is a real page rather than another redirect;
- a slug that never existed still 404s (without this, "everything
  redirects" would pass the test above);
- both redirect kinds still send `HX-Redirect` + 200 under htmx;
- the two statuses differ on plain requests.

### API change

`sdk_lock.golden` gains `func RedirectPermanent(target string) (HTML, error)`.

## FL3 — `Query.Count()` (2026-08-04)

Conformance case first, then both backends — the standing order for
anything with two implementations.

### The mechanisms are completely different, which is the point

`gcp` answers server-side through `runAggregationQuery`, a sibling
endpoint of the `runQuery` the hand-rolled Datastore client already
speaks: the same query object wrapped in
`{aggregations: [{count: {}, alias: "total"}]}`. No new dependency, and
Datastore bills an aggregation per index entry SCANNED rather than per
entity returned — so counting ten thousand matches does not read ten
thousand entities. Doing it client-side would have meant paging the
whole result set to throw it away.

`local` walks the same filter its scan walks, sharing `matches()` with
`Query` rather than re-deriving the predicate. A count that disagrees
with the page it describes is worse than no count: a pager would
confidently render "page 3 of 2".

Two mechanisms, one contract, held together by the conformance suite —
which is exactly the case that suite exists for.

### Count ignores Limit AND Order

`Limit` was the approved call. `Order` came out of writing the gcp side
and is the sharper of the two: Datastore's index-backed sort only sees
entities that HAVE the sort property, so an order surviving into the
aggregation makes the count answer **low** rather than error. A number
that looks like an answer.

Both are conformance cases, so neither can regress in one backend only.

### It refuses to guess

An aggregation response tako cannot read is an error, not a zero. Three
cases are tested — no results, an unexpected alias, a non-numeric value
— because reporting "nothing matched" for "we did not understand the
answer" is precisely the quiet wrongness this stage has spent itself on.
`int64` also crosses Datastore's JSON as a STRING, so reading it is a
parse rather than a cast.

### What demands it

journal's home page renders "Showing 50 of 214". Before this, the page
could say "here are 50" and had no way to say "of 214" — the only route
to the total was reading every matching post and discarding the bodies,
a read per post to render one number.

Its test writes `pageSize + 10` posts, because the decision under test
is only visible past a page boundary. A second test unpublishes a post
and asserts it leaves the count: a count that ignores its filter is not
a count of anything.

### API change

`sdk_lock.golden` gains `func (*EntityQuery[T]).Count() (int64, error)`,
and `backends.Entity` gains `Count` — a backend-interface change, so
every implementation had to move together.

## FL4 — `Query.Page(cursor)` (2026-08-04)

The slice with the sharp edge, and it stayed sharp.

### The refusal is the feature

`Page` requires an explicit `OrderBy` AND an explicit `Limit`, refusing
both rather than guessing. The order requirement is the load-bearing
one: `gcp` falls back to a client-side sort when it cannot push tako's
default id order down beside an inequality filter, and the server cursor
it holds is then a position in the order DATASTORE used rather than the
one the caller asked for. Handed back, it silently skips or repeats
rows.

The refusal is identical on both backends and lives in
`pkg/backends` as `ErrPageNeedsOrder` / `ErrPageNeedsLimit` — shared
because the WORDING is contract too. Meeting a different message on
local than in the cloud would be its own bug.

### Two cursors, one meaning

`gcp` hands back Datastore's own cursor — which `Query` has always read
and thrown away at the API boundary — and does NOT drain batches: one
call, one page. `local` computes a keyset position, `(sort value, id)`,
base64-encoded so it is opaque. Opaque on purpose: a cursor that looks
parseable invites being built by hand for a different query, which gcp
would refuse and local would silently mis-page.

The id rides in the cursor because the sort value is not unique, and the
id tiebreak is ALWAYS ascending on both sides — the same `__key__`
ascending gcp pushes down. Reversing it with the sort direction would
make a descending page skip rows whenever two share a sort value.

The conformance case is the one the design exists for: between page 1
and page 2, insert a row before the cursor, insert one after, delete a
third. A keyset cursor is unmoved by the write before it; an offset
cursor would shift and serve a row twice.

### What demands it, and what it taught

gallery's `GET /api/photos` takes `?cursor=` and returns the next one.

**The cache had to change shape, and that is a finding worth keeping.**
The feed was `Cache[[]Photo]`; caching a first page while paging beyond
it meant the cached page could never say what came after it, because a
cursor cannot be rebuilt from the rows it points past. It is now
`Cache[PhotoPage]` — items and cursor cached together. Anyone adding
paging to a cached list will hit this, so it is in the reference.

Only the first page is cached. Caching beyond it would mean one entry
per cursor: a key space as large as the feed and a hit rate near zero.

**A test of mine was wrong before the code was.** The HTTP walk asserted
exact page sizes against a server with no `DrainQueues`, so it raced the
thumbnail worker and read 24 of 25 — which looked exactly like a dropped
row. It now walks until the walk settles, with a deadline. Worth
recording because the failure was indistinguishable from the bug the
test was written to catch.

### API change

`sdk_lock.golden` gains `EntityPage[T]` and `EntityQuery.Page`.
`backends.Entity` gains `Page` — a backend-interface change, so both
implementations moved together, as with FL3.

`Photo` gains an indexed `Created`: a cursor names a position in an
order, so the field the feed is ordered by has to be indexed.

## FL2 — `SiteConfig{NotFound: "404.html"}` (2026-08-04)

Last of the four. The three calls in the proposal were taken as
recommended: template first with a static-file fallback, 500s out of
scope, htmx gets the document.

### One field, because it is one experience

Two entirely different paths 404 today: `pageError` for a handler's
`tako.NotFound()`, and the site handler for a static miss. A
handler-side result type could never have closed this — on a static miss
NOTHING RAN, so there is nothing to return a status from. That is the
whole argument for it being site config, and it is why the field covers
both rather than the pages half only.

Cheaper than it looked, as the proposal guessed: `RegisterSiteTemplates`
already receives `SiteOptions` and installs the renderers as package
state, so both paths reach one `writeNotFoundPage` with no codegen
restructuring.

### The failure policy is the part that matters on a bad day

A missing 404 page, one that does not parse, or one that fails at render
all fall back to today's plain text. **A 404 never becomes a 500.** The
visitor already could not find what they wanted; an error page that
errors turns "we don't have that" into "we are broken", which is a worse
thing to say and a harder one to debug. All three failure shapes are
tested.

500s keep plain text, and that is a decision rather than laziness: a 500
means something in this process is already wrong, and running the
template engine to report it is the worst moment to depend on it.

### A mistake caught by an existing test

The first version exported `WriteNotFoundPage`, and `TestRuntimeLock`
failed — that surface is imported by generated code in users'
repositories. Both callers are inside `package runtime`, so it had no
business being exported. The lock did exactly what it is for.

### Coverage the goldens did not have

journal has no codegen golden, so `NotFound`'s trip from analyzer to
generated main was pinned by nothing. `TestSiteOptionsCarryEveryDeclared
Field` covers it: a `SiteConfig` field the analyzer reads and codegen
drops is an option that silently does nothing, which reads as the
feature not working rather than as a bug.

The journal harness also had to grow the site mount it never had — the
generated main mounts the site at "/", and without that a mistyped URL
was answered by the mux rather than by tako.

### API change

`sdk_lock.golden`: `SiteConfig` gains `NotFound string`.

## Stage 11 — FL1–FL4 all landed (2026-08-04)

Ordering ran as suggested: FL1 → FL3 → FL4 → FL2. Every example test
passes against `local`, conformance included.

What the four taught, beyond their own features:

1. **A cursor cannot be rebuilt from the rows it points past.** FL4's
   cache had to change shape, and anyone adding paging to a cached list
   will meet the same wall.
2. **`Count` had to ignore `Order` as well as `Limit`** — an ordered
   Datastore count silently drops entities missing the sort property,
   which answers LOW rather than failing.
3. **A test can be wrong before the code is.** FL4's HTTP walk raced an
   async worker and read 24 of 25, which is exactly what a dropped row
   would look like.
4. **`trimZeros` had been rendering p50 as "p5" since Z3** — found in
   FA3 only because a new alert used a quantile with a trailing zero.

Z6 (publish) is what waits on these; its blocker was the flautas
friction logs, and FL1–FL4 are those logs answered. The verdicts still
need to travel back to `flautas/docs/friction.md` under its ADR 0008,
which is a flauta-session job — tako never patches flauta.

## Z7 — `tako docs`, built (2026-08-04)

Approved by the owner ("proceed with the documentation server") against
the proposal above. Shipped as proposed, with three deviations and one
correction, all below.

### Where the embed had to live

`//go:embed` patterns cannot escape the directory of the package that
declares them, and no `..` is allowed. So neither `cmd/tako` nor
`pkg/docserver` can embed `docs/guide`; the only package that can is
`docs` itself, which is why `docs/embed.go` exists and holds nothing
else. The alternative — embedding from the module root — would have put
284KB of markdown in the SDK package that **every tako application
imports**. Verified it does not:

```
$ go list -deps github.com/gsandoval/tako | grep -c tako/docs
0
$ go list -deps ./cmd/tako | grep tako/docs
github.com/gsandoval/tako/docs
```

The CLI carries the docs; a user's binary does not. 284KB against a
21.5MB binary, and it is what makes the command work for someone who ran
`go install` and has no checkout.

### The api page, and the copy it reads

The api section needed the exported surface as *data*, and the one place
the surface is written down is `testdata/sdk_lock.golden` — which the
docs package also cannot reach (`..` again, and `testdata` is invisible
to the go tool besides). So `docs/api/surface.txt` is a copy, and
`TestEmbeddedSurfaceMatchesTheSDKLock` pins it byte-for-byte with a
`-update` path. **Copying under equality was the deliberate choice over
re-deriving**: two renderings of "the exported surface" can disagree,
one copy under equality cannot.

What the lock does not carry is where each symbol is *explained*, so
`symbolPage` says — 110 entries, one per top-level symbol, methods
following their type. That table looked like a maintenance cost until
the test was written, and then it turned out to be the point: **a new
exported symbol with no reference page now fails a test.** Mutation-
verified rather than assumed:

```
$ echo "func Ghost() error" >> docs/api/surface.txt
$ go test ./pkg/docserver/ -run TestEveryExportedSymbolHasAReferencePage
    docserver_test.go:121: Ghost is exported and no reference page documents it — add it to symbolPage
```

One symbol is mapped to nothing on purpose. `tako.Handler` is what
`Cron`, `Worker`, `Subscribe` and `Singleton` return and what an alert
can target; every page that produces one mentions it in passing and none
of them defines it. It prints on the api page under **"Not on a
reference page yet"**, so the gap is visible to a reader and not only to
us, and the test holds the list of such symbols to exactly that one.

### The link check, which was the reason to build this

The proposal singled it out: `reference/alerts.md` gained links to
`observability.md` and `footprint.md` during Y2 and nothing verified
they resolved. They do. So do the other 124, the 1 same-page anchor, and
all 54 links into the repository:

```
checked 125 links between docs, 1 anchors, 54 into the repository; 0 external, unchecked
```

Both arms mutation-tested, because a checker that has never failed is a
checker nobody has tested:

```
    docserver_test.go:58: reference/cli.md links to "queue.md#errors-you-will-meet" — reference/queue.md has no section with that anchor
    docserver_test.go:69: reference/alerts.md links to "observabilty.md#the-two-metrics-you-never-declare", and docs/reference/observabilty.md does not exist
```

The anchors exist because the renderer turns headings into IDs
(`parser.WithAutoHeadingID`) and the sanitizer is told to keep them —
without that every `#section` link in the docs would silently land at
the top of a page and nothing would have noticed.

### Links to files the binary cannot serve

54 of them: `../../examples/shop/app.go`, `../../validate/shop.md`,
`../domain-options.md`. There is nothing to serve them from, and a dead
`<a>` tells a reader less than a path does — so they render as the
repo-relative path in monospace, next to the sentence that linked them.

Except when the sentence **is** the path. "From
`[examples/shortlink](../../examples/shortlink/app.go)`:" appears all
over the reference, and printing the path after text the path already
contains says the same thing twice. A link text the target contains is
replaced by the target rather than followed by it.

### Sanitizing our own documentation

goldmark renders, bluemonday sanitizes — the pipeline `pkg/runtime`
already has (settled decision #13). The input here is tako's own docs,
which is exactly the argument for sanitizing it anyway: a renderer with
an exception for trusted input is a renderer with an exception, and this
one listens on a port. It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, for the same
reason.

### Deviations from the approved proposal

1. **Grouping** is read out of `reference/README.md` at build time
   rather than restated in code — the proposal said "grouped the way
   `docs/reference/README.md` already groups them", and parsing that
   file is the only version of that sentence with no second copy to keep
   true. A heading whose bullets are prose is not a group, which is what
   keeps the "What is API, and what is not" section from becoming one.
2. **The error text prints `tako: port 8090 is already in use — pass
   --port to pick another`**, not `tako docs:`. Every CLI error in tako
   goes through one `fail()` with one prefix, and inventing a
   per-command prefix for this one error would be the deviation.
3. **The symbol count in the startup line is computed, not fixed.** The
   proposal said 171; the lock is 189 lines today. A hand-counted number
   in a banner is a number that goes stale.

### A correction the docs needed

`reference/cli.md` listed `tako alerts` under **Cloud, mutating**. It
touches no cloud — FA2's own doc comment opens "Nothing here touches the
cloud" — and `tako` help has always had it under Local. Moved, along
with `tako docs`. Also dropped "148 entries" from `reference/README.md`:
the lock has 110 top-level symbols and 189 lines, the number had been
wrong for some time, and a count restated in prose is a count that
drifts. The api page carries it now, generated.

### One bug the tests did not have

`referenceOrder` listed the index twice — the leftovers sweep matched on
`Name + ".md"`, and the index's `Name` is `""`. It surfaced as
`reference (25 pages)` in the startup banner for a reference of 24, i.e.
in the one place a reader would see it. `TestEveryEmbeddedPageRenders`
now asserts the page count equals the file count, each page once.

### Validation

`validate/docs.md`, run in full. The step that matters:

```
$ go build -o /tmp/tako ./cmd/tako && cd /tmp && ./tako docs --port 8091
📖 tako docs → http://localhost:8091
   guide (9 chapters) · reference (24 pages) · api (189 symbols)
   ^C to stop
```

Served every page from `/tmp`, with no tako source anywhere near it. If
that step needs the repository the feature does not exist.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **`tako.Handler` is undocumented.** Above; the api page says so out
  loud now. A reference page — or a paragraph in an existing one — would
  close it.
- **No search.** Find-in-page over one reference page is enough for
  twenty-four of them; a search index waits for a demand. Recorded in
  `cli.md` under "Not yet" rather than left as a silent absence.

### API change

None. `docs` and `pkg/docserver` are internals, like everything outside
the root package.

## Z7a — `tako.Handler` documented (2026-08-04)

Discovered work from Z7, closed the same day. The api page had one
symbol under **"Not on a reference page yet"**; that heading is empty
now, and the `known` list in
`TestEveryExportedSymbolHasAReferencePage` is empty with it — so the
next undocumented export is a test failure with nowhere to hide.

### Where it went

`docs/reference/handler.md`, filed under **Async** in the reference
index. It bends the rubric and says so, the way `cli.md` does: a
`Handler` is not a feature you declare, it is the value five features
return — `Worker`, `Subscribe`, `Runner`, `Cron`, `Singleton`. **Five,
not the four the Z7 entry said**: `Runner` returns one too, which the
type's own doc comment has said all along.

The page is reachable from where a reader actually is, not only from
the index: each of the five producer pages now names the type in its
Declare section. That took the link count from 125 to 145, all
resolving.

### What was worth writing down

- **The var name is the identity.** `MakeThumb` in package `gallery`
  deploys as `gallery-makethumb` — `pkg.Name + "-" + ToLower(varName)`
  in `pkg/analyzer/workers.go`. The handler FUNCTION's name is a log
  label; the type's own comment records that using it as an identity
  once gave crons a second name that disagreed with the deployed one.
- **A Handler is a name, not a callable.** No exported methods, on
  purpose: invoking a worker directly would be a second way to run the
  work, one that skips the queue that gives it retries, a dead letter
  and at-least-once delivery.
- **Not every Handler is a service.** `Runner` becomes a Cloud Run
  **Job**; the other four become services. The first draft of the page
  said "each Handler becomes its own Cloud Run service" and `job.md`
  contradicted it — caught by reading the page it linked to.

### Three claims the draft got wrong, and how

Every one was caught by checking the code rather than by review, which
is the argument for writing reference prose next to a grep:

1. **"Nothing is registered by declaring a Handler."** False:
   `handlers.go` keeps an `asyncRegistry` so `NewTestApp` can wire every
   worker without a handler list. It is read only by tests — the
   approved rule-1 carve-out — and the page now says exactly that
   instead of overstating the purity.
2. **"Renaming a Handler var … classifies as a REPLACE."** False.
   `provision.go` marks a same-kind orphan+create pair a **rename
   suspect**; a replace is a different class. The page now describes the
   orphan, the suspect line, and that compute orphans are stateless and
   pruned.
3. **Snippets that would not analyze.** The alert examples were written
   without windows; `tako/window` requires a period on a Count reading.
   They now match the forms `examples/siren` actually declares.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **`cache.md` documents an option that does not exist.** "‍`WithTTL` is
  the only Cache option" — there is no `WithTTL` anywhere in the tree;
  the TTL is the second argument to `tako.Cache`. Found while reading
  the page for house style. The docserver's link check cannot catch
  prose that names a symbol which never existed; **an api-surface check
  over the reference's inline `tako.X` mentions would**, and that is
  worth its own slice rather than a patch here.

### API change

None.

## Z7b — the api-surface check over the docs (2026-08-04)

Discovered work from Z7a, closed the same day. The docs name the SDK 522
times across the guide and the reference, and nothing checked that the
things they name exist. Three of them did not.

### The check

`TestEveryTakoSymbolTheDocsNameExists` scans every embedded page for
`tako.X` and requires X in the lock — as a declaration or as a method.
Methods count because the docs legitimately write `tako.Percentile` for
a reading method, and a `tako/quantile` error text tako itself emits
does the same.

The pattern requires a capital after the dot, which is what keeps the
image labels (`tako.app`, `tako.service`) out of the sweep. Mutation-
verified rather than assumed:

```
reference/lock.md:103: the docs name tako.WithLease, and tako exports no such symbol
```

### What it found

1. **`tako.Absent`** (alerts.md) — the constructor is `tako.WhenAbsent`,
   which the same page writes correctly four times elsewhere. One
   sentence kept a name that never shipped.
2. **`tako.On`** (footprint.md) — the constant is `tako.ToggleOn`, and
   the very next clause says `tako.ToggleOff` correctly.
3. **`tako.ServiceLatency`** (alerts.md) — in a "Not yet" bullet
   promising three shorthands tako does not have. **One of the three has
   since shipped**: `tako.ServiceInstances` is in the lock. So the
   bullet was stale in the direction that matters least to a compiler
   and most to a reader — it told them to write `ServiceMetric` by hand
   for something with a constructor. Rewritten to name the one that
   exists and point at `tako metrics <search>` for finding the rest.

Worth noticing about #3: prose that names an ABSENT feature is a real
category, and writing it as `tako.X` makes it indistinguishable from a
claim that the symbol exists. The rule this test creates is a good one —
if tako does not have it, do not write it with the `tako.` prefix.

### What it deliberately does not check

**The `WithX` vocabulary.** The reference alone has 59 mentions —
`WithProfile`, `WithFootprint`, `WithSingleflight`, `WithAuth`,
`WithPrivate`, `WithDelay` — and tako exports no `With` anything;
options are fields on config structs. That looked like 59 more bugs
until the spec and the API reviews turned out to use the same names:
§4 of the tech spec discusses "conflicting `WithProfile` values",
`api-review-2.md` groups the surface by `WithBuild` / `WithAuth` /
`WithParallel`. They are the project's names for option FAMILIES, not
claims about Go symbols.

So the check requires the qualifier: **`tako.X` asserts "this is API",
bare `WithX` does not.** Whether the docs should keep a vocabulary the
Go surface does not share is a question about the docs' voice, not a
correctness bug, and it is not one to settle inside a test.

### The limit, stated

cache.md said "`WithTTL` is the only Cache option" — which motivated
this whole slice — and this check does **not** catch it. Not because of
the vocabulary rule but because the sentence is wrong about something
subtler: `tako.Cache` has no options at all. The TTL is a required
second parameter, deliberately (`cache.go`: "a cache without an expiry
policy is a decision, not a default worth making silently"), and the
page also claimed you could omit it. Fixed by hand.

**No symbol check catches a sentence that is wrong about a symbol that
exists.** That is the honest ceiling here, and the reason the reference
rubric puts real transcripts and verbatim error texts on every page.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **The `WithX` vocabulary question**, above. Either the docs adopt the
  config-struct names, or the vocabulary is stated somewhere as
  deliberate. Today it is neither, and a reader who greps for
  `WithSingleflight` finds nothing.

### API change

None.

## FL5 — DX proposal: the session surface, mounted method-scoped (2026-08-04) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Source: flauta's friction log, entry `2026-08-04 — the session route has
no method, and the mux refuses it beside a wildcard page`. The first gap
from that log that **stopped** a task (its M2-01) rather than shaping
one, and the only one it promoted since FL1–FL4 landed.

### The failure, reproduced here

Not taken on the consumer's word. journal already declares `tako.Auth`;
giving it the permalink shape a blog actually wants —
`GET /{year}/{slug}` — is enough:

```go
var (
	Home    = tako.Page("GET /", home)
	Read    = tako.Page("GET /p/{id}", read)
	...
	Perma   = tako.Page("GET /{year}/{slug}", perma)   // the whole repro
)
```

```
$ tako dev
tako dev · journal

  analyzing   1 service, 7 endpoints, 1 site
  generating  .tako/gen/journal/main.go
  starting    http://localhost:8080

  GET / → Home (app.go:61)
  GET /p/{id} → Read (app.go:62)
  GET /write → Write (app.go:63)
  POST /p → Save 🔒 (app.go:64)
  POST /p/{id}/publish → Publish 🔒 (app.go:65)
  POST /p/{id}/rename → Rename 🔒 (app.go:66)
  GET /{year}/{slug} → Perma (app.go:67)
  entity posts (indexes: Published, Created)
  entity moved_urls
  site ./web
  auth (google)

panic: pattern "GET /{year}/{slug}" (registered at …/.tako/gen/journal/main.go:65)
conflicts with pattern "/api/_session" (registered at …/.tako/gen/journal/main.go:32):
	GET /{year}/{slug} matches fewer methods than /api/_session, but has a more
	general path pattern

goroutine 1 [running]:
net/http.(*ServeMux).register(...)
	/opt/homebrew/…/net/http/server.go:2882
main.main()
	…/.tako/gen/journal/main.go:65 +0x5b4
```

Read that transcript as a user would. tako prints a clean, confident
route table — every declared endpoint, the site, the auth — and then
panics into a stack trace through **generated code the user did not
write**, naming a route (`/api/_session`) that appears nowhere in their
source. Nothing in the app's own code ran. There is no tako error text
here at all; the framework's last word is `starting`, and the runtime's
is a stdlib panic.

### The cause, and how small it is

Codegen mounts the session exchange without a method
(`pkg/codegen/codegen.go:329`), while both of its siblings are
method-scoped:

```go
mux.Handle("/api/_session", runtime.SessionHandler())              // no method
mux.Handle("POST /api/_session/signout", runtime.SignOutHandler())
mux.Handle("GET /api/_session/signin", runtime.SignInPage("google"))
```

Go's `ServeMux` orders patterns by specificity and refuses a pair where
neither wins on both axes: `/api/_session` is more specific on path,
`GET /{year}/{slug}` is more specific on method. It cannot order them,
so it panics **at registration** — a startup crash, not a request-time
404, and not a warning.

`SessionHandler` already switches on exactly two methods internally
(`pkg/runtime/session.go`: POST at :133, DELETE at :172, everything else
falling to a 405 default). So the method-less mount claims all nine
methods to serve two.

### The change

```go
mux.Handle("POST /api/_session", runtime.SessionHandler())
mux.Handle("DELETE /api/_session", runtime.SessionHandler())
```

Verified against stdlib `ServeMux`: registered this way, `/api/_session`
coexists with `GET /{year}/{slug}` **and** the site handler at `/`, and
requests route as they did — `POST` reaches the session handler, the
wildcard page still gets its own URLs. One line becomes two in the
generator's output; no SDK symbol changes, no analyzer rule, no
conformance case. `pkg/codegen/testdata` goldens move by two lines.

### The one call for the owner

**What answers an unlisted method.** Today `PUT /api/_session` gets
`SessionHandler`'s own `405 method not allowed`. Mounted method-scoped,
it no longer matches either pattern and falls through to the site
handler at `/`. Two halves, both checked separately: the fallthrough
itself against stdlib `ServeMux`, and journal's site handler answering a
miss — `curl -i /no-such-file.css` → `404` + `text/html`, the styled
page FL2 shipped, not plain text. Today the same request gets
`405 Method Not Allowed`, plain text, from `SessionHandler`'s default.

- **Recommended: accept the fallthrough.** `/api/_session` is an
  internal endpoint tako injects; it is not in the guide, not in the
  reference, and nothing tells a user to type it. A 404 for a method
  that endpoint never served is not a worse answer than a 405, and it
  costs one pattern instead of three.
- The alternative, if the 405 is worth keeping: also register
  `GET /api/_session`. It does not conflict with the wildcard page
  (same method, more specific path), so it is available — it is just
  three mounts and a special case to explain.

### What this is NOT

- Not a change to auth, sessions, cookies, or the sign-in flow. The
  handler's body is untouched; only the pattern it is registered under
  moves.
- Not a fix for route conflicts in general. An app can still declare two
  of its own patterns that `ServeMux` refuses to order, and it will
  still learn about it as a panic. Turning *that* into an analyzer error
  is a real slice and is not this one — noted below.
- Not the wildcard-shadows-site-files warning from the same friction log
  (a different entry, flagged workaround-fine there, unscheduled here).

### The example demanding it

**journal**, which is where the transcript above came from. It already
declares `tako.Auth`; FL5 gives it `Perma` permanently, so the
combination that cannot boot today is in the acceptance suite. The
regression is a startup test — the generated service is built and run —
so this cannot come back quietly. `GET /p/{id}` stays; a permalink and a
short id-URL coexisting is the realistic shape, and the two do not
conflict.

### Gate FL5 (agent-side, no cloud)

1. journal boots with auth and the wildcard both declared, and the
   route table above is followed by `starting`, not a panic.
2. Sign in and sign out through the dev bar still work — the POST and
   the DELETE paths both exercised.
3. `GET /2026/some-post` reaches `Perma`; `POST /api/_session` reaches
   the session handler.
4. The codegen golden shows two patterns where it showed one.
5. Full example suite plus conformance green against `local`.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **Route conflicts should be an analyzer error, not a panic.** The
  analyzer knows every declared pattern and every pattern codegen will
  inject. `ServeMux`'s ordering rule is documented and mechanical, so
  the conflict is decidable at analysis time and could read
  `app.go:67:12: route "GET /{year}/{slug}" conflicts with the injected
  session route (tako/ROUTE-CONFLICT)` instead of a stack trace through
  generated code. FL5 removes today's only *framework-caused* instance;
  it does not remove the class.
- **`tako dev` prints its route table before the service is proven to
  start.** The confident listing above was already on screen when the
  process died. Printing it after a successful bind, or marking it
  provisional until then, would stop the output from vouching for a
  service that never ran.

### API change

None. `docs/reference/auth.md` gains a sentence naming the two methods
`/api/_session` answers, since that becomes observable.

## FL5 — revised DX proposal: `/_tako/`, a namespace with rooms (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Supersedes the method-scoping proposal above, at the owner's direction.
That draft fixed the panic flauta hit; this one fixes the class it
belongs to, and the difference was worth the redraft.

### What changed the shape

The first draft treated `/api/_session` as an endpoint mounted wrong.
It is really an endpoint in the wrong *namespace*: codegen already
injects three routes under `/_tako/` — `POST /_tako/push`,
`/_tako/signed/`, `POST /_tako/cron/{cron}` — and the session surface
is the only injected route that sits outside it. The convention exists;
one route never joined it.

**A prefix alone does not create precedence.** `ServeMux` resolves
conflicts structurally — which pattern is more specific on path and on
method — and has no notion of a reserved word. Measured:

| framework pattern | vs `GET /{a}/{b}` | vs `GET /{a}/{b}/{c}` |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/_session` (today) | **panic** | ok |
| `/_tako/session` (prefix only) | **panic** | ok |
| `/_/api/session` (deeper prefix) | ok | **panic** |
| `POST` + `DELETE /_tako/session` | ok | ok |

A deeper prefix does not remove the collision, it relocates it to a
different arity. Any fixed-depth path loses to a wildcard of matching
depth.

**And the bug is already in the tree twice.** `/_tako/signed/` is
mounted method-less and panics against any app declaring a three-or-more
segment wildcard GET route — a gallery with `GET /{user}/{album}/{photo}`
and a bucket cannot boot, exactly as journal with auth cannot. `push`
and `cron` escape only because they happen to be `POST`-scoped, which is
luck, not design. FL5 as first written would have fixed one instance and
left the other.

### The change: two muxes, one dispatch

Framework routes leave the app's mux entirely.

```go
takoMux := http.NewServeMux()   // everything tako injects
appMux  := http.NewServeMux()   // everything the user declared, plus the site at "/"

top := http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	if strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/_tako/") {
		takoMux.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		return
	}
	appMux.ServeHTTP(w, r)
})
```

No two patterns share a mux, so a conflict is not merely avoided — it is
**unrepresentable**, at every arity and every method, for every endpoint
tako injects later. This is what "the framework's routes take precedence"
actually requires; specificity rules cannot express it.

It also dissolves the first draft's one open question. With a mux of its
own, the session route stays method-less and `SessionHandler`'s own
`405 method not allowed` survives — no fallthrough to the site's 404, no
choice to make.

### The rooms

`/_tako/` alone would be a junk drawer. Sub-namespaces, so every future
endpoint has an obvious home and the surface stays readable:

```
/_tako/api/…       machine-facing: JSON, tokens, form posts, OIDC triggers
/_tako/z/…         human-facing diagnostics (reserved, empty in v0.1.0)
/_tako/<page>      the framework's own pages — signin today, few ever
```

Three rooms and a doorstep. `api` is everything a program talks to;
`z` is everything a person reads about a running service; a bare name
under `/_tako/` is a page the framework itself serves, and there is
exactly one of those.

Mapped onto what exists today, with the moves marked:

| route | methods | from |
|---|---|---|
| `/_tako/api/session` | POST, DELETE | **moved** from `/api/_session` |
| `/_tako/api/session/signout` | POST | **moved** from `/api/_session/signout` |
| `/_tako/api/push` | POST | **moved** from `/_tako/push` |
| `/_tako/api/signed/{token}` | GET, PUT, OPTIONS | **moved** from `/_tako/signed/` |
| `/_tako/api/cron/{cron}` | POST | **moved** from `/_tako/cron/{cron}` |
| `/_tako/signin` | GET | **moved** from `/api/_session/signin` |
| `/_tako/z/…` | — | reserved, serves 404 |

Verified end to end — 6 framework routes and 5 app routes including
`GET /{a}/{b}`, `GET /{a}/{b}/{c}`, `GET /{a}/{b}/{c}/{d}`, a user's own
`POST /api/orders`, and a site at `/`:

```
registered: 6 framework routes, 5 app routes, every wildcard arity — no conflict

POST    /_tako/api/session           -> 200 session
DELETE  /_tako/api/session           -> 200 session
PUT     /_tako/api/session           -> 405 method not allowed
POST    /_tako/api/session/signout   -> 200 signout
POST    /_tako/api/push              -> 200 push
PUT     /_tako/api/signed/tok123     -> 200 signed
POST    /_tako/api/cron/nightly      -> 200 cron cron=nightly
GET     /_tako/signin                -> 200 signin
GET     /_tako/z/                    -> 404 404 page not found
GET     /_tako                       -> 404 404 page not found
GET     /opinion/nota                -> 200 page2 a=opinion b=nota c=
GET     /2026/01/nota                -> 200 page3 a=2026 b=01 c=nota
GET     /a/b/c/d                     -> 200 page4 a=a b=b c=c
POST    /api/orders                  -> 200 user-api
GET     /foo/../_tako/signin         -> 307 → /_tako/signin
```

The last two lines are the reserved namespace holding its edges. A bare
`/_tako` with no trailing slash is answered by tako's mux, not leaked to
the app's; and a path that only *becomes* `/_tako/…` after cleaning is
redirected to the clean form, which re-enters through the prefix check
rather than sliding past it.

### Decisions taken (owner, 2026-08-05)

Both open calls answered, and one name shortened.

1. **`cron` moves inside `api`** — `/_tako/api/cron/{cron}`. The draft
   argued that leaving it beside `api` was a judgment nobody could
   restate as a rule, given that `push` is equally OIDC-only and
   machine-only. Taken: the rule wins over the judgment.
2. **`zpages` becomes `z`** — `/_tako/z/`. Same room, shorter name, and
   `zpages` was a borrowed word (App Engine's) that would have needed
   explaining in the reference.
3. **`signin` stays at `/_tako/signin`**, and the shape is now a stated
   rule rather than a one-off: **plain pages live at the root of the
   namespace.** Rooms are for families of endpoints; a page is a page.
4. **The framework always wins under `/_tako/`**, unconditionally and by
   design — "the user should never want an endpoint whose first segment
   is `_tako`". This is what the two-mux dispatch encodes, and it is a
   claim on the **whole URL space** under the prefix, static files in a
   site directory included, not only on declared `Page`/`API` routes.
   Note the two properties are independent: the panic is a
   *registration-time* conflict that separate muxes remove on their own,
   while precedence is the *request-time* rule this decision settles.
   With it, the analyzer rule below is no longer load-bearing for
   correctness — it exists so a `GET /_tako/…` typed by mistake is a
   build error rather than a handler that silently never runs.

**Not a security boundary, and the proposal will not claim it is.** The
rooms are organizational. Authentication stays per-endpoint: the session
exchange is public by necessity (the ID token *is* the credential),
signed URLs authenticate by the token in the path, push and cron verify
OIDC. The one room that will carry a policy is `z` — diagnostics must
never be public in cloud — and stating that once, in advance, is most of
why it is worth reserving before it has contents. The owner's position,
recorded: `z` is off in the common case and will require auth if and
when it has contents, so nothing ships unguarded by reserving the name.

### Why reserve `z` while it is empty

Because reserving it later is this same breaking change again. A
namespace that only becomes reserved when something needs it has never
been reserved. It serves 404 in v0.1.0 and appears in exactly two
places: the analyzer's reserved-prefix rule, and one sentence in the
reference saying it is tako's.

### Mounting: is there a sub-mux, and why this is not one

Asked directly, and worth recording because the obvious answer is
wrong. `http.ServeMux` **is** an `http.Handler`, so mounting one inside
another looks like the idiomatic move:

```go
appMux.Handle("/_tako/", takoMux)   // ← this panics
```

It does not work here, and it fails for the *same reason as the bug
being fixed*. Registration goes through the parent mux's conflict check
first, and `/_tako/` is a subtree pattern with no method, so against a
wildcard page route neither is more specific on both axes:

```
pattern "/_tako/" conflicts with pattern "GET /{a}/{b}":
/_tako/ and GET /{a}/{b} both match some paths, like "/_tako/b".
But neither is more specific than the other.
```

Measured: `/_tako/` panics beside `GET /{a}/{b}` and beside
`GET /{a}/{b}/{c}`; `/_tako/{rest...}` panics too. There is no pattern
spelling that mounts a sub-router on the app's mux and survives, because
a mounted sub-router is just another pattern to the parent, and Go's
mux has no mount primitive and no fallthrough — a matched pattern is
the end of routing.

So the dispatch has to happen **before** either mux sees the request,
which is the whole design. In generated code that is one readable line
via a runtime helper, keeping `.tako/gen/` legible (settled decision 3):

```go
// framework routes are answered before the app's router is consulted;
// nothing under /_tako/ can be declared, shadowed or reordered by the app.
runtime.Serve(runtime.WithDevBar(runtime.Reserved(takoMux, mux)))
```

`Reserved(framework, app)` is ~6 lines in `pkg/runtime`, holds the
prefix constant, and is where the `/_tako`-without-slash case is
handled. It is also the seam a test can assert directly, rather than
asserting through a generated `main`.

### The analyzer rule, which is now a courtesy rather than a fix

A user route under the prefix becomes silently unreachable — verified,
a declared `GET /_tako/sneaky` gets tako's 404 and never sees its
handler. Per decision 4 that is correct behaviour, not a bug; what is
wrong is the silence. The same complaint flauta made about a wildcard
route shadowing its stylesheet applies here — the rule is one sentence,
the gap is that nothing tells you. The pattern is a string literal, so
it is decidable at analysis time:

```
app.go:41:12: route "GET /_tako/sneaky" is inside /_tako/, which the framework
reserves for the endpoints it injects (session, cron, signed URLs, push);
choose a path outside it (tako/RESERVED-PREFIX)
```

### The cost, stated

83 references to `/api/_session` across the runtime's dev bar and
sign-in page, `docs/guide/04-journal.md`, `reference/auth.md`,
`reference/client-ts.md`, and journal's and shop's HTML. Mechanical, but
public: after a v0.1.0 tag those paths are API, and Z6 has not published
yet. This is the cheapest hour this move will ever have.

### The examples demanding it

- **journal** — declares `tako.Auth`, gains `GET /{year}/{slug}`. The
  combination cannot boot today (transcript in the proposal above).
- **gallery** — declares a bucket with signed URLs; a
  `GET /{user}/{album}/{photo}` route is the second instance, and the one
  the first draft would have missed.

### Gate FL5 (agent-side, no cloud)

1. journal boots with auth and a two-segment wildcard page; gallery boots
   with signed URLs and a three-segment one. Both are startup tests.
2. Sign in and sign out through the dev bar; a signed upload PUT and a
   signed download GET both round-trip.
3. `PUT /_tako/api/session` still answers 405 from the handler, not 404
   from the site.
4. A user route under `/_tako/` fails analysis with the text above
   (golden, file:line asserted).
5. Full example suite plus conformance green against `local`.

### API change

No exported SDK symbol changes. The injected URL surface changes, which
is user-observable and gets a table in `docs/reference/auth.md` plus a
note in `client-ts.md`.

## FL5 — the `/_tako/` namespace, shipped (2026-08-05)

Approved as the revised proposal above, with decisions 1–4 folded in.
Framework routes now live under a reserved prefix, on a mux of their
own, answered before the app's router is consulted.

### What shipped

**`internal/routes`** — the one definition of every URL tako mounts.
This is an addition to the approved proposal, which put the prefix
constant in `runtime.Reserved`. It moved because the paths are agreed on
by parts of the system that never call each other: codegen writes the
mount, the local signer builds URLs pointing at one, the provisioner
targets three of them from Cloud Scheduler / Cloud Tasks / a Pub/Sub
push subscription, alert queries match one as a `route` label, and the
analyzer refuses to let a user declare any. Six spellings that used to
agree by hand — the identical argument `internal/metrics` was created
for in FA1, and `testdata/lock.golden.txt` plays the same role: a rename
here is a failing test rather than a Scheduler POST quietly becoming a
404.

**`runtime.Reserved(framework, app)`** — the dispatch. Nine lines, and
the only new exported symbol (`runtime_lock.golden` +1).

**The mounts**, all moved:

| now | was |
|---|---|
| `/_tako/api/session` | `/api/_session` |
| `POST /_tako/api/session/signout` | `POST /api/_session/signout` |
| `GET /_tako/signin` | `GET /api/_session/signin` |
| `POST /_tako/api/push` | `POST /_tako/push` |
| `/_tako/api/signed/` | `/_tako/signed/` |
| `POST /_tako/api/cron/{cron}` | `POST /_tako/cron/{cron}` |
| `/_tako/z/…` | — (reserved, 404s) |

**`tako/reserved-prefix`** — analysis refuses a route inside the
namespace, with a fixture covering four shapes (namespace root, a bare
