page, the `api` room, the `z` room) and one lookalike, `/_takoish/page`,
that must NOT trip it.

### The finding that changed an example

The proposal named gallery's demand as `GET /{user}/{album}/{photo}`,
three segments. Building it showed that is not a demand at all, and the
reason is worth keeping: **moving a mount deeper moves the arity that
collides with it, one segment at a time.** Measured against one shared
mux, with the real route sets:

```
journal's real routes + tako's NEW auth mounts   → ok
journal's real routes + tako's OLD auth mounts   → PANIC
gallery's real routes + tako's NEW bucket mounts → PANIC
```

So the path move **alone** would have rescued journal — `/_tako/api/session`
is three segments where `/api/_session` was two, and journal's wildcard
page is two. It does nothing for gallery, whose `/_tako/api/signed/`
subtree matches four-segment paths and therefore still collides with a
four-segment wildcard. gallery's permalink shipped as
`GET /{owner}/{album}/{photo}/{size}` — a sized image URL, which is what
a gallery wants anyway — so that the example genuinely cannot boot
without `Reserved` rather than merely commemorating a bug.

Stated plainly, because it is the whole argument for the design that was
chosen: **journal is the historical reproduction; gallery is the live
demand; the two-mux separation is what makes the class of failure
unrepresentable at every arity, which no path is deep enough to do.**

### Tests

- `pkg/runtime/reserved_test.go` — parameterized over every mount in
  `routes.All`: which ones panic on a shared mux beside wildcards at
  four arities (Session and Signed do; the method-scoped three do not),
  that `Reserved` registers all of them beside all of those, that each
  side routes to its owner, that a user route under the prefix is
  unreachable, that an unlisted method still gets the handler's own 405,
  and that `/foo/../_tako/signin` redirects into the namespace instead
  of sliding past the check.
- `internal/routes/routes_test.go` — the URL lock, plus: every mount is
  inside the prefix it claims, the mounts coexist on one mux, and
  `IsReserved` refuses lookalikes.
- `examples/journal` — the pre-FL5 pair still panics (kept as the record
  of what was fixed), a three-segment wildcard still conflicts with the
  new session mount (kept because it is why depth is not the fix), and
  journal's real shape registers clean. Plus: the permalink and the
  short URL both resolve, and the namespace answers on the real server
  with tako's 404 rather than the site's.
- `examples/gallery` — the same in the arity that still bites, and the
  permalink resolving a photo for its owner and 404ing for another's.
- `pkg/analyzer/testdata/errors/reservedprefix/` — the rule's golden.

### Validation

`validate/reserved-namespace.md`, executed end to end. §1, the whole
point — the combination that used to panic:

```
tako dev · journal

  analyzing   1 service, 7 endpoints, 1 site
  generating  .tako/gen/journal/main.go
  starting    http://localhost:8080

  GET / → Home (app.go:61)
  …
  GET /{year}/{slug} → Perma (app.go:73)
  entity posts (indexes: Published, Created)
  site ./web
  auth (google)

ready in 947ms — watching (backends: local, in-process)
```

§3, live against that server:

```
HTTP/1.1 303 See Other          ← POST /_tako/api/session (dev_user=alice)
Location: /
Set-Cookie: _session=654bc718…; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
signin       200
PUT session  405     ← the handler's own refusal, not the site's 404
z/x          404     ← tako's mux, not journal's 404.html
bare _tako   404
signout      204
app root     200
app /write   200
permalink    404     ← /2026/nope reaches Perma, which finds no post
```

§5, the analyzer rule through the CLI rather than through a golden:

```
tako: app.go:239:24: route "GET /_tako/sneaky" is inside /_tako/, which tako
reserves for the endpoints it injects (session, sign-in, cron, signed URLs,
push) — the framework answers that namespace before this app's routes, so
Sneaky would never run; choose a path outside it (tako/reserved-prefix)
exit status 1
```

§7: `go test ./...` green, and all seven example suites green.

**What was NOT validated: the cloud half.** The move changes three
deployed targets — the Scheduler job `uri`, the push subscription
`endpoint`, the Cloud Tasks queue target — and the `route` label alert
queries match. Plan-level assertions are unit-tested
(`shortlink_plan_test.go`, `alerts_test.go`, `promql_test.go`,
`siren_queries.golden.txt`), but no deploy has run against these paths.
It belongs to the next `release-cycle` walk, and is stated here rather
than implied covered.

### Deviations from the approved proposal

1. **`internal/routes` exists**, where the proposal put the constant in
   `pkg/runtime`. Reason above; the proposal's `Reserved` signature and
   composition line are otherwise exactly as approved.
2. **gallery's permalink is four segments, not three** — the proposal's
   three would not have demanded the fix. Reason above.
3. Examples use path literals rather than the constants, because
   `internal/` is not importable from an example module. This is the
   better outcome: an example showing the real URL is documentation.

### Discovered work (unscheduled)

- **Route conflicts should be an analyzer error, not a panic.** FL5
  removed the framework's instances; an app can still declare two of its
  own patterns Go refuses to order and learn about it as a stack trace
  through generated code. Decidable at analysis time — the patterns are
  string literals and the ordering rule is documented.
- **`tako dev` prints its route table before the service is proven to
  bind.** During the pre-fix reproduction the full, confident listing was
  on screen when the process died. Printing it after a successful bind
  would stop the output vouching for a service that never ran.
- **`/_tako/z/` is reserved and empty.** Whatever lands there needs an
  auth story before it serves anything; the owner's position is recorded
  in the proposal.

### API change

No root-package symbol changed (`sdk_lock.golden` unmoved).
`pkg/runtime` gained `Reserved` (+1 in `runtime_lock.golden`). The
injected URL surface changed, which is user-observable: documented as a
table in `docs/reference/api.md` under "`/_tako/` is not yours", with
the paths updated across `reference/auth.md`, `bucket.md`, `cron.md`,
`queue.md`, `topic.md`, `testing.md`, `observability.md`,
`client-ts.md`, `guide/04-journal.md`, `guide/cloud.md`, eleven
`validate/*.md` scripts, and two lines of the tech spec.

## FL6 — DX proposal: the shadow warning (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Promoting the friction log's "workaround-fine, warning worth asking for"
entry at the owner's direction. flauta declared
`GET /{section}/{slug}` and `/assets/site.css` stopped being served —
no error, no warning, an honest 404 for a stylesheet. It was caught by
`TestDocumentAndAssetHeaders`, written for another purpose; without that
test the site deploys unstyled.

### Why a heuristic is the wrong shape

The obvious version is "warn when a Page pattern has the same segment
count as files the site serves" — depth arithmetic, the way the friction
log described it. That is guesswork, and it is guesswork about a
question `ServeMux` already answers exactly.

So the check **asks the mux**. Build the real thing — every declared
route pattern, plus `"/"` for the site handler, exactly as codegen
mounts them — then walk the site directory and, for each file, ask the
mux which pattern claims its URL. A file whose `GET` lands on anything
other than `"/"` is shadowed, by definition, with the same resolver that
will serve production traffic. No false positives, no depth rule to get
wrong, and it stays correct when Go's precedence rules change.

### The message

Positional, because the fix is at the declaration:

```
app.go:31:2: ⚠ GET /{section}/{slug} shadows 2 files the site serves — /assets/site.css and /assets/app.js reach articleRead instead, and answer 404; move them deeper than the route's 2 segments (/assets/css/site.css) or narrow the pattern (tako/site-shadow)
```

Three files named at most, then `and N more`. It names the handler
because the 404 comes from there, and it names the depth because moving
the file is the fix that costs nothing.

### Warning, never an error

Shadowing is legitimate — an app that serves no files at that depth is
doing nothing wrong, and flauta's own `/media/{key}` (M3) will shadow a
depth-2 URL space it deliberately owns. Nothing fails the build. It
prints and the exit code is unchanged.

### Where it runs

`tako dev` on every analyze pass (this is a local-feedback problem;
flauta hit it in development) and `tako deploy` beside `warnCallEdges`
and friends. Both call it **after** the site build has run — an unbuilt
`Out` directory has no files to enumerate, and a check that ran before
the generator would report nothing and mean nothing.

Placement: `analyzer.ShadowedSiteFiles(graph) []Shadow` — the pattern
knowledge is the analyzer's, the printing is the caller's, which is how
the deploy warnings are already split. No root-package symbol; no
change to the `tako` surface.

### Tests

Golden analyzer cases, message text asserted exactly per the standing
rule: a two-segment wildcard over a depth-2 asset (warns, names it), the
same route over depth-3 assets only (silent), a route shadowing more
than three files (`and N more`), a site with no files (silent), an app
with no Site at all (silent). Plus the case flauta shipped as its
workaround — assets moved to depth 3 — which must stay quiet.

---

## FL7 — DX proposal: reading the declared domain (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

The friction log's last open entry, filed as "no candidate feature worth
asking for" and re-opened at the owner's direction — correctly, because
the entry conceded more than it had to. It argued that analysis-time
configuration is load-bearing and that a duplicated string held by a
test is the smaller price. The first half is true and is not in
question. The second half assumes the app cannot *read* what it
declared, and nothing requires that.

```go
var web = tako.Service(tako.ServiceConfig{Domain: "1dos3porti.com"})

func canonical(path string) string { return "https://" + web.Domain() + path }
```

The literal stays a literal — the analyzer reads the source, the deploy
plan is still computed without running the app, `tako/config-literal`
still refuses a variable. Nothing about the constraint moves. The
handle simply stops hiding the value it was given, and flauta's
duplicated string plus the test that guards it both go away.

### Against the six rules

Rule 3 governs *operations* — anything that can do I/O takes `Ctx` and
returns an error. A record read is not one, and the surface already
says so: `CounterHandle.Count() Metric`, `HistogramHandle.Mean()`,
`RequestsHandle.Rate()` are all ctx-less, error-less reads of a
declaration. `Domain()` joins that family. Rule 1 is untouched —
`Service` remains a side-effect-free record, and reading a field of it
cannot depend on initialization order.

The doc comment on `ServiceHandle` currently reads "It carries no
methods: the declaration IS the value, read at analysis time." That
sentence needs rewriting to say what stays true: the declaration is the
value, read at analysis time **and readable by the app that declared
it**.

### Undeclared domains

`Domain()` returns `""` when no `Domain` was declared, and the doc
comment says so in the same breath. The alternative — resolving to the
run.app URL or to `localhost:8080` so absolute URLs "just work"
everywhere — is rejected: it would make the return value differ by
environment, which is exactly wrong for the things flauta wants it for
(canonical tags, RSS `<link>`, sitemap entries, share URLs all name the
public domain regardless of where the code is running). One declared
string, the same everywhere, or the empty string. **Open question for
the owner** — this is the one judgment in FL7 worth disagreeing with.

### Tests

`compile_check_test.go` for the shape, an SDK-lock regeneration (its own
review, per the standing rule), a unit test for the undeclared case, and
`docs/reference/domains.md` gains a "Reading it back" section.

---

**2. `docs/reference/domains.md:10` names a symbol that no longer

## FL6 — the shadow warning, shipped (2026-08-05)

Approved as proposed ("A warning on shadows is good"). Built as
described: no depth heuristic, the real `ServeMux` asked instead.

### What landed

`analyzer.ShadowedSiteFiles(moduleDir, graph) []Shadow`
(`pkg/analyzer/shadow.go`) builds the router codegen builds — every
declared pattern for the service, plus `"/"` for its site — and asks it
which pattern claims each file under the served directory. A file whose
`GET` lands anywhere but `"/"` is shadowed. `Shadow.Warning()` renders
the line, so `tako dev` and `tako deploy` cannot drift into two
descriptions of one problem.

Callers: `pkg/devserver` (every cycle, after `build.Sites`, before
codegen) and `cmd/tako/deploy.go`'s `warnSiteShadows` beside
`warnCallEdges`/`warnFootprints`/`warnDomains`. Both run after the site
build, since an unbuilt `Build` output has no files to shadow.

Asking the mux paid for itself immediately in cases a depth rule would
have got wrong: `POST /{a}/{b}` does not shadow a GET stylesheet,
`GET /` does not swallow the site (codegen's `{$}` anchoring), and
patterns that cannot coexist are declined rather than reported over
(that is a startup panic with its own message).

### It found a real one

`examples/journal` has flauta's exact shape — `GET /{year}/{slug}` at
`app.go:73` over a site with `/assets/…` at depth 2 — and has been
serving its own stylesheet as a 404:

```
  app.go:73:2: ⚠ GET /{year}/{slug} shadows 3 files the site serves — /about/index.html, /assets/htmx.min.e209dda5.js, /assets/site.9f86d081.css reach Perma instead of the site, and answer 404; move them deeper than the route's 2 segments, or narrow the pattern (tako/site-shadow)
```

Confirmed live, not inferred: `curl localhost:8080/assets/site.9f86d081.css`
→ **404**, `curl localhost:8080/` → 200. `TestFingerprintedAssetIsImmutable`
(`site_test.go:39`) passes throughout, because `siteHandler()` mounts the
site **alone** — no declared routes, so nothing to shadow. That is the
blind spot the friction log described, sitting in tako's own acceptance
suite. Logged under Discovered work below rather than fixed here.

### Validation

`validate/site-shadow.md`, written and run.

- **Step 1** (fires on a real app), live transcript above: warning
  between `analyzing` and `generating`, position real, claim true, dev
  server starts and serves — a warning, not a rule.
- **Step 2** (quiet when the files clear the route): moving
  `site.9f86d081.css` to `/assets/css/` drops it from the line, which
  goes from 3 files to 2. This is flauta's own workaround, and it has
  to be silent or the warning trains people to ignore it.
- **Step 3** (deploy): **not run** — `deploy --plan` stops at
  `tako: no project set` before analysis. Belongs to a release-cycle
  walk with credentials, like FL5's cloud half. The wiring is three
  lines calling the same function step 1 covers.
- **Step 4**: 11 automated cases pass, message text asserted exactly.

### Docs

`reference/errors.md` gains warnings as a fourth kind of message that
is not an analysis error, with the full text and the reason it is worth
reading. `reference/site.md`'s "Use" section — where a reader learns
that declared routes beat the site — now says what that costs and how
to clear it.

---

## FL7 — reading the declared domain, shipped (2026-08-05)

Approved, including the judgment the proposal flagged: `Domain()`
returns `""` when undeclared, and never substitutes a run.app URL or a
localhost ("I'm ok with the domain() function returning empty string").

`func (s *ServiceHandle) Domain() string` — one symbol, the SDK lock
regenerated deliberately for it (`go test . -update`, `go test ./docs
-update`; the diff is exactly `+ func (*ServiceHandle).Domain() string`).
The lock test caught the change before the regeneration, which is what
it is for.

Analysis-time configuration is unchanged in every respect: the analyzer
still reads the literal, `tako/config-literal` still refuses a
variable, the plan is still computed without running the app. Only the
read-back direction is new.

`reference/domains.md` gains "Reading it back", stating both the use
(canonical tags, RSS, sitemap, share links) and the deliberate refusal
to vary by environment.

**flauta's side**, when a flauta session next runs (tako never patches
flauta): the config seam's `domain` can now come from the
`ServiceConfig` literal, and the M6 test asserting the two agree has
nothing left to guard.

## Review pass — docs, API surface, live cloud (2026-08-05)

Owner-requested full review after FL5b–FL7. Three tracks; two complete,
one blocked at a permission boundary.

### Track 1 — documentation

The existing checks were all green and stayed green: every `tako.X` the
docs name exists (533 mentions), every link resolves, every exported
symbol has a reference page, the api page matches the lock. What they
cannot see is a sentence that is wrong about a symbol that exists —
Z7b said so in its own entry, and that is exactly where every finding
landed.

**Self-contradictions, fixed** (commit `9a8b1a7`):

1. `cron.md` denied a per-cron timezone knob 100 lines below the
   section documenting `CronConfig.Timezone`, complete with an
   `America/Mexico_City` example and its own `tako/timezone` error.
2. `pages.md` still said styled error pages were a later slice. FL2
   shipped `SiteConfig{NotFound}` and site.md was rewritten the same
   day; pages.md was not. The truth is narrower than either page had
   it, and is now stated: the 404 wears the site's design, every other
   status is plain text because `tako.HTML` carries no status.
3. `client-ts.md`'s backtick opened before `tako gen client` and closed
   after `tako gen client ts`, rendering a sentence as a code span that
   swallowed its own prose.

**The WithX vocabulary, settled** (commit `f1dc5ab`). Z7b logged the
question and declined to answer it: 84 mentions across 22 spellings of
an option namespace X2 deleted, none of them anything a user could
write. Settled toward the config-struct names at the owner's direction,
which is also what tako's analyzer already says when it refuses one
(`Cloud Run enforces Route.Private at the service level`).

Two of the 84 were not vocabulary but **shipped output**:

- `preflight.go` told users to "drop tako.WithDomain" — never a symbol,
  and `domains.md` already documented the corrected sentence. The doc
  had been fixed; the code had not. This is the same class as FL5b: a
  rename that updated the docs and left the emitting code behind.
- a Cloud Tasks routing error blamed "a WithDelay publish site"; the
  method is `PublishAfter`.

And two were **error texts tako no longer emits at all** — X2 deleted
the `invalid-option` rule (`pkg/analyzer/config.go` says so) and both
`singleton.md` and `job.md` kept documenting its message, in the
"Errors you'll meet" sections the reference rubric says carry verbatim
texts. Replaced with the `config-literal` messages actually emitted.
`cache.md`'s "any option but `WithTTL`" went too: `tako.Cache` has no
options, the TTL is a required parameter.

`TestTheDocsDoNotNameRetiredWithOptions` now guards the vocabulary.
The existing symbol check could not: its pattern requires the `tako.`
qualifier and these were bare, which is precisely how they survived.

**Attempted and rejected:** a scanner that extracts quoted error texts
from the docs and greps the code for them. It reported 76 misses, most
of them false — messages built with `fmt.Sprintf("tako.%s name must
be…")` never appear literally in source. Not shipped; a real version
needs the analyzer's message construction, not a regex over prose.

### Track 2 — API quality

The surface holds up against the six rules. Rule 3's shape ("Ctx first,
returns error") is deviated from in three deliberate, coherent
families, all of which read as records rather than operations:
accessors (`CounterHandle.Count`, `SecretHandle.Value`, and now
`ServiceHandle.Domain`), fire-and-forget metrics (`Add`, `Observe`),
and `EntityTx`'s methods, where the ctx is the transaction.

Two observations, neither urgent, both logged rather than acted on:

- **`ServiceInstances(t) Metric` returns a reading directly** while its
  neighbours `Requests(t)` and `RequestMs(t)` return handles you take a
  reading from. Defensible — instances is a gauge with one reading —
  but it is the one platform metric shaped differently from the rest.
- **`tako.HTML` still cannot carry a status for markup**, which is the
  403 gap the friction log has open. Worth restating precisely because
  the plumbing is already there: `HTML.status` exists (`site.go:75`),
  `HTMLParts` already returns it (`page.go:291`), and the markup arm
  simply never calls `WriteHeader`. FL1 built the transport when it
  added `RedirectPermanent` and nothing else picked it up.

### Track 3 — live cloud

**hello, full cycle on tako-test-01: PASS.**

```
✓ hello → https://hello-cgbk74ip3q-uc.a.run.app
  (22s)
```

Against `validate/deploy.md`: preflight green; the plan created a
service account, a run service and one grant and nothing else; the real
deploy reached a live URL in **22s** against a ~2 min target; all three
endpoints answered exactly as `tako dev` does (`/hello`, `/greet/memo`,
`POST /echo`); a second deploy was `0 creates, 0 updates, 6 skips` and
`✓ no changes (8s)`; `tako logs --since 30m` showed all three request
lines with timings; `tako destroy` demanded the typed app name and
refused an empty one, then removed everything. Verified in the console
after: no run services, no tako service accounts, no artifact repo, no
framework bucket. The stateless-reconcile claim holds end to end.

The security summary printed the converted vocabulary
(`⚠ 1 mutating route(s) without Route{SignIn: true}: POST /echo`),
which is the docs change reaching real output.

**gallery release-cycle walk: BLOCKED, not failed.** Step 1 needs
`gcloud secrets create x1-notifier-key`, and creating a secret was
refused by this session's permission classifier. What the attempt did
validate is the step the script leads with — preflight honesty:

```
tako: preflight found 1 gap(s):
  secret x1-notifier-key does not exist in tako-test-01 — create it: printf '<value>' | gcloud secrets create x1-notifier-key --data-file=- --project tako-test-01
```

It stopped **before building anything**, named the exact secret, and
gave the exact command — the "Cloud errors & permissions" rule made
good. Everything past it is unrun: the X1 cron-identity check, the P2
URL-construction paths, the five-service deploy, and destroy over a
real resource graph.

### Discovered work

**6. `tako logs` prints each request twice** — once tagged `INFO` and
once untagged, with different durations (`GET /hello → 200 (3.2ms)` /
`(0.6ms)`). Almost certainly Cloud Run's request log alongside tako's
own middleware line, in which case the fix is a filter, not a bug in
either. Seen on every request of the hello walk. Not investigated.

## Release-cycle walk, gallery on tako-test-01 (2026-08-05) — one FAILURE

Ran in full after the owner created the secret the earlier attempt was
blocked on. `validate/release-cycle.md`, all five sections.

| § | What | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Five services deploy | **pass** — 51 creates, 0 orphans, 5m58s (3m14s of it the Datastore index) |
| 2 | X1: cron carries its variable's name | **pass** |
| 3 | The cron actually runs under that name | **pass**, first fire |
| 4 | P2: paths that only run against the real API | **FAIL** on the live request; convergence half passes |
| 5 | Destroy leaves nothing | **pass** |

§2 and §3, the two the walk exists for:

```
x1-gallery-cron-cleanup  https://x1-gallery-….run.app/_tako/api/cron/Cleanup  0 0 * * *
14:11:45 x1-gallery INFO POST /_tako/api/cron/Cleanup → 200 (514.5ms)
14:11:46 x1-gallery INFO cron ok
```

No `cleanupOrphans` in either column, and the route resolved on the
first fire with no invoker-propagation window. §4's other half
converged exactly — `0 creates, 0 updates, 59 skips, 0 orphans` — so
P2's observation paths and creation paths agree about every URL. §5
destroyed cleanly and nothing `x1-`prefixed survived in Run, Scheduler,
Pub/Sub or IAM.

### The failure: derived composite indexes miss a conditional query

`GET /api/photos` on the deployed service answers **500**.

```
err=HTTP 400 from /v1/projects/tako-test-01:runQuery: no matching index found.
recommended index is:
- kind: photos
  properties:
  - name: ready
  - name: created
    direction: desc
```

The analyzer derived, for `photos`:

```
composites: [[owner, ready], [owner, ready, -created]]
```

Neither serves the shape Datastore is asking for. The cause is one
function building its query **conditionally**
(`examples/gallery/app.go:384`):

```go
q := photoStore.Query(ctx).Where("Ready", "=", true)
if owner != "" {
    q = q.Where("Owner", "=", owner)
}
return q.Limit(100).All()
```

Two runtime shapes — `ready` alone, and `ready`+`owner` — and the
analyzer, which groups every `Where` in a function into one shape, emits
indexes for the wider one only. The anonymous caller takes the narrower
path, and there is no index for it. An unauthenticated `GET
/api/photos` is exactly that caller, which is why the walk's own
one-line smoke test is what found it.

**It contradicts a stated invariant.** `pkg/analyzer/appgraph.go:124`:

> Grouping per function can over-index a function running two separate
> queries; it never under-indexes a shape (the aggregate-per-entity
> scheme this replaced did — shop, R0).

It under-indexes here. The claim holds for a function running two
*complete* queries; it does not hold for one query assembled across a
branch, and nothing distinguished the two cases.

**Why every other tier was green.** The local backend is bbolt and
needs no indexes, so the conformance suite — the contract between
`local` and `gcp` — cannot express this, and gallery's own tests pass
locally. Index derivation is the one part of the entity story where
"conformance is law" has no purchase, because the thing being derived
does not exist on one side. Only real Datastore rejects the query, and
only for the branch an anonymous request happens to take.

**Not fixed here.** The fix is an analyzer change with a real design
question behind it — emit one index per reachable filter subset (correct
but combinatorial: n conditional filters is 2ⁿ indexes, and Datastore
caps at 200 per project), or refuse to derive from a branch-assembled
query and say so at analysis time. That is its own task with its own
DX proposal, per the standing rules. Logged as discovered work.

### Discovered work

**7. Conditional queries under-index (above).** Release-blocking by the
walk's own verdict rule (§4 failing blocks a release). Needs a DX
decision between the two shapes above before any code moves.

**8. `tako logs` does not surface the error behind a 500.** The walk's
diagnosis needed `gcloud logging read`: `tako logs` showed
`ERROR GET /api/photos → 500 (80.6ms)` and nothing else, while the
`err=…` payload with Datastore's exact remediation sat one query away.
pages.md promises "an opaque 500 with the request id, real error only
in your logs" — the error IS in the logs, and tako's own reader is the
thing that hides it. The request id is in the payload too (`req=759268`),
so the correlation the design intends is right there.

**9. `tako logs` prints each request twice** — once `INFO` with tako's
duration, once untagged with Cloud Run's. Cosmetic beside #8, same
reader.

## RC1 — DX proposal: index derivation follows the branches (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Discovered work #7, promoted. The gallery walk's one-line smoke test
(`curl $URL/api/photos` → 500) traced to composites derived from a
query assembled across an `if`.

### The user code does not change — that is the point

```go
func readyPhotos(ctx tako.Ctx, owner string) ([]Photo, error) {
	q := photoStore.Query(ctx).Where("Ready", "=", true)
	if owner != "" {
		q = q.Where("Owner", "=", owner)
	}
	return q.Limit(100).All()
}
```

This is ordinary Go, it is what `examples/gallery` has shipped since
R0, and nothing about it should have to move. What moves is what tako
derives from it. Today `scanQueries` runs a flat `ast.Inspect` over the
function body and folds every `Where` into **one** chain per (entity,
function) — a filter inside an `if` is recorded exactly like one on the
straight-line path. Two runtime shapes, one derived shape, and the
narrower one goes unindexed.

### Why this is tractable at all

Two rules the analyzer already enforces bound the problem to a finite,
small space:

- `Where`'s field must be a **string constant** (`tako/const-query-field`)
  — there is no dynamic field name to reason about.
- The field must be tagged **`entity:"index"`** (`tako/unindexed-query`)
  — the universe of filterable fields per entity is declared.

So this needs no SSA and no dataflow lattice. It needs the AST walk to
notice which block it is standing in.

### The rule

A `Where`/`OrderBy` on the function's **unconditional path** is
MANDATORY. One inside the body of an `if`, `switch`, `select`, `for`
or `range` is OPTIONAL. The shapes a function produces are
`mandatory ∪ S` for every subset `S` of the optional filters; each
shape derives a composite exactly as today (struct order, then
OrderBys, dedup, skip shapes under two distinct properties).

gallery then derives what Datastore asked for, plus what it already
had:

```
+ create  datastore index photos (ready, -created)
+ create  datastore index photos (owner, ready, -created)
```

The first line is the fix. The second is today's only line.

**Deliberate over-indexing.** `if/else` arms adding different filters
are treated as independently optional, so the combination that can
never occur together is still derived. Over-indexing is the safe
direction and SSA-grade exclusivity is not worth the weight — but it
is a cost, and the "Not yet" section should say so.

### Answering the plan question directly

The owner asked to show the derived indexes at plan time. **They are
already shown** — `KindDatastoreIndex` is fourth in `reconcileOrder`
and `gallery_plan_test.go:91` pins the rendering. What the plan cannot
tell you is which query each index serves, which is exactly what a
reviewer needed to notice one was missing. Proposed:

```
  plan
    + create  datastore index photos (ready, -created)          ← app.go:385 readyPhotos
    + create  datastore index photos (owner, ready, -created)   ← app.go:385 readyPhotos
```

The position is the query that needs it. An index with no arrow is one
nothing asks for any more — the orphan case, visible for free.

### The cap, and the refusal

Over-indexing is not free: Datastore allows **200 composite indexes per
project** and each takes minutes to build (measured: 3m14s for one, over
half that deploy's wall clock). `k` optional filters in one function
yield `2^k` shapes. Real code sits at k=1–3; nothing should silently
generate 256 indexes.

So past a threshold tako refuses at analysis time rather than deriving:

```
app.go:385:7: readyPhotos assembles one query from 6 conditional filters — that is 64 composite indexes for a single function, and Datastore allows 200 in a project; split it into separate queries whose filters are unconditional (tako/query-shapes)
```

Proposed threshold **k > 4** (16 shapes). Generous for real code,
loud for the pathological. This turns today's silent production 500
into a build error, which is the posture every other analyzer rule
takes.

### Tests

Golden analyzer cases (input package + expected AppGraph JSON), per the
standing rule, with error text and position asserted exactly:

1. unconditional filters — today's output, unchanged (regression guard)
2. one optional filter — gallery's shape, two composites
3. `if/else` adding different filters — the unreachable combination is
   derived, pinned as deliberate
4. optional filter plus `OrderBy` — both tuples carry the order
5. filter inside a `for` body — optional
6. k over the threshold — the refusal above
7. a shape whose tuple another shape already covers — deduped

Plus the one that matters most: **an invariant test asserting every
enumerated shape is served by some derived tuple.** That is the check
whose absence let this ship, it is pure static analysis, and it needs
no cloud and no emulator — which is the only way this class can be
covered, since the local backend is bbolt and has no notion of an
index. `validate/release-cycle.md` §4 stays the live backstop.

### Non-goals, stated

- **SSA path sensitivity.** See above.
- **Cross-function query assembly.** `chains` are per-function, so a
  helper that takes a `*EntityQuery` and adds filters forms its own
  chain and misses the caller's. That hole predates this task and is
  not closed by it; the invariant test cannot see it either. Worth its
  own entry rather than a silent widening of scope here.
- **Changing `entity:"index"`.** The field-level tag stays exactly as
  it is; only tuple derivation moves.

## RC2 — DX proposal: `tako logs` shows the error, not the label (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Discovered work #8 and #9, folded together — one reader, one pass.

Diagnosing RC1 needed `gcloud logging read`. That is the finding:
tako's own log reader had the answer and printed a label instead.

### The confirmed defect

`pkg/provision/gcp/logs.go:77`:

```go
if msg, ok := e.JSONPayload["message"].(string); ok {
    text = msg
}
```

A handler error's payload is
`{err: "…", message: "handler error", req: "759268"}`. The reader takes
`message` — the least informative field present — and discards `err`,
which held Datastore's exact remediation, and `req`, which is the id
that ties the entry to its request line. `pages.md` promises "an
opaque 500 with the request id, real error only in your logs." The
error is in the logs. tako's reader is what hides it.

Proposed rendering — message first, then the payload it came with:

```
14:12:20 x1-gallery  ERROR  handler error [req=759268]
                            err: HTTP 400 from /v1/projects/tako-test-01:runQuery: no matching index found.
                                 recommended index is:
                                 - kind: photos
                                   properties: ready, created desc
```

Continuation lines indent under the entry rather than collapsing, since
the useful payloads here are multi-line by nature (Datastore's
recommendation is a YAML block). Unknown keys print as `key: value`
after the known ones, so a payload shape this command has not met is
degraded rather than dropped — the current `fmt.Sprint(map)` fallback
produces Go map syntax with random key order.

### The duplicate request lines (#9)

Every request prints twice — once `INFO` with tako's middleware
duration, once with Cloud Run's:

```
14:11:45 x1-gallery  INFO  POST /_tako/api/cron/Cleanup → 200 (514.5ms)
14:11:46 x1-gallery        POST /_tako/api/cron/Cleanup → 200 (0.5ms)
```

Proposed: keep **Cloud Run's** line — it is what the client actually
experienced, platform overhead included — and drop tako's duplicate
when both are present for one `req`. The judgment worth confirming:
that discards the handler's own timing, which is the more useful number
when you are hunting a slow handler rather than a slow request. The
alternative is one line carrying both (`→ 200 (514.5ms total, 0.5ms in
handler)`), which is more informative and more machinery.

### What I could not diagnose, stated plainly

The `handler error` entry did not appear in `tako logs` output **at
all** — not even as the bare label. The filter
(`resource.type="cloud_run_revision"` minus audit logs) looks broad
enough to include it, and `gcloud logging read` returned it from the
same window. I could not chase it further: the walk had already
destroyed the deployment, and re-deploying gallery to find out is a
six-minute cycle plus a secret.

So RC2's validation **starts** by reproducing the omission against a
live service. If the entry is being filtered or paged out, the payload
rendering above lands on a line that never prints, and the real fix is
elsewhere. Sequencing this after RC1 is convenient: RC1's live
verification needs a gallery deployment anyway, and that deployment is
where this reproduces.

### Tests

`pkg/provision/gcp/logs_test.go` against recorded API responses (the
package already tests against a fake server): a handler-error payload
renders `err` and `req`; a multi-line `err` indents; an unknown-key
payload degrades readably; a request logged by both Cloud Run and tako
prints once. The live half is the reproduction above, in
`validate/logs.md`.

## RC1 + RC2 — shipped and verified live (2026-08-05)

Both approved as proposed and implemented as approved. Commits
`b90ac51` (RC1) and `1ad390e` (RC2).

### RC1, live

The plan showed the fix before anything was applied — the two indexes
that survived the env-scoped destroy skipping, the missing one being
created, each naming the query that asks for it:

```
    skip    datastore index photos (owner, ready)             ← app.go:384 readyPhotos
    skip    datastore index photos (owner, ready, -created)   ← app.go:404 readyPage
  + create  datastore index photos (ready, -created)          ← app.go:404 readyPage
```

Then the request that started all of this:

```
GET /api/photos → 200
{"photos":[]}
```

**§4 of validate/release-cycle.md now passes.** The same URL that
answered 500 four hours ago answers 200, from an index tako derived
because the filter that produces it sits inside an `if`.

Index build was 3m8s, consistent with the ~4 minutes entity.md
promises, and the deploy overlapped it with the image push as designed
(6m5s total).

### RC2, live

The structured rendering works on real entries. tako's cron line now
arrives with its fields instead of just its message:

```
20:30:54 x1-gallery   INFO    cron driven by Cloud Scheduler
                              cron: Cleanup
                              schedule: every 24h
```

Before RC2 that was one line reading `cron driven by Cloud Scheduler`,
with `cron` and `schedule` dropped — the same discard that hid
Datastore's remediation.

Not exercised live: the multi-line `err` path, because after RC1 there
is no handler error left to provoke on this app. It is covered by
`logs_test.go` against the exact payload gallery wrote.

Incidental: hammering `tako logs` tripped Cloud Logging's read quota,
and the retry narration behaved — `↻ POST entries:list: HTTP 429 —
retrying in 1s`, then a clean 429 error naming the quota when the
retries ran out.

### Discovered work #9 — diagnosed, NOT fixed

The duplicate request lines reproduce on `hello` and **not** on
gallery. One curl, two entries:

```
20:33:47 hello        INFO    GET /hello → 200 (8.8ms)
20:33:47 hello                GET /hello → 200 (0.7ms)
```

The blank-severity line with the handler-only duration is tako's own
`logRequest` `fmt.Printf`. It should never run in the cloud —
`logging.go:156` returns early when `traceProject` is set — so
`traceProject` is empty, so `useCloudLogging` never ran, so `BootGCP`
never ran. And it never ran because **codegen does not emit `Boot()`
for this service** (`codegen.go:316`):

```go
if hasResources(g, svc) || hasAuth(g) {
	b.WriteString("\truntime.Boot() …")
}
```

hello declares no resources and no auth. The guard reasons about
BACKENDS — nothing to wire when nothing is declared, which is correct —
but cloud logging setup rides inside `Boot` and is not a backend
concern. So a resource-less service in production:

1. writes plain text instead of Cloud Logging JSON, so **every line has
   no severity** — `tako logs` shows a blank column, and severity
   filtering in the console matches nothing;
2. carries no trace, so handler lines do not nest under their request;
3. double-logs every request, which is only the visible symptom.

This is why `hello` duplicated and `gallery` did not, and it is a
framework bug rather than the reader cosmetic #9 was filed as. The fix
belongs in codegen or in `Boot`'s split — install cloud logging
unconditionally, wire backends conditionally — and it changes generated
code for every resource-less service, so it is its own task. Renamed
from "prints each request twice" to what it actually is:

**#9 (revised). A service with no resources never installs cloud
logging.** Severity, tracing and request-log de-duplication all ride on
`Boot()`, which codegen omits when there is nothing to wire.

### Cleanup

hello and gallery destroyed, `x1-notifier-key` deleted, project
verified clean of `x1-`/`hello` run services, service accounts and
secrets. The three Datastore composite indexes remain by design —
env-scoped destroy says so on the tin ("shared repo, indexes, and
framework bucket stay") and they are derivable, never data.

## RC3 — DX proposal: every deployed service is observable (2026-08-05) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Discovered work #9 (revised), promoted, and it grew a second half on
the way. What began as "tako logs prints each request twice" is two
defects sharing one root: **a service is only wired for observability
if it happens to declare something else.**

### What is confirmed

Observed live, on `hello` deployed to tako-test-01:

```
20:33:47 hello        INFO    GET /hello → 200 (8.8ms)
20:33:47 hello                GET /hello → 200 (0.7ms)
```

One request, two entries. The blank-severity line with the
handler-only duration is tako's own `logRequest` `fmt.Printf`, which
`logging.go:156` returns early from whenever `traceProject` is set. It
is not set, so `useCloudLogging` never ran, so `BootGCP` never ran —
because codegen never emitted the call (`codegen.go:316`):

```go
if hasResources(g, svc) || hasAuth(g) {
	b.WriteString("\truntime.Boot() …")
}
```

`hello` declares no resources and no auth. The guard reasons about
BACKENDS, correctly — there is nothing to wire. But three things ride
inside `Boot` that are not backends, and they go with it:

1. **Cloud Logging JSON.** Every line the service writes is plain
   text, so **every line has no severity**. Console severity filters
   match nothing, and `tako logs` prints a blank column — visible in
   the transcript above.
2. **Trace correlation.** Handler lines never nest under their request.
3. **Request metrics.** `SetRequestMetrics` is called from `BootGCP`
   and nowhere else, and `recordRequest` opens with
   `if requestMetrics == nil { return }` — so a service that never
   booted exports **no `requests` and no `request_ms`**.

(3) is the one that matters. `http.go:225`'s comment says wiring it in
Boot "is what makes 'every service exports requests and request_ms'
true of deployed services and not only of tests". For a resource-less
service it is not true, and an alert built on those metrics —
`tako.RequestsErroring`, `tako.RequestsSlow` — watches a series nothing
writes. An alert that cannot fire looks exactly like an alert that is
not firing.

The duplicate log line, the thing originally filed, is the least of it.

### The second half — the grant does not match what the runtime writes

Following (3) turned up a wider mismatch. `grants.go:94` grants
`roles/monitoring.metricWriter` **only when the app declares a Counter
or Histogram**:

```go
if hasMetrics {
	for _, svc := range g.Services { add(…, "roles/monitoring.metricWriter", …) }
}
```

But `recordRequest` writes `requests` and `request_ms` from **every
service that booted**, declared counters or not. Of the six examples,
only gallery declares a Counter. So shortlink, journal, shop and blog
deploy services that boot, wire request metrics, and attempt writes
their identity was never granted.

**Status: inferred from code, NOT yet observed.** The flush is every
60s (`metricsFlush`), so confirming it means deploying one of those
apps, serving a request, and waiting a flush. It is the first
validation step below rather than a claim being made here.

Two details argue it is real. `client.go:78` already knows what this
looks like:

> `permission denied by %s — this service's grants derive from the app
> graph at deploy time, so a runtime 403 is a tako deploy bug: re-run
> tako deploy, and file it if it persists`

A metricWriter 403 would print exactly that, and it would be right: by
tako's own standard, a runtime 403 IS a deploy bug. And the comment
above the grant already describes the intended shape —
"Package-wide, like secrets" — so only the condition is wrong, not the
design.

### Part A — observability installs unconditionally

Generated main for a resource-less service, today and proposed:

```go
 func main() {
+	runtime.Boot() // observability always; backends when this package declares any
 	mux := http.NewServeMux()
```

One unconditional line, which is also simpler than the conditional it
replaces. Safe to call with nothing declared, and I checked rather than
assumed: `gcpb.New` only builds an authenticated HTTP client (no API
call), the declared-secrets loop is empty, hook wiring touches nothing,
and the single boot-time call — `gcpb.WhoAmI` against the instance
metadata server — is instance-local and needs no IAM. Its failure path
already degrades to log-only metrics rather than refusing to boot.

`Boot` itself gains the ordering the comment in `BootGCP` already
implies: observability first, backends after, so a failure wiring a
backend is reported through a logger that works.

**Local is unchanged, deliberately.** `BootLocal` still installs no
JSON handler — the dev console is a product and JSON in it is a
regression — and `logRequest` keeps printing the dev line, because
locally `traceProject` stays empty. That asymmetry is the existing
design and this must not disturb it.

**One local consequence worth your call.** `Boot()` in local mode is
`BootLocal(".tako/data")`, so `tako dev` on a resource-less app would
begin creating an empty `.tako/data`. Harmless and gitignored, but
untidy. The tidy alternative is making the directory lazily, on first
backend use. I lean lazy; it is a small change and it is strictly more
honest about what the app uses.

### Part B — grant what the runtime writes

```go
-if hasMetrics {
-	for _, svc := range g.Services { add(…metricWriter…) }
-}
+// Every service writes requests and request_ms from the middleware,
+// whether or not the app declares a counter of its own.
+for _, svc := range g.Services { add(…metricWriter…) }
```

The security summary already explains this posture for apps that
declare metrics; it will now say it for all of them. `metricWriter` is
write-only and project-scoped, which is the true minimum given what
the middleware does — narrowing it further would mean not exporting
request metrics, and those are the ones every alert in
`reference/alerts.md` is built on.

Deployed effect for an app like journal: one added grant per service,
and `requests`/`request_ms` start arriving where today they are
attempted and refused.

### Tests

- **codegen golden**: a resource-less service's generated main contains
  `runtime.Boot()`. `pkg/codegen` already goldens generated mains, so
  this is a golden update plus one new fixture — the case that has no
  coverage today precisely because nothing was emitted.
- **grants**: `pkg/provision` asserts every service SA receives
  `roles/monitoring.metricWriter` for an app declaring no Counter. The
  existing grant tests cover the declared-counter path only.
- **runtime**: `recordRequest` records through a fake sink after a boot
  with nothing declared — the unit-level statement of "every service
  exports requests".
- The security-summary text changes for four examples' expected output;
  those are goldened and will be regenerated deliberately.

### Validation

1. **Confirm the 403 first** — deploy `shortlink` (boots, declares no
   Counter), serve a request, wait one 60s flush, read logs. If the
   metric write is failing, Part B is a fix; if it is somehow
   succeeding, Part B is unnecessary and the proposal shrinks to Part
   A. This is the step that decides the shape, so it runs before any
   code moves.
2. Deploy `hello` after Part A: one request, one log line, severity
   present, and `requests` visible in Cloud Monitoring for a service
   that declares nothing.
3. `validate/logging.md` gains the resource-less case; it is the gap
   that let this ship.

### Non-goals

- **The `httpKey` constant** (`logging.go:40`) is dead — a leftover
  from when tako wrote its own request entry alongside Cloud Run's.
  Deleting it is a one-line cleanup that belongs to whoever is next in
  that file, not to a task about grants.
- **Making request metrics optional.** They are what every alert in the
  reference is built on; an app that silently exports none is the bug,
  not the configuration.

## RC3 — shipped and verified live (2026-08-05)

Approved with the lazy-directory option taken. Validation step 1 ran
first, as the proposal required, and it changed nothing about the shape
— it confirmed Part B rather than eliminating it.

### Step 1: the 403 is real

`shortlink` deployed (boots, declares no Counter), one request, one
flush interval:

```
21:40:06 shortlink  WARNING  tako: metrics flush failed — the totals are cumulative, so a later flush recovers unless this was the last one
                             err: permission denied by /v3/projects/tako-test-01/timeSeries — this service's grants derive from the app graph at deploy time, so a runtime 403 is a tako deploy bug: re-run tako deploy, and file it if it persists (Permission monitoring.timeSeries.create denied…)
                             final: false
```

Every 60s, in production, for four of the six examples.

**RC2 is why that was readable.** Before it, this line printed its
message and dropped `err` — the diagnosis would have needed
`gcloud logging read` again. The previous task paid for itself inside
one day.

### What shipped

**Part A** — `runtime.Boot()` is now emitted unconditionally
(`codegen.go`). The guard asked "does this service have backends to
wire", which is right for backends and wrong for the three things that
ride along: Cloud Logging, trace correlation, and request metrics.

**Part B** — `roles/monitoring.metricWriter` goes to every service, not
only apps declaring a Counter, because the middleware exports
`requests`/`request_ms` from all of them. The security summary's reason
text was written for the counter case and is now accurate for the real
one: "every service exports requests and request_ms from the request
middleware, and counters derive no usage edges".

**The lazy directory** — `local.OpenEntity` and `local.NewURLSigner`
create nothing at boot; the bolt file, the signing key and `.tako/data`
itself appear on first use. The cost, named in the proposal and
accepted: a database another process holds is now reported at the first
query rather than at boot, with the same message.

### Verified live

| Claim | Evidence |
|---|---|
| resource-less service logs with severity | `21:55:28 hello INFO GET /hello → 200 (4.9ms)` — **one** line where there were two, the second previously with no severity at all |
| resource-less service exports metrics | Monitoring API: 1 series for `job=hello`, `custom.googleapis.com/tako/requests{route: GET /hello, status: 2xx} = 1` |
| the 403 is gone | 0 flush failures in 6m of shortlink logs, where the same window previously held one per minute |
| metrics actually land | `custom.googleapis.com/tako/requests{route: GET /api/links, status: 2xx}` present for shortlink |
| local unchanged, no data dir | `tako dev` on hello serves `/hello` and `/greet/{name}`; `.tako/` holds `bin` and `gen` only |

Both apps destroyed; project verified clean of `hello-`/`shortlink-`
run services and service accounts.

Incidental confirmations along the way: preflight caught a disabled

### Still open

`httpKey` (`logging.go:40`) remains dead code, named as a non-goal in
