## FL8 — DX proposal: the app identifier is derived, not assumed (2026-08-06) — AWAITING APPROVAL

flauta's entry, promoted. tako builds Google-facing identifiers out of
the Go module path and never asks whether Google will accept them.

### What is confirmed

`pkg/provision/desired.go:100`:

```go
func (c Config) Labels() map[string]string {
	return map[string]string{"tako-app": c.App, "tako-env": c.Env}
}
```

`c.App` is `graph.Module` at every call site (`deploy.go:157`,
`destroy.go:43`, `lifecycle.go:33`, `logs.go:41`, `alerts.go:60`), so
for a normally-named module it is `github.com/gsandoval/flauta`. GCS
label values admit `[\p{Ll}\p{Lo}\p{N}_-]{0,63}`, so the first create
fails:

```
tako: create the framework bucket: Invalid user label: tako-app with value
github.com/gsandoval/flauta. Reason: … character "." at position 6 is not a
non-uppercased letter … (HTTP 400 from storage.googleapis.com)
```

That value reaches eleven reconcilers — Artifact Registry, Run
services, Run jobs, domain mappings, buckets, topics, both
subscription kinds, both alert kinds, and the lease — via
`cfg.Labels()`. Each has its own rules; none of them accepts a dot.

### The blind spot, which is the finding

Every example declares a bare module name. I checked all seven:
`blog gallery hello journal shop shortlink siren`. Every one is
already label-legal, so **no example can produce this failure**. Tako
has deployed twice to a real project and met no bug that fires on the
first create of a normally-named app, because the acceptance corpus
contains no app that is named like an app. flauta's correction to its
own entry says this better than I did, and it is the reason FL8 ships
an example rather than only a function.

### What flauta has not hit yet, and would hit next

The label is not the only unsanitised use. `pkg/backends/gcp/naming.go:25`:

```go
func BucketName(project, app, env, base string) string {
	return project + "-" + app + "-" + Prefixed(env, base)
}
```

A declared `tako.Bucket` on flauta would ask GCS for
`tako-test-02-github.com/gsandoval/flauta-media` — a slash is illegal
in a bucket name outright, and a dot demands domain verification.
flauta declares no bucket today, which is the only reason the label
failed first; the framework bucket is `<project>-tako` and carries no
app segment. **Sanitising the label alone unblocks flauta and strands
the next app one `tako.Bucket` in**, so FL8 covers names too.

### The rule

One derivation, in `pkg/backends/gcp/naming.go` — the file whose
header already states why it exists: *"shared verbatim by the runtime
and the provisioner so the names services read are the names deploys
create."* The app identifier has exactly that property.

```go
// AppID is the app's machine identifier: what Google is asked to
// store when Google constrains the characters. The module path stays
// the app's NAME — it is what a person reads in the plan header, the
// alert doc and a service account's description, none of which Google
// validates.
//
// A module path that is already a legal identifier is its own id, so
// every app deployed before this existed keeps the labels and bucket
// names it already has. Anything else is derived from its last
// segment plus a hash of the whole path: short enough for a bucket
// name, unique because the hash covers what truncation dropped, and
// stable because both halves are pure functions of go.mod. Same
// discipline as SAName (desired.go:74), applied one level up.
func AppID(module string) string
```

- `hello` → `hello` · `shortlink` → `shortlink` (identity, all seven examples)
- `github.com/gsandoval/flauta` → `flauta-a70a87`
- `github.com/Me/My_App.v2` → `my-app-v2-<hash6>`
- a 41-char bare name → truncated to 22 + `-<hash6>`

Legal-as-is means `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,29}$`. The 30-char bound is
not cosmetic: a bucket name is capped at 63 and already spends
`project` + `env` + the declared name.

`AppID` replaces the raw module path in the four places Google
constrains characters — both label values, the app segment of
`BucketName`, the lease object path (a slash there is a path separator
in every GCS tool), and the metric namespace `<app>-<env>`. The
namespace moves on both sides at once: the runtime writes it from
`TAKO_APP` and `pkg/provision/alerts.go` spells the same string into
every matcher, so they must change together or every alert silently
stops matching. That is what the FA1 lock golden and the twins test
are for, and both are in the test list below.

### The env half, deliberately different

`--env` has the same exposure — `--env Staging` produces the same
illegal label, and `Prefixed` puts it in every resource name — but it
is **typed by a person, not read from go.mod**. Silently deriving
`staging` from `Staging` would make `tako destroy --env Staging`
address something the user did not name. So env is validated, not
sanitised:

```
tako: --env "Staging" is not a valid environment name

    environments become part of every resource name and every label,
    so they are limited to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens
    (1–20 characters), starting with a letter

    did you mean --env staging?
```

The "did you mean" line appears only when sanitising the input yields
something legal, which is the common case (a capital, a slash).

### What the user sees

Unchanged for every app whose module is already an id — no example's
output moves. When the id is derived, the plan header says so once:

```
tako deploy · github.com/gsandoval/flauta → tako-test-02 (us-central1)
              id flauta-a70a87 — labels and bucket names use this

  analyzing    1 service · 33 endpoints · 1 site
  generating   .tako/gen
  preflight    ok (run, iam, artifactregistry, storage, datastore, identitytoolkit)
```

Stated once, at the top, where someone about to read a plan full of
`flauta-a70a87` finds out why. Not repeated per object.

### Cloud errors & permissions

No new permission: FL8 changes the *value* of a label tako already
writes with the roles it already holds, and the deployer setup in
`docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md` is untouched.

The failure modes it removes are all HTTP 400s from a resource create
— the class where Google's message is precise about the character and
useless about the cause, because the offending value was derived by
tako and never appears in the user's code. The one it adds is the
`--env` rejection above, raised in argument parsing before any network
call, so a bad env costs nothing.

Preflight gains one check, because a derived id can still be too long
once a project and a bucket name are added to it:

```
tako: bucket "originals" would be created as
  tako-test-02-flauta-a70a87-staging-originals (67 characters)

    Google caps bucket names at 63. The name is
    <project>-<app id>-<env>-<declared name>; shorten the declared
    name, the env, or the project id.
```

Raised in preflight, before the first create, alongside the API-enabled
probes — the existing rule that a deploy fails before it changes
anything or not at all.

### Tests

- `pkg/backends/gcp/naming_test.go` — `AppID` table: identity for all
  seven example modules, the flauta case, uppercase, trailing
  punctuation, an over-long bare name, a path whose last segment is
  empty. Stability asserted by hashing twice, uniqueness by two module
  paths sharing a last segment.
- A **new example with a host-shaped module path**. This is the part
  that keeps FL8 fixed: the corpus that could not catch it becomes the
  corpus that can. Cheapest honest form is `examples/hello`'s module
  becoming `github.com/gsandoval/tako-example-hello` — one line of
  `go.mod`, its golden moves once, and every future label change is
  measured against a realistic name. (Alternative: a new
  `examples/module-path` fixture. I prefer moving hello — a fixture
  nobody deploys is a fixture that rots.)
- `pkg/provision` — a `Labels()` case asserting the derived value, and
  a `BucketName` case for a derived app.
- FA1's metric lock golden and `pkg/provision/testdata/twins` re-run
  unchanged: the namespace must still be spelled identically on both
  sides. A twins diff is the failure signal for the alerts half.
- `--env` validation: the exact error text, the `did you mean` line
  present and absent.
- Preflight: the over-long bucket name, exact text.

### Validation

`validate/app-identifier.md`, new, run by me before the gate: `tako
deploy --plan` on an example with a host-shaped module (header shows
the id, plan is otherwise identical), `tako destroy --plan` on the
same (finds the same objects by the same label — the round trip is the
point, since the label is the state), and `--env Staging` rejected
without a network call. The live half — an actual create against a
real project with a derived label — belongs to the next release-cycle
walk, and I will say so rather than claim it.

### Non-goals

- Renaming or migrating anything already deployed. Identity on legal
  module paths means there is nothing to migrate; an app that cannot
  have deployed cannot have state.
- Sanitising the module path in human-facing text. The plan header,
  alert docs and SA descriptions keep `github.com/gsandoval/flauta`,
  because Google does not validate those and a person reading them
  wants the name they typed.
- Datastore namespaces (env only, no app) and Cloud Run service names
  (`Prefixed(env, service)`, no app) — neither carries the app, and
  neither changes.
- Multi-app projects. The dedicated-project doctrine holds
  (`RepoName`, `desired.go:55`); the hash is uniqueness insurance, not
  a multi-tenancy feature.

## FL9 — DX proposal: an index note belongs to its index (2026-08-06) — AWAITING APPROVAL

The Datastore work RC1 left half-shipped. RC1 added the attribution
that names the call site behind each derived composite; the
attribution is attached to the wrong index.

### The confirmed defect

`pkg/analyzer/analyzer.go:344` appends in lockstep:

```go
res.Composites = append(res.Composites, tuple)
res.CompositeSources = append(res.CompositeSources, c.source)
```

and `analyzer.go:349` then sorts one of them:

```go
sort.Slice(res.Composites, func(i, j int) bool {
	return strings.Join(res.Composites[i], ",") < strings.Join(res.Composites[j], ",")
})
```

`appgraph.go:130` states the invariant that breaks: *"CompositeSources
runs parallel to Composites."* After the sort it does not. An entity
whose walk order already matches sorted order is unharmed, which is
why flauta's revisions pair reads correctly and its articles pair is
swapped:

```
+ create  datastore index articles (section, state, -publishAt)  ← entity.go:231 publishedArticles
+ create  datastore index articles (state, -publishAt)  ← entity.go:238 publishedInSection
```

`publishedArticles` filters on `State` alone; it is the two-property
index. Both notes are one row off.

### Why no test caught it

There is no analyzer golden containing `CompositeSources` at all —
`grep` finds it in `analyzer.go`, `appgraph.go`, `desired.go` and one
provision test. RC1 shipped a parallel-slice invariant with nothing
asserting the pairing survives the sort. That is the real defect; the
sort is just where it shows.

### The fix

Sort the pair as one thing. `Composites []([]string)` and
`CompositeSources []string` stay as they are on `AppGraph` — they are
the JSON shape `tako gen graph` prints and changing it is an API
change, which is its own task — but the analyzer builds
`[]struct{tuple []string; source string}`, sorts that, and unzips into
the two slices at the end. The invariant then holds by construction
rather than by remembering to sort twice, and `appgraph.go:130`'s
comment gains the sentence saying where the pairing is established.

### What the user sees

The same two lines, correctly paired:

```
+ create  datastore index articles (state, -publishAt)  ← entity.go:231 publishedArticles
+ create  datastore index articles (section, state, -publishAt)  ← entity.go:238 publishedInSection
```

No new surface, no new flag, no changed ordering of the plan itself.

### Tests

- A new analyzer golden whose entity's **walk order differs from its
  sorted order** — flauta's exact shape: a two-property query written
  first, a three-property one written second, sorting the other way.
  This is the case every existing golden lacks, and it fails on
  today's code before the fix.
- The golden asserts the full `CompositeSources` array, not just its
  length: a length check passes on swapped notes, which is how this
  survived.
- `pkg/provision/gallery_plan_test.go` extended so a note is asserted
  against its tuple rather than its position.

### The rest of the Datastore work, named so it is not lost again

Two items stay open after FL9, both recorded, neither in scope here:

1. **Cross-function query assembly.** RC1's stated non-goal: a helper
   that takes a `*EntityQuery` and adds a filter forms its own chain
   and misses the caller's, so the derived set can still be short.
   Same failure class as the 500 RC1 fixed, one call frame away. It
   needs its own proposal — the analysis is interprocedural and the DX
   question (warn? derive? refuse?) is not obvious.
2. **The `query-shapes` ceiling.** `maxOptionalMods = 4` refuses at 5
   optional modifiers with an exact message. Nothing has hit it; it is
   listed so a future reader knows the number was chosen, not
   inherited.

### Non-goals

Changing what is derived. FL9 moves no index; the composite set before
and after is identical, and both flauta indexes were always correct.
This is an attribution bug in output a person reads while deciding
whether a query shape is right — which is exactly why a confidently
wrong `file:line` is worse than none.

## FL8 — shipped (2026-08-06)

Approved as proposed, with the owner's direction to move hello's module
path. Everything below is measured, not asserted.

### What shipped

`gcp.AppID` (`pkg/backends/gcp/appid.go`), in the file whose header
already says why it exists — the runtime and the provisioner must
derive names identically. A module path that is already a legal id is
its own id; anything else is its last segment, sanitised, plus six hex
digits of sha256 over the whole path.

Applied at four places, all of them ones Google constrains:
`Config.Labels()`, the app segment of `BucketName` (four call sites
across `desired.go` and `grants.go`), the lease object, and the metric
namespace — the last one on BOTH sides at once (`TAKO_APP` at
`desired.go:262`, the four matcher spellings in `alerts.go`), because a
namespace written by the runtime and matched by the provisioner has to
move together or every alert silently stops matching. The twins test
and the FA1 lock golden both stayed green, which is the signal that
they did.

NOT applied where Google validates nothing and a person reads the
value: the deploy banner, alert docs, notification subjects, service
account descriptions, the scheduler marker, and the OCI image label.
Those keep the module path. The rule is one sentence — the id is for
Google, the module path is the name.

`--env` is validated rather than derived (`cmd/tako/env.go`), because
it is typed by a person and `tako destroy --env Staging` silently
addressing `staging` is not a thing to ship. The repair is offered only
when there is one.

`provision.CheckNames` refuses an assembled bucket name past 63
characters. It runs before the frontend build, before codegen and
before the first network call — earlier than the proposal's "alongside
the preflight probes", which was the wrong place: nothing about it
needs the network.

### The second wall, found by the example move

`module hello` → `module github.com/gsandoval/tako-example-hello` and
codegen broke immediately:

```
generated main for service hello does not format: 13:6: missing import path
```

`pkgAlias` used the last segment of the import path as the Go import
alias, and `tako-example-hello` is not an identifier — it emitted
`tako-example-hello "github.com/…"`, a parse error at the hyphen. Any
app whose repository name contains a hyphen could not generate a
service at all. **flauta never hit this** because `flauta` happens to
be identifier-shaped; it would have hit it the day it was renamed.
This is the corpus blind spot closing on the first day, exactly as the
proposal argued it would.

Fixed twice over. `pkgAlias` now takes the graph and uses the
package's OWN name — which is what `Handler.Var` has always been
prefixed with, and is an identifier by definition — so hello's
generated main differs from before by exactly one line, the import
path, and every reference stays `hello.Hello`. `aliasFromPath` is the
fallback for a service with no handler to read a name from, and it
sanitises: hyphens and dots to underscores, a `pkg` prefix ahead of a
leading digit, a trailing underscore on a keyword. Its table is
`pkg/codegen/alias_test.go`.

The first cut sanitised the path instead, which compiled and read
`tako_example_hello.GreetReq` throughout — legal, and worse than what
it replaced. Generated code is a product (settled decision 3).

### Tests

- `pkg/backends/gcp/appid_test.go` — identity for all seven example
  modules, flauta's path, the new hello path, uppercase, an empty last
  segment, an over-long bare name; plus legality of every derived id
  against the rule, idempotence (what lets `TAKO_APP` round-trip),
  separation of two modules sharing a last segment, and stability.
- `pkg/codegen/alias_test.go` — the alias table, `token.IsIdentifier`
  as the oracle rather than a restated rule, and the two paths through
  `pkgAlias`.
- `pkg/provision/names_test.go` — realistic names pass, an over-long
  one is refused with all four parts named, the check follows the env
  (prod fits where a long env does not), and example-shaped names pass
  so a false positive cannot block a deploy.
- `cmd/tako/env_test.go` — valid names, the three illegal shapes with
  their repairs, no repair when there is none, the length bound, and
  `parseTarget` doing the check so every cloud command inherits it.

### Validation

`validate/app-identifier.md`, written and run. Real transcripts:

Section 1 — the header, on the moved example:

```
tako deploy · github.com/gsandoval/tako-example-hello → tako-test-01 (us-central1)
              id tako-example-hello-812a9c — labels and bucket names use this

  analyzing    1 service, 3 endpoints
  generating   .tako/gen
  preflight    ok (run, iam, artifactregistry, storage)
  building     1 service image(s), digest-pinned
  plan
    + create  artifact repo tako
    + create  service account hello-sa
    + create  run service hello
    + create  iam grants bucket tako-test-01-tako
    ~ update  iam grants project
      skip    iam grants run hello
    + create  iam grants serviceAccount hello-sa@tako-test-01.iam.gserviceaccount.com
    5 creates, 1 updates, 1 skips, 0 orphans
```

and `examples/gallery` (module `gallery`) prints no id line at all —
the quiet case is quiet.

Section 2 — `tako dev` on hello, generated import and two live
responses:

```
	hello "github.com/gsandoval/tako-example-hello"

$ curl localhost:8080/hello      → {"message":"Hello from Tako!"}
$ curl localhost:8080/greet/memo → {"message":"Hello, memo!"}
```

Section 3 — the env rejections, all three before any network call:

```
tako: --env "Staging" is not a valid environment name

    environments become part of every resource name and every label,
    so they are limited to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens
    (1–20 characters), starting with a letter

    did you mean --env staging?
```

`--env feature/x` offers `feature-x`; `--env ...` offers nothing,
because there is nothing to offer.

### What is NOT validated, stated plainly

The create. `--plan` never creates an object, so nothing run here
exercised the HTTP 400 FL8 exists to fix — the label is rejected at
create time. Proving it end to end needs one real deploy of a
host-shaped module plus a destroy, and that belongs to the next
release-cycle walk. Everything up to the create is verified; the create
is not.

### Discovered work

**10. `Prefixed` has no bound of its own.** `checkEnv` caps an env at
20 characters, but that is a CLI check: a caller constructing
`provision.Config` directly (tests, and `cmd/tako/lifecycle.go`'s
paths) can still set any env. The names it would produce are caught by
`CheckNames` for buckets and by nothing for topics or Run services.
Not promoted: no path in tako reaches it without going through
`parseTarget` today.

## FL9 — shipped (2026-08-06)

The Datastore index work RC1 left half-shipped, closed.

### The test came first, and failed

`pkg/analyzer/testdata/indexnotes/` is a fixture module with flauta's
exact shape: `publishedArticles` (two properties) written first and
sorting second, `publishedInSection` (three) written second and sorting
first. On the unfixed analyzer:

```
composite "section,state,-publishAt" is credited to "app.go:38 publishedArticles", want the note for publishedInSection
composite "state,-publishAt" is credited to "app.go:46 publishedInSection", want the note for publishedArticles
```

Both notes one row off, which is what flauta reported. Every other
fixture in the tree — gallery included — has an entity whose walk order
already matches its sorted order, or two shapes from the SAME function
whose notes are identical, so none of them can tell a correct
implementation from this one.

### The fix

`analyzer.go` now builds `[]struct{tuple, source}`, sorts that, and
unzips into the two slices on the way out. The invariant holds by
construction rather than by remembering to sort twice, and
`appgraph.go` says where it is established and what breaking it costs.

Nothing about WHICH indexes are derived changed. Both of flauta's were
always correct; only the attribution was wrong.

### Validation, on the app that found it

flauta builds against `replace => ../tako`, so tako's working tree is
its dependency. `tako gen graph --json` in `~/Programming/flautas`:

```
articles
   (section, state, -publishAt)  <- entity.go:238 publishedInSection
   (state, -publishAt)  <- entity.go:231 publishedArticles
revisions
   (targetKind, targetSlug, -created)  <- revision.go:199 latestRevision
   (targetKind, targetSlug, cause, -created)  <- revision.go:208 latestRevisionOfCause
```

`publishedArticles` filters `State` alone and is credited with the
two-property index; `publishedInSection` adds `Section` and is credited
with the three-property one. The revisions pair, which was right by
luck before, is still right.

### Tests

- `pkg/analyzer/composites_test.go` — the pairing asserted as a map
  from tuple to function, not by position, plus a case pinning that
  composites stay sorted (sorting is what broke it, so the order is
  part of the contract now).
- `pkg/provision/gallery_plan_test.go` — the entity carries two
  composites with two different sources instead of one, so the plan's
  rendering has a pairing to get wrong. It had exactly one before,
  which is why the render test could not catch this either.

### The Datastore work still open, named again so it is not lost

1. **Cross-function query assembly.** A helper taking a `*EntityQuery`
   forms its own chain and misses the caller's. Interprocedural, and
   the DX question (warn / derive / refuse) is unanswered. Needs its
   own proposal.
2. **The `query-shapes` ceiling.** `maxOptionalMods = 4`; nothing has
   reached it. The number was chosen, not inherited.

## Program: FL10 → FL13, then release (2026-08-06) — DESIGN, AWAITING APPROVAL

Owner-directed, in the order proposed and approved: cross-function
query assembly, the 404-nil-data gap **taken as a class rather than a
fix**, the per-route cache policy, the docs mention check. Then: update
all three doc trees, run comprehensive local **and live** validation,
`make build` / `make install`. The loop itself becomes a skill.

Four slices, four gates. Each has its own DX proposal below; approving
this design approves the order and the shape, and each slice still
reports before the next begins.

---

## FL10 — a query assembled across a function boundary

### The defect

`scanQueries` (`resources.go:211`) walks `file.Decls` and collects
modifiers **per `*ast.FuncDecl`**. A query value that crosses a
function boundary breaks the chain in both directions:

```go
// The caller's derived shape is (section) — State is missing.
func list(ctx tako.Ctx, section string) ([]Article, error) {
	return published(articles.Query(ctx).Where("Section", "=", section)).
		OrderBy("-PublishAt").Limit(50).All()
}

// This helper derives a shape of its own that never runs alone.
func published(q *tako.EntityQuery[Article]) *tako.EntityQuery[Article] {
	return q.Where("State", "=", "published")
}
```

Under-derivation is the RC1 failure again — a composite only serves a
query that constrains its leading properties, so the real query has no
index and Datastore answers 500 in production. Over-derivation is
cheaper but not free: every derived index is ~4 minutes of build and
one of a project's 200.

### Why this is worse than it looks

**tako's own example already does this, and gets away with it by
accident.** `examples/journal/app.go:92`:

```go
published := func() *tako.EntityQuery[Post] {
	return posts.Query(ctx).Where("Published", "=", true)
}
list, err := published().OrderBy("-Created").Limit(pageSize).All()
```

That derives `(published, -created)` correctly (`journal_appgraph.golden.json:30`)
— because a **closure** lives inside the enclosing FuncDecl's body, so
`ast.Inspect` walks straight through it. Promote the same closure to a
package-level func and the index silently changes. The user cannot see
which of the two they wrote, nothing warns, and the difference only
appears as a production 500.

### The three options

1. **Warn.** RC1 proved the failure mode is silent under-indexing that
   surfaces as a 500 in production. A warning that can be ignored is
   the state we are already in.
2. **Refuse** — an analyzer error on any query value crossing a
   function boundary. Cheap and safe, and it outlaws a helper, which is
   ordinary good Go and which tako's own example uses.
3. **Derive, and refuse only what cannot be followed.** Recommended.

Option 3 is the framework's existing posture (derive what is derivable,
refuse the rest loudly, never silently under-derive), and the shape is
narrower than "interprocedural analysis" sounds: a query value has a
**known type** (`*tako.EntityQuery[T]`), so `go/types` finds every
function that takes or returns one without any dataflow. Within a
package, resolving a direct call by identifier is the same machinery
`scanQueries` already uses for `entityQueryMethod`.

### The rule

- A function whose parameter or result is `*tako.EntityQuery[T]` is a
  **query fragment**, not a query. It contributes no chain of its own —
  which also deletes today's phantom indexes.
- At a direct call to a fragment, the fragment's modifiers are inlined
  into the caller's chain, in call order, carrying their own
  guarded/unconditional classification. A fragment called inside an
  `if` makes all of its modifiers optional at that site.
- Fragments compose (a fragment may call a fragment), bounded by a
  recursion depth and by the existing `maxOptionalMods` ceiling, which
  the inlined optional modifiers now count against.
- A query value tako **cannot follow** — assigned to a struct field, a
  package-level var, sent on a channel, passed as an interface, or
  handed to a function in another module — is refused:

```
app.go:118:9: this query is built somewhere tako cannot follow (stored in a struct field), so the composite indexes it needs cannot be derived — build the query in one function, or in helpers that take and return *tako.EntityQuery[Article] (tako/query-escapes)
```

- Cross-PACKAGE fragments: same package only in this slice, since
  package = service and a query crossing a service boundary is not a
  query. Named as a non-goal, with the escape rule covering it.

### Tests

Golden fixtures under `pkg/analyzer/testdata/`: the caller/fragment
pair above (derives the full shape), a fragment called under an `if`
(its modifiers become optional), a fragment chain two deep, a fragment
that is never called (contributes nothing — today it contributes a
phantom), the closure form (unchanged, so journal's golden must not
move), and the escape cases with exact error text. Plus `examples/journal`
gaining the promoted-helper form so an example demands the feature.

### Non-goals

Cross-package fragments; queries built in loops accumulating a variable
number of filters (already the `query-shapes` ceiling's business);
proving that a derived shape is reachable (over-indexing stays the safe
direction, per `shapesOf`).

---

## FL11 — tako's own pages are the app's pages

**Taken as a class, per owner direction. The specific 404-nil-data fix
is a symptom, and shipping only the symptom guarantees the next entry.**

### The class

tako answers some requests **itself**, without reaching the app's
handlers, and every one of those answers is a dead end that does not
look like the app:

| Where | Today | Filed as |
|---|---|---|
| `writeNotFoundPage` (`page.go:393`) | renders `SiteConfig.NotFound` with **nil data** | friction 2026-08-04 |
| `pageError` non-404 status (`page.go:371`) | `http.Error` — **plain text** | friction 2026-08-04 (the 403) |
| `pageError` 500 (`page.go:375`) | plain text, deliberately | — |
| site static miss (`site.go`) | same nil-data 404 | friction 2026-08-04 |
| `SignInPage` (`session.go:419`) | tako's own markup, app cannot touch it | — |
| every future one: 405, 413, 429, CSRF failure, maintenance | plain text by default | not yet |

Flauta filed two of these separately, three days apart, as if they were
different problems. They are one: **the app has no way to tell tako
what a page it owns should look like.** Every future status tako learns
to answer arrives as a new friction entry until that seam exists.

### The seam

One field, one function, every page tako renders on the app's behalf:

```go
var site = tako.Site("web", tako.SiteConfig{
	Status: statusPage,
})

// Called for every response tako produces itself. The app decides
// what it looks like and what data it carries; tako decides when.
func statusPage(ctx tako.Ctx, s tako.Status) (tako.HTML, error) {
	return tako.Render("status.html", shell(ctx, statusData{
		Code:  s.Code,
		Title: titles[s.Code],
		Nav:   navFromConfig(),
	}))
}
```

`tako.Status` carries what a status page can honestly know: `Code`,
`Path`, `RequestID`, and `Err` (nil unless the app's own handler
produced it — never populated for a 5xx, where the message is logged
and the visitor gets the request id). It is a struct so later fields
are additive.

`SiteConfig.NotFound` stays, and stays the easy path: name a template,
get a 404. `Status` is the seam for anything more, and `NotFound`
becomes shorthand for a `Status` function that renders that template
for 404 only. One mechanism, two spellings, the simple one unchanged.

### The rule that governs all of it

**A status page must never become a 500.** Today's contract — "a
missing or broken 404 template must never turn a 404 into a 500" — is
generalised: `Status` is called with recover, its failure is logged,
and the fallback is today's plain text. It is called for 4xx AND 5xx;
`page.go:365` currently argues against rendering during a 500, and the
guard is what makes that argument moot — a 500 page in the site's
chrome is what a visitor wants, and a broken one costs nothing it did
not already cost. A `Status` function that itself 500s does not
re-enter.

### This is an API task

Per CLAUDE.md, adding `SiteConfig.Status` and `tako.Status` is an SDK
change and therefore its own task, which is what this slice is. It
lands with `sdk_lock_test.go` and the api reference page updated in the
same commit.

### Tests

The conformance-shaped question here is the fallback: a `Status` that
panics, one that returns an error, one that returns empty HTML, and one
that is absent — all four produce the plain-text answer with the right
code. Then one case per call site (handler 404, static miss, 403, 500,
sign-in required), asserting the app's chrome is present. `examples/journal`
grows the masthead-and-nav 404 flauta wants, which is the example that
demands the feature.

### Non-goals

Letting `Status` change the status code (it renders an answer, it does
not decide one); a per-route status page; theming tako's sign-in page
beyond wrapping it in the app's shell.

---

## FL12 — a page can say how long it may be cached

### The defect

`page.go:315` sets `Cache-Control: no-cache` on **every** SSR render,
unconditionally. There is no way to say otherwise. A read-heavy site
that publishes twice a week revalidates every reader request against
the app and the entity store — which on Datastore is a billed read per
visitor per page. flauta calls it "an inherited default, nobody's
decision," and it is: `site.go:170` already gives fingerprinted static
assets `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so the static half was
thought about and the rendered half was not.

Not in the friction log — it is in flauta's backlog as SR-6. Worth
recording that the friction log is not the whole picture.

### The surface

`Route` is the config struct for "settings that belong to a single
route", which is exactly what this is:

```go
var Article = tako.Page("GET /{section}/{slug}", article, tako.Route{
	MaxAge: 5 * time.Minute,
})
```

Zero keeps today's `no-cache`, so nothing existing moves. Non-zero
emits `public, max-age=<seconds>`.

### The interaction that makes it an analyzer rule

`MaxAge` on a route with `SignIn: true` is a **cache-poisoning bug**: a
shared cache would serve one user's authenticated page to another. It
is refused at analysis time, not documented as a caution:

```
app.go:64:2: Article sets MaxAge on a route that requires sign-in — a shared cache would serve one signed-in user's page to another; drop MaxAge, or drop SignIn (tako/cache-signin)
```

### Tests

Golden for the analyzer refusal; runtime tests for the header on a
plain page, a `SignIn` page (refused before it can run), a fragment
response, and a redirect. `examples/journal`'s public article page
takes a `MaxAge`, since it is the case that motivated it.

### Non-goals

`s-maxage`/CDN split, `stale-while-revalidate`, ETag-based
revalidation for rendered pages, and per-route cache policy on API
routes (JSON clients cache differently; no example asks).

---

## Z8 — the docs check catches names as they are written

`pkg/docserver/mentions_test.go` keys on `tako.X`. Prose naming
`WithDomain` without the qualifier walks straight past it, which is how
all four retired-symbol mentions survived until they were found by
hand. Widen it: an identifier-shaped word in prose or a code span that
looks like SDK surface (`WithFoo`, `PascalCase` adjacent to a tako
term) is checked against the lock, with an allowlist for the words that
legitimately are not SDK symbols. Cheap, and it belongs before a
v0.1.0, because after the tag the docs are what people read first.

## Closing sequence, after the four gates

1. **Documentation, all three trees.** `docs/guide/` (the narrative —
   FL11 and FL12 change what a site author writes), `docs/reference/`
   (site.md, pages.md, entity.md, errors.md gain the two new rules),
   `docs/api/` (the `SiteConfig.Status`, `tako.Status` and `Route.MaxAge`
   entries, plus the lock). Z7b's check and Z8's widened one are what
   keep this honest.
2. **Comprehensive validation, local and live.** The full `validate/`
   suite locally; live means a real deploy to `tako-test-01` — which
   also finally exercises **FL8's create**, the one step `--plan`
   cannot reach, with a host-shaped module path. Destroy after, and
   confirm the project is clean.
3. **`make build` / `make install`.**

### The skill

The loop the owner described — take a requirement, hold the whole plan
without dropping items, build to the end, validate local **and** live,
update the docs, cut a build — is written as `~/.claude/skills/ship-loop/`.
It is deliberately project-agnostic: the tako specifics (three doc
trees, `validate/`, `make install`) are what it asks the project for,
not what it hardcodes.

### Order, and what is NOT in this program

FL10 → FL11 → FL12 → Z8 → docs → validate → build.

Deliberately excluded, and why: **Z6 (publish)** is owner-only (no git
remote, tag, push). **flauta's M4 request** — expose codegen's
generated request binders so their 2,837-line `pages_test.go` stops
hand-mirroring them — is a real gap and a real API question, and it is
its own program, not a tail on this one. **Discovered work #10**
(`Prefixed` has no bound) stays logged and unpromoted. The four
`workaround-fine` friction entries other than the 404 are covered by
FL11 or stay settled. The parked list (load balancer, multi-service dev
routing, `tako rename`, session cache, VPC, per-command `--help`) is
unchanged.

### The list — the contract for this program (2026-08-06)

Approved with one addition: "and cleanups related to not found." Eight
items. This is what the closing report is checked against.

1. **FL10** — cross-function query assembly.
2. **FL11** — status pages as a class (`SiteConfig.Status`, `tako.Status`).
3. **FL11c** — the NotFound cleanups, folded into FL11 rather than
   scheduled beside it, because they are the same seam:
   - **Two 404 writers with different security headers.**
     `writeNotFoundPage` (`page.go:400`) sets CSP-Report-Only and
     Referrer-Policy; `writeStaticNotFound` (`site.go:113`) sets
     neither. Which one a visitor gets depends on whether the declared
     404 resolved as a template or as a static file — invisible from
     the app, and a security-header difference rather than a cosmetic
     one.
   - **A third writer**, `http.NotFound` (`site.go:99`), with no
     headers at all.
   - **A fourth**, `cron.go:117`, writing its own plain-text 404.
   - **Package-level mutable state**, `notFoundPage` (`page.go:383`),
     a second global beside `renderSite`.
   - **404 is special-cased** in `pageError` (`page.go:368`) while
     every other explicit status falls to `http.Error`.
   One status writer replaces all of it: headers decided once, the
   app's shell applied once, the plain-text fallback in one place.
4. **FL12** — per-route cache policy (`Route.MaxAge` + `tako/cache-signin`).
5. **Z8** — the docs mention check catches unqualified names.
6. **Docs** — guide, reference, and api, all three.
7. **Validation** — full local suite and scripted validation, plus
   LIVE against a real project (which also finally exercises FL8's
   create).
8. **Build** — `make build`, `make install`.

## FL10 — shipped (2026-08-06)

Item 1 of 8. A query assembled across a function boundary now derives
the shapes that actually run.

### The rule, as built

A function with an `*EntityQuery[T]` parameter or result is a
**fragment**: `pkg/analyzer/fragments.go` finds every one of them from
`go/types` alone, with no dataflow analysis, because a query value has
a known type. A fragment contributes no chain of its own; its modifiers
are spliced into each caller at the call's position, carrying that call
site's branch context (`optional = fragmentOptional || guarded(stack)`).
Fragments compose, memoized, with a cycle guard.

A query tako cannot follow is refused, in three wordings under one rule
(`tako/query-escapes`): stored in a struct field, a package-level var,
a map or slice element, a pointer's target or a composite literal; sent
on a channel; or passed to something that does not resolve to a
declaration in this package.

### What the slice found on the way

**Two OrderBys were recorded backwards.** Not in the design, not in the
friction log, found by writing the fixture:

```
OrderBy("Section").OrderBy("-PublishAt")   derived   (state, -publishAt, section)
```

`ast.Inspect` visits a chained call **outermost-first**, so the last
`OrderBy` written was the first one collected. A composite whose sort
suffix is in the wrong order is one Datastore will not use — the same
production 500 as a missing index, from a different clause.

It is the same class as FL10 and was fixed inside it: modifiers now
carry a `token.Pos` and are sorted by source position, which is what
"in call order" was always supposed to mean. Traversal order was
standing in for it and happened to agree in every case any example or
fixture had.

### What did NOT change

`examples/journal`'s derived index. The example used a **closure**,
which worked for a reason nobody could see: a closure lives inside its
enclosing function, so the analyzer never crossed a boundary. FL10's
commit promotes it to a package-level fragment and the tuple is
identical — `(published, -created)`, before and after. That is the
proof the two spellings now mean the same thing, and it is why the
example moved.

### Tests

- `pkg/analyzer/testdata/queryfragments/` + `fragments_test.go` — the
  caller/fragment pair with a conditional filter, a two-deep chain, two
  OrderBys, a fragment called under an `if` (everything it carries
  becomes optional), and an uncalled fragment that must ask for
  nothing. All three tests fail on the pre-FL10 analyzer, each for its
  own reason.
- `pkg/analyzer/testdata/errors/queryescapes/` — both refusals, exact
  text and position.
- Every example green, which is the false-positive check: an escape
  rule that fires wrongly blocks a deploy.

### Validation

`validate/query-fragments.md`, written and run. Step 1, live:

```
$ cd examples/journal && go run ../../cmd/tako gen graph --json | …
posts: (published, -created)  <- app.go:101 home
```

Step 4's two refusals are the golden above. Step 5 is the full suite,
green.

### Correction to the design

The design predicted `byAuthor` would derive `(author, state, -publishAt)`.
It derives `(state, author, -publishAt)`: filter order is STRUCT order
and always has been (gallery's `(owner, ready)`, flauta's
`(section, state, -publishAt)`), and only the OrderBy suffix follows
call order. The test asserted the wrong thing and was corrected, not
the code.

### Non-goals held

Cross-package fragments (package = service; a query crossing that
boundary is not a query — the escape rule covers it), and proving a
derived shape is reachable.

## FL11 — shipped (2026-08-06)

Items 2 and 3 of 8: the class, and the NotFound cleanups folded into
it because they are the same seam.

### The spelling changed from the design, for a reason

The design said `SiteConfig{Status: statusPage}`. **That cannot be
built.** `SiteOptions` reaches the runtime as a struct LITERAL rendered
by codegen from the AppGraph (`siteOptionsLiteral`), and a func value
is not a literal; the generated main is package `main`, so it can only
name exported identifiers, and every example's site var is lowercase.

What shipped instead obeys settled decision 1 exactly:

```go
var Status = tako.StatusPage(status)
```

A package-level var via a constructor, like every other handler, named
from the generated main the same way `journal.Home` is. No new wiring
mechanism, and the analyzer gets to enforce the constraints: exported
(`tako/unexported-status`) and one per package (`tako/one-status`).

### What it covers

Every response tako produces for itself, through one writer
(`pkg/runtime/status.go`):

| was | now |
|---|---|
| `writeNotFoundPage` — template, CSP + Referrer-Policy | `writeStatus` |
| `writeStaticNotFound` — static file, **neither header** | `writeStatus` |
| `http.NotFound` — no headers at all | `writeStatus` |
| `pageError` non-404 — `http.Error`, plain text | `writeStatus` |
| `pageError` 500 — plain text by policy | `writeStatus` |
| CSRF 403 ×2 — `http.Error` | `writeStatus` |
| a page's 401 — `http.Error` | `writeStatus` |
| site 405, site read 500 ×2 — `http.Error` | `writeStatus` |

The 401 was **not in the design**. It surfaced during live validation:
`POST /p` on a `SignIn` route answered before CSRF could, still in
plain text. Same class, same slice.

Deliberately NOT converted: `cron.go`'s four (machine-facing, OIDC
triggers from Cloud Scheduler — a person never sees them) and
`http.go`'s API 401 (a client parses JSON; rendering it a page would
break the parse).

### The rule that pays for the risk

`page.go` used to argue that a 500 must stay plain text, because
running the template engine when the process is already broken is the
worst moment to depend on it. Right about the risk, wrong about the
remedy: `renderStatus` recovers from a panicking status page and falls
through to the same plain text. The downside is bounded, so the app's
own page can answer the 500 too.

`tako.Status` has **no error field**, and `Message` is cleared for any
5xx before the page is called. Leaking a 500's detail is not something
the type permits.

### Live, on examples/journal

```
$ curl -s -i localhost:8080/no-such-page
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Cache-Control: no-cache
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

  <title>Not found · journal</title>
  <header><h1><a href="/">journal</a></h1>
    <nav><a href="/write">write</a> · <a href="/about">about</a> ·
  <h2>Not found</h2>
  <p><a href="/">Back to the journal</a> — 3 published posts.</p>
```

**"3 published posts" is the whole feature.** That number is a live
query from the status page's Ctx; before FL11 the 404 rendered with
`nil` and a shell built from data rendered its bands empty, which is
exactly what flauta filed. `POST /about` answers 405 as HTML (1209
bytes), `POST /p` answers 401 as HTML (1261), and `/p/does-not-exist` —
a handler's `tako.NotFound()` — renders the identical page as the
static miss.

### Tests

`pkg/runtime/status_test.go`: the fallback (panics / errors / renders
nothing → plain text, right code), every code wearing the app, the
header set identical on the rendered AND static paths, the 5xx
non-leak, and the bare floor. They render through a **real site**
rather than a test-only HTML constructor — adding `tako.RawHTML` just
to test would have widened the API for nobody.

### API and docs, in this commit

`sdk_lock.golden` (+5), `runtime_lock.golden` (+1,
`RegisterStatusPage` — generated code in users' repos names it),
`docs/api/surface.txt`, `symbolPage`, and `reference/site.md`'s new
"Status pages" section. Per CLAUDE.md an API change is its own task,
and this slice is it.

### Examples

`examples/journal` declares the status page and its `404.html` becomes
`status.html` with real data. `examples/blog` takes
`SiteConfig{NotFound: "404.html"}` — Hugo emits the file already — so
the one-line spelling keeps an example demanding it.

## FL12 — shipped (2026-08-06)

Item 4 of 8. flauta's SR-6, which was in their backlog rather than the
friction log — worth recording, because it means the friction log is
not the whole inventory.

### What shipped

`tako.Route{MaxAge: 5 * time.Minute}` on a Page renders
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`. Zero — every route that does not
ask — keeps `no-cache`, so no existing app moves. The value is a
constant (1s–1y), because it is baked into the header at build time.

Two analyzer refusals:

```
app.go:17:10: Dashboard sets MaxAge on a route that requires sign-in — a shared cache would serve one signed-in visitor's page to another; drop MaxAge, or drop SignIn (tako/cache-signin)
app.go:26:60: tako.Route.MaxAge takes a constant between 1s and a year — it is baked into the Cache-Control header at build time, not decided per request (tako/max-age)
```

`cache-signin` is the reason this is more than a field. A shared cache
holding an authenticated page hands it to whoever asks next, and
nothing about that failure is visible from the app — tests pass, the
page renders, and one day a reader sees someone else's page. Refused,
not documented as a caution.

### Live, on examples/journal

```
$ curl -s -i localhost:8080/2026/<slug> | grep -i cache-control
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
$ curl -s -i localhost:8080/ | grep -i cache-control
Cache-Control: no-cache
```

The permalink opts in — a published post does not change between
requests and a reader arriving from a shared link is the common case.
The home page does not, and gets exactly what it got before.

### API

`Route` gains one field, so `sdk_lock.golden` moves; `runtime_lock`
gains `CacheFor` (generated code names it). Both deliberate, both in
this commit with `reference/api.md` and `reference/pages.md`.

### Non-goals held

`s-maxage`/CDN split, `stale-while-revalidate`, ETag revalidation for
rendered pages, and MaxAge on API routes — a JSON client decides its
own caching, and no example asks.

## Z8 — shipped (2026-08-06)

Item 5 of 8. Discovered work #5, and the answer turned out to be
narrower and better than "check bare names".

### What the gap actually was

#5 said the mention check keys on `tako.X`, so prose naming
`WithDomain` bare escapes it. That specific hole was already closed by
`TestTheDocsDoNotNameRetiredWithOptions` (the WithX retirement). What
was still open is **what replaced the WithX vocabulary**: the docs now
spell options as `Route.SignIn`, `CronConfig.Singleflight`,
`SiteConfig.Build` — 93 qualified members across the guide and
reference — and nothing checked a single one of them. A renamed field
would rot exactly the way `WithDomain` did, silently, reading like
documentation the whole time.

Checking any capitalised word would have meant an allowlist arms race.
A QUALIFIED member is a claim about API precise enough to verify and
specific enough not to fire on prose.

### The check

`pkg/docserver/members_test.go` parses `api/surface.txt` — the same
lock the api page is generated from — into type → fields + methods,
then scans the guide and reference for `Type.Member`. Unknown types are
skipped (that is prose); a known type with an unknown member is an
error.

It refuses to pass vacuously: zero mentions checked is a failure, not a
clean bill, because a scanner that finds nothing is broken rather than
satisfied.

### Verified by mutation, not by passing

A check that has never failed is worth nothing. Two bogus names added
to `reference/api.md`:

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryFieldTheDocsNameExists
    reference/api.md:172: the docs name Route.Nonexistent, and Route has no such field or method
    reference/api.md:172: the docs name SiteConfig.Missing, and SiteConfig has no such field or method
    checked 95 Type.Member mentions against the lock
```

Reverted; the tree is clean at 93.

### The limit, stated

Same one the file above it states: no symbol check catches a sentence
that is WRONG about a symbol that exists. `cache.md` once said
"`WithTTL` is the only Cache option" when Cache has no options at all.
Three checks now cover three claims — the type exists, the retired
vocabulary is gone, the member exists — and none of them reads English.

Item 6 of 8. The reference and api pages moved with their slices (an
API change lands with its docs, per CLAUDE.md); this closes the guide
and the cross-cutting reference pages.

- **guide/02-shortlink.md** — "per query" means per SHAPE, not per
  function, with the fragment form and the escape rule. The guide

- **guide/04-journal.md** — a new "The pages tako writes" section
  (`tako.StatusPage`, what it covers, the never-worse guarantee) and

- **reference/entity.md** — query fragments beside the branch rule.
- **reference/errors.md** — four new rules in the tables they belong

### Discovered work

**11. A deploy can lose a race with IAM propagation.** journal's first
deploy failed here:

```
tako: update iam grants project: write the IAM policy of project tako-test-01: Service account journal-sa@… does not exist. (HTTP 400 from cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com)
```

The SA was created seconds earlier in the same run. IAM's create is
eventually consistent and the project-scope grant (RC3's) is reconciled
right after it. Re-running succeeded with no changes — the reconciler
is idempotent, which is why this is a retry-shaped bug rather than a
correctness one. hello's deploy won the same race minutes earlier, so
it is intermittent. **Not this program's class**; it belongs with the
provisioner's retry policy. Worth fixing before a v0.1.0, because
"run it again" is a bad first experience.

**12. Three `photos` Datastore indexes remain on tako-test-01** from a
gallery deployment in an earlier session, all READY. Either that
destroy was env-scoped (`destroy.go:216` keeps shared repo, indexes and
framework bucket by design for a non-prod env) or destroy missed them.
Recorded as a thing to CHECK rather than a claim — I did not create
them and did not verify which.

## FL13 + the FL12 verification — shipped (2026-08-06)

Owner-directed follow-ups: verify FL12 for real, fix discovered #11,
clear #12's leftovers.

### FL13 — the project grant survives IAM propagation (#11)

The retry was already there, and already written for this exact
failure — `apply` loops four times, 15 seconds apart, with a comment
saying it exists because "a policy write can 400 on a MEMBER the IAM
backend hasn't seen yet". The bug was one clause in `applyOnce`:

```go
if isAPI && typ != provision.TargetProject && (ae.Status == 403 || ae.Status == 400) {
```

The project target could never set `retry`. Two different things
answer 403/400 there and the condition conflated them: a NON-project
target that no longer reads back is GONE (converge — that carve-out is
what stops a half-destroyed app failing forever), and a member that is
not propagated yet is EARLY (retry). RC3 then made a project-scope
grant part of every service, so the one target that could not retry
became the one applied soonest after a fresh identity exists.

Split: the gone-check runs only for non-project targets; the retry runs
for all of them. `grantRetryDelay` is a var now so a test can shrink it.

Verified by mutation, not by passing: with the old clause restored the
new test fails with the live error text, character for character.

```
--- FAIL: TestAProjectGrantWaitsForAFreshServiceAccount
    the project grant gave up on an unpropagated member: write the IAM policy of project p: Service account new-sa@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com does not exist. (HTTP 400 …)
```

Live: journal redeployed from nothing — fresh SA, fresh grant — and
completed in one run.

### FL12 verified live, and it was broken

The owner was right to insist. To reach a cacheable page in the cloud I
seeded a published post straight into Datastore with tako's own
encoding (`_doc` blob + indexed properties, namespace `prod`). The
permalink then answered:

```
HTTP/2 200
cache-control: private, max-age=300
set-cookie: __tako_csrf=b656810e346edf653fe286623ea9b05a; …
```

**`private`, not `public`.** tako emits `public`; something rewrote it.
Tested rather than assumed — the same URL with the cookie already
held:

```
$ curl -H "Cookie: __tako_csrf=…" …
cache-control: public, max-age=300
```

**Cloud Run's frontend downgrades `public` to `private` whenever the
response carries a Set-Cookie.** Sane proxy behaviour, and it made
FL12's whole point unreachable on the FIRST visit — the one a shared
cache exists for. Nothing local could show it: the header tako writes
was correct, and the rewrite happens above the process.

It also exposed a correctness bug FL12 would have shipped: a page
declared cacheable must carry no per-visitor state, and a CSRF token is
exactly that. Minting one bakes one visitor's token into a page a
shared cache hands to the next.

One fix for both: a page with `MaxAge > 0` mints no CSRF cookie on a
safe method. The trade — `{{ csrf }}` renders empty, so a cacheable
page cannot carry a form — is the same bargain as `tako/cache-signin`,
and for the same reason.

Live, after the fix, first visit, no cookie held:

```
HTTP/2 200
cache-control: public, max-age=300
```

with no Set-Cookie. The home page still mints its cookie and still
answers `no-cache`.

### #12's leftovers, cleared

`cd examples/gallery && tako destroy --project tako-test-01` removed
all three:

```
✗ datastore index photos (owner, ready)
✗ datastore index photos (owner, ready, -created)
✗ datastore index photos (ready, -created)
```

So destroy was never broken — an earlier session simply left gallery
deployed, or destroyed it env-scoped. The project now lists four
indexes in DELETING and nothing else: no services, no buckets.

### The pattern worth keeping

Both of today's real defects were invisible below the cloud boundary.
`private, max-age=300` cannot be reproduced locally at all, and the IAM
race only fires against a real, eventually-consistent IAM. A green
local suite says nothing about either.

## FL14 — DX proposal: a declared provider is a scoped door (2026-08-06) — AWAITING APPROVAL

flauta's first **security** entry, taken as a task.

### The finding holds, verified line by line

`pkg/runtime/session.go:281` unmarshals exactly:

```go
var claims struct {
	Iss, Aud string; Exp int64; Sub, Email, Name string
}
```

There is no `firebase.sign_in_provider`, and `tako.User` (`ctx.go:39`)
carries `ID`, `Email`, `Name` — nothing else. So **any** Identity
Platform token for the project verifies, whatever provider minted it.

The other half is in the provisioner. `EnsureAuthClient`
(`preflight.go:318`) enables a declared provider — *"declared →
enabled: the declaration is the decision"* — and **never disables an
undeclared one**. A project where email/password is on (Firebase's
default, another app's deploy, or a console click) accepts password
sessions for an app that declared `AuthConfig{Google: true}`.

flauta's own words for why this matters: *"the declaration reads like
a restriction and is not one."* An author writing `Google: true`
believes they have scoped their door. tako-test-02 had self-service
password sign-up open, so a self-registered account would have produced
a session tako accepted; only an allowlist string comparison stood
behind it.

### What ships

**1. The session is scoped to the declared providers.** `verifyIDToken`
reads `firebase.sign_in_provider` and refuses a token whose provider
the app did not declare:

```
sign-in refused: this token was minted by password, and this app declares google — tako.AuthConfig{Google: true}
```

The claim is already in the token. This is a comparison tako is
positioned to make and the app is not.

The declared set reaches the verifier the way every other declaration
reaches the runtime: codegen passes it, so
`runtime.SessionHandler()` becomes `runtime.SessionHandler("google")`.
That is a `runtime_lock` change — generated code in users' repos names
it — and therefore deliberate and called out.

**2. The claims an app cannot otherwise see.** `tako.User` gains:

```go
// Provider is the sign-in method that minted this session:
// "google", "email". Scoping already refused anything undeclared;
// this is for an app that declares more than one and treats them
// differently.
Provider string
// EmailVerified is the provider's claim about the address. A Google
// identity is verified by Google; a password account is whatever
// Identity Platform was configured to require.
EmailVerified bool
```

`EmailVerified` is not decoration. An allowlist keyed on **email** —
which is what flauta's `editors` is, and the obvious shape — is only as
strong as the guarantee that the address is real. For Google that
guarantee is Google's; for password it is a project setting nobody in
the app can see. Exposing the claim is what lets an app say
`if !u.EmailVerified { deny }` instead of trusting a string.

Both halves are one change to one function, which is why they ship
together rather than as 1-then-2.

### The behaviour change, stated loudly

An app declaring `Google: true` whose users have been signing in with
password will start refusing those sign-ins. **That is the fix**, not a
side effect. It is a sign-in-time check, so sessions already
established in the entity store keep working until they expire or are
revoked — the change cannot log anybody out mid-visit.

`tako dev` is unaffected: the dev bar establishes sessions at
`session.go:136` without going through `verifyIDToken` at all.

### Not in scope (the fence)

- **Disabling undeclared providers at the project level.** flauta's
  workaround (`client.permissions.disabledUserSignup`) is a real
  control, and tako reaching in to turn off a provider it did not
  declare would be tako deciding something about a project it shares.
  Scoping the session gets the security property without that.
  Recorded as a candidate, not built.
- `anonymous`, phone, or any provider tako does not declare — they are
  refused by the same rule, with no per-provider handling.
- Re-verifying live sessions against a provider list that changed after
  they were minted.

### Tests

- `verifyIDToken` with a `password` token against a `google` app →
  refused, exact text; the same token against an app declaring both →
  accepted.
- `Provider` and `EmailVerified` populated from the claim on both
  paths, and absent-claim defaults (`EmailVerified` false when the
  claim is missing — the safe direction).
- A token with no `firebase` object at all → refused, not accepted as
  "no provider".
- The runtime lock and SDK lock move; both deliberate.

### Validation

`validate/auth.md` gains the scoping step. The live half needs a
password account on a project with both providers enabled — which is
exactly the configuration flauta found, and which I can reproduce on
tako-test-02 rather than tako-test-01.

## FL14 — shipped (2026-08-06)

flauta's first security entry, closed. Taken through `/senior-task`,
which is where the re-confirm step earned its place: three of their
seven open items had already been closed by FL11 and FL13 after their
review was written.

### The finding held, and had a second half

Verified line by line before writing anything: `verifyIDToken`
unmarshalled `Iss, Aud, Exp, Sub, Email, Name` and nothing else, and
`tako.User` carried `ID, Email, Name`. So any Identity Platform token
for the project verified.

The half flauta did not name is in the provisioner: `EnsureAuthClient`
(`preflight.go:318`) *enables* a declared provider — "declared →
enabled: the declaration is the decision" — and **never disables an
undeclared one**. The gap is therefore not a missing check on an
unlikely configuration; it is the ordinary one.

### What shipped

`userFromClaims` reads `firebase.sign_in_provider`, maps Identity
Platform's names onto the ones an app declares (`google.com` → google,
`password` → email), and refuses anything not declared. Split from
`verifyIDToken` deliberately: the signature check is Google's business
and needs a key, this rule is tako's and needs nothing, so it is
testable on its own.

An absent provider claim is refused too. "No provider" is not "any
provider" — it is a token tako cannot place.

`tako.User` gains `Provider` and `EmailVerified`. The second is the one
that matters: an allowlist keyed on email — flauta's `editors`, and the
obvious shape — is only as strong as the guarantee the address belongs
to whoever signed in. Google guarantees it; email/password guarantees a
project setting no app can see.

The declared set reaches the verifier through codegen:
`runtime.SessionHandler("google")`. Runtime lock and SDK lock both
move, both deliberate.

### Live, on tako-test-02 — the real attack

The project is the configuration flauta described, confirmed first:

```
email: {"enabled": true, "passwordRequired": true}
perms: {"disabledUserSignup": true}
```

journal (declares `Google: true`) deployed there. A password account
created through the admin API, signed in for a real ID token:

```
sign_in_provider: password
email_verified  : False
aud             : tako-test-02
```

A valid, signed, unexpired token for the project — everything
`verifyIDToken` used to check, it passes. Offered to the app:

```
HTTP/2 401
the ID token did not verify: this token was minted by email, and this app declares google — tako.AuthConfig decides which doors exist
```

**Before FL14 that session would have been minted.** Proven by
mutation rather than by assertion: disabling the one condition makes
both refusal tests fail —

```
--- FAIL: TestASessionCannotComeFromAnUndeclaredProvider
    a password token was accepted by an app that declares only google
--- FAIL: TestAnUnknownProviderIsRefusedUnlessDeclared
    an anonymous token was accepted
```

Probe account deleted, deployment destroyed.

### The docs check caught me

Writing `reference/auth.md` I used `tako.Forbidden()`, which has never
existed. Z8's sibling check failed the build on it within the minute:

```
reference/auth.md:64: the docs name tako.Forbidden, and tako exports no such symbol
```

Corrected to `tako.Errorf(403, …)`. Worth recording because it is the
first time that check fired on new prose rather than on old rot — which
is what it was actually built for.

### Fence held

tako does not disable providers at the project level. That would be
tako reaching into a shared project to turn off something it did not
declare; scoping the session gets the security property without it.
flauta's `disabledUserSignup` stays their control.

### Discovered work

**13. `tako logs`' ADC quota-project failure is not just `tako logs`.**
flauta filed it against Logging; I hit the identical 403 against
`identitytoolkit.googleapis.com` while reading the project's auth
config. It is an ADC-wide property — user credentials carry no quota
project — so the fix (send `x-goog-user-project`, or say so in the
error) belongs to the shared client, not to one command. Their entry
understates the scope.

## Wrap-up check (2026-08-06)

### Discovered work

**14. A destroy of ONE app removes the project's SHARED objects.** The
framework bucket (`<project>-tako`) and the Artifact Registry repo
(`RepoName = "tako"`, explicitly "app-agnostic") carry no app label and
are deleted by any app's `tako destroy`. Under the dedicated-project
doctrine that is correct and intended. On a project holding more than
one app — which every tako TEST project does — one app's teardown takes
the lease bucket and the image repo out from under the others.

Nothing was harmed today, and the audit log is the reason I can say so
rather than assume it:

```
15:09:33-39  flauta-web + SA + framework bucket deleted   (flauta's own destroy)
15:12:37     journal-sa created                            (my deploy's first write)
15:16:41     journal created
15:18:21-25  journal + SA + framework bucket deleted       (my destroy)
```

flauta's teardown finished three minutes before my deploy wrote
anything, and `RunServices.List` filters by the `tako-app` label
(`run.go:89`), so an orphan sweep could not have reached their service
either. Two independent reasons, one of them structural.

The hazard is still real: had flauta still been deployed at 15:18, my
journal destroy would have deleted the bucket their deploy lease lives
in. Both objects are recreated on demand, so the blast radius is a
failed concurrent deploy rather than data loss — but a destroy that
says "✓ destroyed" while removing another app's infrastructure is not
honest. Candidate fix: name shared objects in the destroy preamble as
shared, or skip them when another app's labels are present in the
project.

### Cleanup

tako-test-01: no services, no buckets, no indexes. tako-test-02: the
`orders` (shop) and `photos` (gallery) indexes left by earlier sessions
were cleared by running each example's own destroy, as the owner
directed for the tako-test-01 leftovers; both now DELETING. The FL14
probe account was deleted immediately after the test.

## Code review 2 — reviewed and landed (2026-08-06)

Owner-requested health review: structure, simplicity, duplication, dead
documents, readability for a newcomer. Taken through `/senior-task`.
The findings and the numbers are `docs/code-review-2.md`; this is what
changed.

**No backlog handle** — the request was the whole brief, so acceptance
was sharpened before starting and written into the review: every
duplication claim a measured pair, every dead document dead by a stated
test, every readability finding naming the file a newcomer opens, and
every code change **hardening** (behaviour provably unchanged).

### The headline number

`code-review-1` measured 29.5k lines of Go outside `examples/` and 38
analyzer rules on 2026-08-01. Today: **45,260 and 52** — half again as
much code in five days — with `TODO`/`FIXME`/`XXX` still at **zero**.
The code is healthy. The documentation was where the rot was.

### A — hardening, three de-duplications

1. **`urlEscape`** was written byte-for-byte twice
   (`alertdoc.go`, `gcp/descriptorsearch.go`), hand-rolled in both
   because `url.QueryEscape` turns a space into `+` and the Logs
   Explorer reads its query from a path segment. One home
   (`provision.URLEscape`, which `gcp` already imports), with the
   reason stated once instead of in one copy of two.
2. **The package-qualifier split** existed four times.
   `analyzer.ShortName` is now the one, called by `ShortVar`, codegen
   and `provision.shortNames`. `gcp.lastSegment` splits a different
   separator for a different domain and stays.
   **`codegen.shortVarName` was mine**, added five commits ago in FL11
   because `ShortVar` took a `Handler` and I had a `Resource`. Writing
   the review found my own duplicate, which is the argument for
   measuring rather than remembering.
3. **The security-header set** was written in three places
   (`page.go`, `site.go`, `status.go`). Now `securityHeaders(h,
   fragment)`, with the fragment rule — nosniff yes, CSP and
   Referrer-Policy no, because a partial is swapped into a document
   that already declares both — stated once.

(3) is the one that had already failed: FL11 existed because a declared
404 got the CSP as a template and not as a static file. FL11 unified
the four *writers* and left the *list* in triplicate. It now has the
test that absence deserved, and the test was checked against the
mistake a real implementer makes — re-inlining one path:

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryHTMLDocumentCarriesTheSameSecurityHeaders
    site: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only = "", want "default-src 'self'"
    site: Referrer-Policy = "", want "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
```

Behaviour unchanged: the full suite passes untouched.

### B — three dead documents, 814 lines

Dead by a stated test: **its stated purpose is to instruct work that
has since shipped.** Deliberately stronger than "nothing links to it",
because an unlinked review is still dated reasoning the code obeys.

- `stage7-handoff.md` (315) — "a brief for whoever implements Stage 7"
- `stage7-resume.md` (119) — "Resume here — U2, U3, U4"
- `stage10-resume.md` (380) — "FL1–FL4 are next and still unapproved.

**Everything else stays.** The reviews are cited from the shipped

### C — the finding that actually cost a newcomer

`README.md` is good and gets someone to a URL. Their second step is

### Discovered work

**15. `internal/hooks` is 22 mutable package vars** bridging the SDK
and the runtime, assigned at boot. It is the one structure in the tree
a newcomer will find surprising, and it is load-bearing: it is how the
