task, not a cleanup, and it stays on the fence's far side.

## FL15–FL19 — DX proposals: the fourth friction review (2026-08-08) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Five tasks from `docs/tako-agent-plan.md` Stage 12. Presented together
because the owner asked for all of them; **each still ships behind its
own gate**, and FL15 is the only one whose surface a v0.1.0 would
freeze. Every finding below was re-verified against this tree at
`7a40353` before it was written up.

---

### FL15 — a form may repeat a field

**The finding holds.** `bindableTypes` (`pkg/analyzer/handlers.go:18`)
holds exactly five entries; anything else fails `tako/bind-type` at
`handlers.go:326`. `FormString` is `r.FormValue(name)`
(`pkg/runtime/bind.go:92`), which returns the **first** value of a
repeated field. So a group of checkboxes named alike — the native HTML
shape of "select some rows" — loses N-1 of its values before the app
runs, silently.

**What ships.** `[]string` becomes bindable for `form:` and `query:`:

```go
type BulkArchive struct {
	Selected []string `form:"selected"`
	Reason   string   `form:"reason"`
}
```

```html
<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="hello-world">
<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="second-post">
```

Two runtime helpers beside the existing ten:

```go
// FormStrings returns every value of the named form field (nil when
// absent). A repeated field is the HTML shape of "select some rows".
func FormStrings(r *http.Request, name string) []string {
	_ = r.ParseForm()
	return r.Form[name]
}

// QueryStrings returns every value of the named query parameter.
func QueryStrings(r *http.Request, name string) []string {
	return r.URL.Query()[name]
}
```

Codegen needs one line: `helperName` (`pkg/codegen/codegen.go:469`)
gains `"[]string": "Strings"`, and the emitter's existing
`bind.Type == "string"` fast path — the one that assigns without an
`err` check — extends to `[]string`, because neither can fail to parse.

**`path:` does not get it.** A route segment is one value by
construction; offering `[]string` there would be a shape the router can
never produce.

**Absent is `nil`, not empty.** A checkbox group with nothing ticked
sends no field at all, so `nil` is the honest answer and `len(x) == 0`
is the test either way.

**The error text is unchanged.** A still-unbindable type keeps saying
what it says today, with the list grown by one:

```
app.go:31:2: field Tags: form:-tagged fields must be string, []string, bool, int, int64, or float64; got []int (tako/bind-type)
```

**The example that demands it.** None of the five does today, which is
why this task carries one: `shop` gains a bulk action on its product
list — N checkboxes named alike, a submit, no JavaScript. That is the
FL8 move, where the corpus was fixed rather than the note.

**Why this one is pre-tag.** It changes what a Req struct may declare.
Before v0.1.0 that is the v0 surface; after it, it is an API change
against a published version.

**Gate FL15 (agent-side).** Analyzer golden for the new binding and for
the unchanged `bind-type` error on `[]int`; a codegen golden showing the
emitted decode line; `shop`'s suite green with two boxes ticked, one
ticked, and none; conformance untouched.

---

### FL16 — the dev server's readiness probe answers for the wrong process

**The filed diagnosis is wrong, and the correction is the task.**
flauta asked tako to "bind the listener before printing ready". `tako
dev` never binds — the child does. `waitReady`
(`pkg/devserver/devserver.go:342`) dials `127.0.0.1:PORT` and returns
`nil` the instant **anything** accepts:

```go
conn, err := net.DialTimeout("tcp", "127.0.0.1:"+port, 100*time.Millisecond)
if err == nil {
	conn.Close()
	return nil
}
```

With a stale example holding 8080, that dial succeeds against the
stranger, `ready in 590ms` (`devserver.go:214`) is printed truthfully
about someone else's server, and the child's own good error arrives
afterwards from `pkg/runtime/http.go:171`. The ordering flauta reported
is a symptom; the probe is the defect.

**tako had already written this down.** `http.go:168`:

> A collision here answers requests with SOMEONE ELSE'S responses —
> mysterious 404s. Name the fix.

The readiness probe is that collision, from the other side.

**What ships.** The probe proves it reached *this* child. `runtime.Serve`
already answers under `/_tako/`; the dev server passes a per-run nonce
in the child's environment (`TAKO_DEV_NONCE`), the runtime answers
`GET /_tako/z/dev` with it under a local backend only, and `waitReady`
accepts only a matching body. A foreign listener answers 404, the wrong
body, or nothing — all three are "not mine".

The child is also watched while waiting, so an exit during startup ends
the wait immediately instead of at the 5s deadline.

```
$ tako dev
  GET  /                      home
  GET  /{year}/{slug}         post
tako: port 8080 is answering, but not with this app — another process
has it. Set PORT (e.g. PORT=8090 tako dev) or free it (`lsof -i :8080`)
```

No `ready` line precedes it. The text names the distinction that
matters: the port is not merely busy, it is busy with something that
will answer your browser.

**Not in scope.** Picking a free port automatically. A dev server that
silently moves is a dev server whose URL you cannot predict, and every
bookmark and OAuth redirect an app has is written against one port.

**Gate FL16 (agent-side).** A devserver test that holds the port with a
foreign listener and asserts the collision text, a non-zero exit, and
that `ready` never appears; a second that kills the child mid-start and
asserts the wait ends on the exit rather than the timeout.

---

### FL17 — a blob carries its headers, and so does a stylesheet

**The finding holds, and the read found a second instance flauta could
not see.** `BlobHandler` (`pkg/runtime/blob.go:20`) writes
`Content-Type` and `Content-Length` (`blob.go:57-59`) and stops: no
`X-Content-Type-Options`, no `Cache-Control`, no validator. A blob is
the one response kind whose bytes came from outside the program.

The second instance: `securityHeaders` (`pkg/runtime/status.go:141`) is
the **only** writer of nosniff in the tree, and the site handler calls
it inside an HTML-only branch (`pkg/runtime/site.go:174-176`):

```go
if strings.HasPrefix(ctype, "text/html") {
	securityHeaders(h, false)
}
```

Every `.css`, `.js` and `.svg` the site serves therefore goes out
without nosniff — while `contentTypeOf`, fifty lines below, carries the
comment *"nosniff is set — types must be right"* (`site.go:229-232`).
An invariant asserted about exactly the files that do not hold it.

**What ships.**

1. `securityHeaders(h, false)` moves out of the HTML-only branch; every
   file the site serves carries nosniff, and CSP/Referrer-Policy stay
   HTML-only where they belong.
2. `BlobHandler` sets nosniff unconditionally.
3. `Route.MaxAge` reaches blob endpoints. **`BlobHandler` already takes
   `...HandlerOption` and already builds a `handlerConf`** (`blob.go:21-24`)
   — it simply never reads `conf.maxAge`. So this is `h.Set("Cache-Control",
   cacheControl(conf.maxAge))` beside the Content-Type, sharing FL12's
   renderer (`page.go:422`).

```go
var media = tako.API(tako.Route{
	Method: "GET", Path: "/media/{key}", MaxAge: 86400,
}, serveMedia)
```

**Freshness stays opt-in.** A blob route that declares no `MaxAge` gets
`no-cache`, which is what every blob answers today by omission — so
replace-in-place keeps working for apps that never asked for caching,
and the ones that do ask get the header the version-in-URL pattern
needs.

**Gate FL17 (agent-side).** One table test, one row per response kind —
page, fragment, HTML site file, non-HTML site file, blob, status,
redirect — asserting the exact header set each carries. FL11 found four
writers and three header sets by counting them by hand; this is the
test that makes a fourth set impossible to add silently. Plus
`gallery`'s photo endpoint declaring `MaxAge` and asserting it round
trips.

---

### FL18 — the dev bar behaves

Two friction entries, one task, both local-only and both invisible in
production.

**The findings hold.** The bar is built at `pkg/runtime/session.go:438`
as a `<div style="position:fixed;bottom:0;…">` — inline styles, no id,
no class. And `barWriter.flush` (`session.go:414`) branches on
`b.html` alone, never on whether the response is a fragment, so an htmx
swap carries a copy of the bar into whatever it swapped into.

flauta's workaround is the tell: it finds the fixed-position child of
`<body>` holding a `[name="dev_user"]` control, because there is
nothing stable to target and an inline-style substring match would be a
guess at something tako never promised.

**What ships.**

```html
<div id="tako-dev-bar" style="position:fixed;bottom:0;…">
```

and injection is skipped for fragments. The runtime already knows one
layer down — `securityHeaders(h, fragment)` at `page.go:359` branches
on exactly that signal — so this is threading a bool that already
exists, not a new concept.

**An app may hide it, and that is supported.** `#tako-dev-bar
{ display: none }` is now a thing an app can write and rely on, which
is the whole ask: any app with its own fixed bottom bar hits this, and
every one of them would otherwise guess at the same selector.

**Not in scope.** A per-route opt-out. An id costs one attribute and
covers the case; a route-level toggle is a declaration surface for a
dev-only affordance, which is the wrong trade before a tag.

**Gate FL18 (agent-side).** Under `tako dev`: a page response contains
exactly one bar and it carries the id; a fragment response contains
none; a non-HTML response is untouched. `shop`'s htmx suite green.

---

### FL19 — `tako logs` bills its reads to the project it was given

**The finding holds.** Nothing in the tree sets a quota project:
`Client.do` (`pkg/provision/gcp/gcp.go:205`) sets `Content-Type` and
nothing else, so every Google API call is metered against whatever the
ADC file carries. For a fresh `gcloud auth application-default login`
that is the project behind gcloud's own shared OAuth client — shared
with every gcloud user on earth, and rate-limited accordingly. flauta
met HTTP 429 on its first deploy while `gcloud logging read` against
the same project worked, because gcloud bills its own reads correctly.

**The permission objection does not apply here, which makes this
smaller than the plan entry assumed.** `x-goog-user-project` requires
`serviceusage.services.use` on the target — and tako's deployer already
requires `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageViewer` for the preflight
(`preflight.go:116`) and `serviceUsageAdmin` for service agents
(`identity.go:41`). Both include it. A credential that cannot set the
header cannot have reached this code path.

**What ships.** One line in `do`, so it covers every API tako calls
rather than Logging alone:

```go
// Bill this call to the project tako was given, not to whatever
// project minted the ADC credentials — gcloud's default is a shared
// OAuth client, and Logging reads against it are rate-limited across
// every gcloud user on earth.
req.Header.Set("x-goog-user-project", c.Project)
```

Plus one classification so the failure, if it ever comes, is not a bare
403: `Classify` learns the `serviceusage.services.use` denial and names
`roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer` as the remedy, in the same
shape as the four already there.

**Gate FL19 (agent-side).** `fake_test.go` asserts the header on a
representative call from each host; a 403 carrying the serviceusage
denial renders the classified text. Live confirmation belongs to the
next release-cycle walk — the 429 needs a real fresh-ADC machine, which
is exactly what a first-deploy walk is.

### FL15 — a form may repeat a field (`a3753dd`)

`[]string` joins the bindable types for `form:` and `query:`.
`path:` refuses it with its own text — a route segment is one value, so
the shape is one the router can never produce. Neither `string` nor
`[]string` can fail to parse, so `infallibleBinding` replaces an
open-coded `b.Type != "string"` in two places, and the cross-package
call stub uses `qs.Add` per element rather than `Set`, which would
collapse the field it exists for.

journal is the example: the home list gets checkboxes and a bulk
unpublish, with no JavaScript in the seam.

```
$ curl -s localhost:8130/ | grep -o '<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="[a-z0-9]*"'
<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="oghrahdyz7imjcwh"
<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="keagtp7cdwpmg6t6"
<input type="checkbox" name="selected" value="lktxmyme4pyevihv"

$ # tick two of the three
$ curl -s -X POST --data-urlencode "selected=lktx…" --data-urlencode "selected=keag…" …
status=303 location=http://localhost:8130/

$ # before: Showing 7 of 7 posts
$ curl -s localhost:8130/ | grep -o "Showing [0-9]* of [0-9]* posts"
Showing 5 of 5 posts
```

Two ticked, two unpublished. **One-of-two is what the old shape
produced**, and it looked like success — which is why the count is the
assertion.

Both refusals, on a real app rather than a fixture:

```
$ go run ../../cmd/tako gen graph
tako: app.go:190:2: field Year: path:-tagged fields cannot be []string — a route segment is one value; a field that repeats binds with query: or form: (tako/bind-type)
app.go:279:2: field Weird: form:-tagged fields must be string, []string, bool, int, int64, or float64; got []int (tako/bind-type)
```

The generated decode is the line the harness writes by hand:

```go
func decodeUnpublish(r *http.Request) (journal.UnpublishReq, error) {
	var req journal.UnpublishReq
	req.Selected = runtime.FormStrings(r, "selected")
	return req, nil
}
```

No `var err error`, because nothing here can fail.

**Two things surfaced while wiring the example, both fixed in this
commit because the suite was red without them.** journal's page harness
never registered the status page FL11 added, so every 404 in the
example fell back to plain text — the example suite has been red on
main since FL11 and nothing said so. And `TestServerErrorsStayPlain`
asserted the pre-FL11 rule; the reasoning survives (renderStatus
recovers a failing status page, pinned in `pkg/runtime/status_test.go`),
so the test now asserts the half an example owes: the declared page is
reached, and reaching it leaks neither the handler's error nor the
chrome.

### FL16 — the readiness probe proves it reached this child (`1d231c3`)

The filed entry asked tako to bind before printing `ready`. **tako dev
never binds; the child does** — so the fix is identity, not ordering.
The loop mints a per-start nonce, passes it as `TAKO_DEV_NONCE`, and
accepts readiness only from a listener that answers `GET /_tako/z/dev`
with that value.

```
$ # journal already serving on 8130
$ cd examples/blog && PORT=8130 /tmp/tako dev
  starting    http://localhost:8130
  …
tako: serve: port 8130 is already in use by another process — set PORT (e.g. PORT=8090 tako dev) or free it (`lsof -i :8130`)
tako: the service exited during startup
exit=1

$ grep -c "^ready in" /tmp/v2.log
0
```

No `ready` line, non-zero exit, and the child's own error last. Before
this the same run printed `ready in 590ms` and then served the OTHER
app's pages to the browser.

Two things came with it. Nothing watched the child, so a service that
died at once still cost the full five-second timeout; `startApp` now
owns the single `Wait` and publishes it as a channel that both
`waitReady` and `stopApp` read. And the probe is tako talking to
itself, so `logRequests` skips it — without that it put a request
nobody made in the dev console and a sample nobody served in
`request_ms`, once per start:

```
GET /_tako/z/dev → 200 (0.0ms)     ← before
(nothing)                          ← after
```

`http.go:168` already carried the comment for this failure mode — *"a
collision here answers requests with SOMEONE ELSE'S responses"* — which
is what the readiness probe had been doing from the other side.

### FL17 — a blob carries its headers, and so does a stylesheet (`fc31684`)

The filed entry is the blob half. **The read found a second instance
the app could not see**: `securityHeaders` is the only writer of
nosniff, and the site handler called it inside an HTML-only branch, so
every `.css`, `.js` and `.txt` it served went out without one — while
`contentTypeOf`'s comment fifty lines below said *"nosniff is set —
types must be right"*.

```
$ curl -s -i localhost:8130/assets/css/site.9f86d081.css | grep -i '^content-type\|^x-content\|^cache-control'
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Content-Type: text/css; charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff        ← was absent

$ curl -s -i localhost:8130/ | grep -i '^x-content\|^content-security'
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
```

CSP stays HTML-only: it describes a document's privileges and a
stylesheet has none.

`Route.MaxAge` reaches blobs. `BlobHandler` already took
`HandlerOption` and already built a `handlerConf` — it never read
`conf.maxAge` — and codegen gated `CacheFor` on `Kind == "page"`, so a
blob route declaring MaxAge had it dropped on the way to the generated
main. Both ends are wired:

```go
// gallery, generated
mux.Handle("GET /api/photos/{id}/thumb", runtime.BlobHandler(gallery.Thumb, decodeThumb, runtime.CacheFor(86400)))
```

The test is **a table with one row per KIND of response** — page, page
with MaxAge, fragment, HTML site file, non-HTML site file,
fingerprinted asset, blob, blob with MaxAge, status page, plain-text
status floor. Per-feature tests could not catch either gap, because
each writer was right about the case it was written for; what was
missing was the comparison. Verified by reverting both fixes:

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryResponseKindCarriesItsHeaders/site_file,_not_HTML
        X-Content-Type-Options = "", want "nosniff"
--- FAIL: TestEveryResponseKindCarriesItsHeaders/site_file,_fingerprinted
--- FAIL: TestEveryResponseKindCarriesItsHeaders/blob
        Cache-Control = "", want "no-cache"
--- FAIL: TestEveryResponseKindCarriesItsHeaders/blob_with_MaxAge
```

### FL18 — the dev bar behaves (`3c29f50`)

Two entries, one task. The bar could not tell a page from an htmx
partial — a fragment has no `</body>`, so it landed at the END of
whatever was swapped in. The runtime already knew one layer down, where
`securityHeaders` branches on `fragment`; that signal now reaches the
bar through a context pointer set by `WithDevBar` and refined inside
the handler, which is the `routeLabel` pattern and for the same reason.

```
$ curl -s localhost:8130/ | grep -o 'id="tako-dev-bar"'
id="tako-dev-bar"

$ curl -s -H "HX-Request: true" -X POST -d "title=fragcheck&…" localhost:8130/p
<article class="card">
  <a href="/p/ljh5vzxv6n3s4xpk">fragcheck</a> <time>2026-08-08</time>
</article>
$ grep -c "tako-dev-bar" /tmp/frag.html
0
```

Skipping injection must not mean skipping the body, so the fragment
path writes its buffer through — asserted, because a middleware that
silently swallows a response is a worse bug than the one it fixed.

The id is the other half: the app that filed this resorted to finding
"the fixed-position child of `<body>` holding a `dev_user` control",
because inline styles are nothing to target. `#tako-dev-bar { display:
none }` is now a supported thing to write, and `reference/auth.md` says
so.

### FL19 — calls are billed to the project they were given (`476c7a0`)

**The proposal treated the permission as the hard part; it is not.**
`serviceusage.services.use` is included in `serviceUsageViewer` (the
preflight's enabled-API check) and in `serviceUsageAdmin` (service
agents), so a credential that cannot set the header cannot have reached
this code. One header in `do()`, covering every call rather than
Logging alone.

It is listed in `tako-cloud-permissions.md` anyway, with its own

meet a 403 naming a service nobody asked tako to touch:

```
cannot bill API calls to p — grant: gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding p --member user:$(gcloud config get account) --role roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer
```

The header test asserts across hosts rather than on one call — the
header is set in `do()` for everything, so a future call site reaching
past `do()` is how this silently comes back. Reverted to check it

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryCallIsBilledToTheTargetProject
    POST logging.googleapis.com/v2/entries:list billed to "", want the target project "p"
    GET run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/p/… billed to "", want the target project "p"
```

## AB1–AB4 — DX proposals: the abstraction review (2026-08-09) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Four tasks from `docs/tako-agent-plan.md` Stage 13. The question the
owner asked is not the friction question: not *what did flauta hit*, but
*what has flauta built that a second tako app would build again*. So
the read went at flauta's code shape (`flautas@2d23ca8`, 25,563 lines of
Go) rather than at its friction log, and every finding below was
verified against this tree at `5e2ca3a`.

**Each ships behind its own gate.** They are presented together because
the ordering argument only makes sense read together: AB1 and AB2 are
coupled, and AB4 is a rider on AB1.

Six more candidates were considered and **not** promoted — a store-side
audit stamp is refused outright, because flauta's `stampMedia` split
exists precisely to undo the bug an automatic stamp causes. The table
with each verdict is in the plan; the reasoning is not repeated here.

---

### AB1 — authorization is declared, not repeated 49 times

**The finding.** `requireEditor(ctx)` appears at **49 call sites across
12 files** in flauta, `renderNoAccess` at 48. Every admin handler opens
with the same four lines:

```go
func adminHome(ctx tako.Ctx, req AdminListReq) (tako.HTML, error) {
	u, ok := requireEditor(ctx)
	if !ok {
		return renderNoAccess(ctx, u)
	}
	// ... the handler
}
```

tako authenticates (`Route{SignIn: true}`, 54 of flauta's 66 routes) and
stops there. Authorization has no seam, so it lives in handler bodies —
which means:

- **it is invisible to every tool.** `tako gen graph` cannot say which
  routes are guarded by what; `tako deploy --plan` prints 🔒 for
  authentication and nothing for authorization. "Which of my 66 routes
  can a stranger reach" is not a question the framework can answer.
- **it is enforced by care.** Nothing refuses a new admin route that
  forgets the preamble. flauta's answer is that four of its handlers
  delegate to shared helpers (`lifecycle`, `bulkAct`) which guard once —
  good practice that also means the guard's presence cannot be read off
  the handler.
- **a refusal cannot say which refusal it is.** flauta had to invent
  `noAccessReason` — a sentinel *string* — because tako's CSRF rejection
  is also a 403, and a signed-in editor who trips CSRF must not be told
  they are at the wrong door (`admin.go`, M3-12).

**What ships.** A policy is a declared record like every other tako
resource — a package-level var, a constructor, no side effects:

```go
// flauta, admin.go — the rule stays the app's, all of it
var Editors = tako.Policy(editorAllowed)

func editorAllowed(ctx tako.Ctx, u tako.User) error {
	if !cfg.IsEditor(u.Email) {
		return tako.Deny("that address is not on the editor list for this site")
	}
	if !providerAllowed(u) {
		return tako.Deny("editors sign in with Google; this session came from a password")
	}
	return nil
}
```

and a route says which door it is behind:

```go
var (
	AdminHome        = tako.Page("GET /admin", adminHome, tako.Route{Allow: Editors})
	AdminArticleSave = tako.Page("POST /admin/articles/{slug}", adminArticleSave, tako.Route{Allow: Editors})
	AdminMediaUpload = tako.API("POST /admin/media/upload", adminMediaUpload, tako.Route{Allow: Editors})
)
```

49 preambles become 49 route fields the analyzer can read, and every
handler starts with its own work.

**`Allow` implies `SignIn`.** A policy takes a `User`, so a route
carrying one is authenticated by construction; `SignIn: true` beside it
is redundant, not an error. `ctx.User()` is guaranteed past the policy
exactly as it is past `SignIn`.

**A policy is enforced by `Endpoint.Call` too, and that is the load-
bearing decision.** The generated mount is not the only way into a
handler: `Endpoint.Call` is the in-package call, the test path, and the
cross-service RPC. If a policy were mount-only then

- every test that calls `AdminSave.Call(ctx, req)` would stop seeing the
  authorization it sees today (flauta's guard is in the body, so its
  tests do exercise it) — a regression dressed as a feature, and
- a **cross-service call would bypass the callee's authorization
  entirely**, which is the one place a trust boundary is actually
  crossed.

So `Call` evaluates the policy first and returns the denial as an error
(`tako.Errorf(403, …)`), while the mount renders it as a page through the
app's `StatusPage`. Same rule, two audiences.

This exposes an existing inconsistency: `Call` does not enforce
`SignIn` either — a `SignIn` route called with an anonymous Ctx reaches
`ctx.User()` and **panics**. AB1 fixes that in passing: `Call` on a
`SignIn`-or-`Allow` route with no user returns a 401 error rather than
panicking. Cheap, and it is the same seam.

**`Status` gains one field**, which retires flauta's sentinel string:

```go
type Status struct {
	Code      int
	Path      string
	RequestID string
	Message   string
	// Policy names the declared policy that refused this request —
	// "Editors" — and is empty for every status tako answers on its
	// own account, CSRF included. A 403 from your policy and a 403
	// from a stale form are different problems with different
	// remediations, and this is how a status page tells them apart.
	Policy string
}
```

**Error texts.** `tako.Deny(msg)` is the refusal constructor: it is a
403 whose message is public by declaration, so a policy author is never
tempted to hand `Status.Message` an internal error. A policy that returns
a non-`Deny` error is a **500**, not a 403 — a store read that failed
while deciding is not a decision — and the message is logged against the
request id, never rendered:

```
tako: policy Editors: entity read failed: context deadline exceeded (request 9f3c…)
```

Analyzer, two new diagnostics with the house format:

```
app.go:118:41: Route.Allow needs a declared policy variable, not a function literal (tako/policy-var)
app.go:118:41: Route.Allow and Route.Private cannot both be set: a policy needs a user, and an IAM-only route has none (tako/policy-private)
```

**Where the code goes.** `Policy`/`PolicyHandle`/`Deny` in a new root
`policy.go`; `Route.Allow` in `config.go` beside `SignIn`; analyzer reads
the var reference the way it already reads `SiteConfig.NotFound`; codegen
emits `runtime.RequirePolicy("Editors", flauta.Editors)` as a third
`HandlerOption` beside `RequireAuth()` and `CacheFor()`
(`pkg/runtime/page.go:39-51`), refusing through the existing
`writeStatus` (`page.go:257`); `Endpoint.Call` (`handlers.go:38`) gains
the same check ahead of the transport lookup. The AppGraph gains
`Route.Policy`, so `tako gen graph` and `--plan` print it.

**The example that demands it.** `journal` — its write routes are
owner-only and it checks ownership inside each handler today, which is
flauta's shape at 1/10th the scale. Its `TestOwnershipAndRevocation`
becomes a policy test, and the guide chapter gains the paragraph the
framework was missing.

**Gate (agent-side).** Golden: the two new analyzer errors at exact
`file:line:col`; the AppGraph carrying the policy per route. Runtime: a
policy refusal renders through the app's status page with `Policy` set,
and CSRF's 403 with it empty. `Call`: denial as an error, and the 401
that used to be a panic. Example suite green with `journal`'s ownership
moved onto the route.

---

### AB2 — an app's real HTTP surface, in its own tests

**The finding, and it is tako's, not flauta's.** Templates compile into
the generated service, so a test that asserts real HTML has to mount the
same handlers the generated main mounts. Nothing in tako offers that, so
apps hand-mirror codegen:

- flauta's `harness_test.go` is **874 lines** — 20 hand-written request
  binders plus 66 `mux.Handle` lines re-typing what
  `.tako/gen/flauta-web/main.go` already emits.
- it drifted **three times in two milestones**: the media blob route
  (M3-10), the status page (M3-12), and **four media write routes that
  no test in the repo drove by any path** — found not by a failure but
  by someone writing a guard (M4-04).
- that guard, `harnessguard_test.go`, **regexes `app.go` against
  `harness_test.go`**, and its own comment explains why it cannot read
  the generated main instead: the file is gitignored and written only by
  `tako dev`/`test`/`deploy`, so a guard that read it would silently
  skip on a clean checkout.
- mount **options** are mirrored by nothing at all. flauta verified this
  by declaring `Route{MaxAge}` on a live route and watching the whole
  suite stay green. `RequireAuth` drift is invisible the same way — and
  after AB1, so is `RequirePolicy`.
- **tako's own acceptance suite has the same 1,052-line file**
  (`examples/journal/pages_test.go`), with `// {$}: exact root, as
  codegen emits` written next to a hand-typed pattern. The framework
  demonstrates the workaround in its own guide.

**What ships.** One method, no new types:

```go
func TestTheAdminDoorIsAPage(t *testing.T) {
	app := tako.NewTestApp(t)
	srv := httptest.NewServer(app.Handler())   // the generated mounts, exactly
	defer srv.Close()

	res, _ := http.Get(srv.URL + "/admin")
	// 401 — through the app's own StatusPage, with its nav and something to click
}
```

`app.Handler()` returns the `http.Handler` **codegen assembled**: every
declared route with its generated binder, `RequireAuth`,
`RequirePolicy`, `CacheFor`, the site handler last, the status page, the
reserved `/_tako/` mux — and no dev bar. Fidelity is by construction
rather than by a second implementation, which is the whole point: a
harness that can disagree with codegen is the bug this closes.

Everything the 874 lines do becomes those two lines, and
`harnessguard_test.go` deletes.

**How it is wired, and the one thing that needs the owner's call.**
Generated code must stay in `.tako/gen/` (decision 3), and a `package
main` file cannot be imported by the app's test. So `tako test` — which
already analyzes and regenerates before running `go test`
(`cmd/tako/main.go:206`) — generates one more file per service,
`.tako/gen/<svc>/harness_test.go` declaring `package <app>`, and runs
`go test -overlay` mapping it into the package directory. The file is
real, human-readable, and lives where generated code lives; the overlay
is what makes it visible to the compiler without writing into the source
tree.

The cost: **`go test ./...` alone cannot see it.** `CLAUDE.md` documents
`go test ./...` as the command, and after this a test using
`app.Handler()` fails under it:

```
tako: app.Handler needs the generated mounts, which `go test` cannot see.
      Run `tako test` (it regenerates first) — or `tako test ./pkg/...`.
```

Two ways to go, and this is the decision to make at approval:

- **(a) `tako test` becomes the documented command** — recommended. It
  exists, it already refreshes generated code, and its output already
  names what it regenerated. `CLAUDE.md`'s Commands block and the
  testing reference change with it.
- **(b) the harness is checked in** — no overlay, no new command story,
  but generated code lands in the app's source tree and decision 3 has
  to be widened. Cheaper today, and it makes a stale checked-in harness
  the exact failure mode we are closing.

**Gate (agent-side).** `journal`'s `pages_test.go` rewritten onto
`app.Handler()` — the assertion is the diff: ~1,052 lines to under 200,
with every existing test preserved and passing. A codegen golden for the
harness file. A test that a route declared and **not** driven by the
suite is still mounted (the four-routes bug, as a positive test). The
unwired error text above, asserted verbatim.

---

### AB3a — a handler can see its client

**The finding.** flauta's `docs/friction.md` has this as its #1 open
entry, and it is the only one the owner flagged "worth asking for".
`tako.Ctx` exposes no request, no headers, no `RemoteAddr`, so the
contact form — the only unauthenticated write path in the product — caps
submissions **site-wide at 30/hour** instead of per sender. flauta wrote
the trade down rather than hiding it: one determined sender can lock the
form for everybody.

**What ships.** One method on `Ctx`, one struct:

```go
// Client is what tako can honestly say about who sent this request.
type Client struct {
	// IP is the caller's address as the platform reports it — the
	// left-most entry of X-Forwarded-For behind Cloud Run, which
	// appends rather than trusts. Empty in a worker, a cron, or a
	// job: there is no client behind those.
	IP string
	// UserAgent is the raw header, unparsed.
	UserAgent string
}

func (c Ctx) Client() Client   // on the interface, beside MaybeUser
```

Deliberately small. No country, no device class, no parsed browser —
each of those is a guess dressed as a fact, and none has an app asking.
`Client{}` in async handlers is the honest zero: a queue message has no
client, and inventing the publisher's would be worse than nothing.

Then flauta's own limiter becomes per-sender, in flauta, where the
policy trade belongs.

**AB3b — `Route{Limit: …}` is designed and blocked, deliberately.** A
declared rate limit needs a counter shared across instances, and
`tako.Cache` is per-instance in-memory even on GCP (`cache.go:11`). A
limit of 5/hour enforced per instance is 100/hour at max=20 — a
framework promise the framework would break, silently, in exactly the
direction that matters. The honest options are a Datastore counter (a
write per request, plus contention on a hot key) or Memorystore (a new
provisioned resource and a VPC connector, which decision 8 keeps as a
later explicit opt-in). That is a backend decision, not a patch, and it
does not block AB3a: with `ctx.Client()` the app can implement the
policy it wants over the store it already has.

**Gate (agent-side).** Runtime: `Client()` populated from a request,
zero in a worker/cron/job Ctx. A test that a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For`
does not become the IP when a trusted hop is present. Conformance: the
zero value is identical local and gcp. `hello` or `shortlink` grows a
line that logs the client, so the guide has somewhere to show it.

---

### AB4 — an app can ask where it is running

**The finding, and it is the one with a security edge.** `admin.go:85`:

```go
func deployed() bool { return os.Getenv("TAKO_BACKEND") == "gcp" }
```

`TAKO_BACKEND` is **tako's private boot switch** (`pkg/runtime/boot.go:30`),
documented nowhere as app surface. flauta reads it at 5 call sites, and
one of them is `editorAllowed`: two dev identities
(`alice@example.test`, `bob@example.test`) are admitted to the admin
**only when that string is not "gcp"**. An app's authorization rule
depends on an undocumented framework env var, and three of flauta's
tests `t.Setenv` it to simulate a deploy.

Any app with a dev seam writes this function. `tako dev`'s own dev bar
mints those identities, so the framework creates the need and then makes
the app guess at the answer.

**What ships.**

```go
// Env is where this process is running. It is a fact about the
// deployment, never a feature flag: use it to decide what a DEV
// affordance may do, not to change what the product is.
type Env int

const (
	EnvLocal Env = iota   // tako dev, tako test, go test
	EnvCloud              // deployed by tako deploy
)

func Environment() Env     // package-level: usable from a constructor
func (e Env) String() string
```

flauta's five call sites become `tako.Environment() == tako.EnvCloud`,
its `deployed()` deletes, and `t.Setenv("TAKO_BACKEND", "gcp")` in three
test files becomes something a test can say out loud. The doc comment
carries the warning that matters: an app that branches its *behaviour*
on this has two products and tests one.

**Why a function and not a `Ctx` method.** `editorAllowed` is pure and
tested without a session; a constructor may want it too. `Ctx` already
carries per-request facts, and this is not one.

**Gate (agent-side).** `EnvLocal` under `NewTestApp` and `tako dev`,
`EnvCloud` with `TAKO_BACKEND=gcp`, and a test pinning that an unknown
value is `EnvLocal` rather than a third state. Docs: `reference/service.md`
gains the paragraph, and the guide's local chapter says the sentence
about not branching the product on it.

---

### What is NOT in this proposal

Listed because a review that only proposes is not a review:

- **A store-side audit stamp is refused.** flauta's `touchMedia` /
  `stampMedia` split exists because an automatic stamp erased the
  uploader on every background write — every processed image in the
  library came out attributed to nobody (M3-08's walk). A store that
  stamps fields the app did not set would ship that bug to every app.
- **Versioned entities are refused.** The framework-shaped kernel inside
  flauta's ~1,000 lines of revision code is optimistic concurrency
  (AB5); the rest is what a CMS is, and decision 11 owns that.
- **A user store, registration and roles wait for AB1.** flauta has no
  user record at all — identity is Identity Platform's, authorization is
  a `config.json` list, and adding an editor is a code edit plus a
  deploy. That is the ask behind "registering users", and the enforcement
  seam has to exist before the store is worth designing. One app's
  requirements are not enough to shape it.
- **Pagination furniture and capability links are parked** with the
  trigger written down: a second app asking.

## AB1 + AB4 — shipped (2026-08-09)

Approved by the owner on 2026-08-09: **AB1 and AB4**, with AB2's wiring
question answered ahead of time (`tako test` + `-overlay`, recorded for
when AB2 runs) and AB3a not in this batch. Two commits, `efcedec` and
`107ac03`.

### AB4 — an app can ask where it is running (`efcedec`)

`tako.Environment()` → `tako.EnvLocal` | `tako.EnvCloud`, plus
`Env.String()`. Anything unrecognised is `EnvLocal`, which is the
direction that costs nothing: a mistyped environment can only turn a
local affordance **off** in production.

Shipped exactly as proposed. Docs: `reference/service.md` gained a
"Where it is running" section, `guide/local.md` a bullet with the
sentence that keeps it honest — a fact about the deployment, never a
feature flag.

**Its example demand arrived with AB1**, as the commit said it would:
journal's moderation door admits `tako dev`'s seeded identities locally
and cannot in the cloud, which is the exact shape flauta reads
`TAKO_BACKEND` for.

### AB1 — authorization is declared (`107ac03`)

Shipped as proposed, with three additions, each called out here rather
than left in the diff:

1. **`tako.IsDenied(err)`** — the caller-side twin of `Status.Policy`.
   `Endpoint.Call` returns a denial as an error, and a caller has to be
   able to tell "you may not" from "it broke" without string-matching.
   Without it the distinction the whole task is about would exist for
   status pages and not for callers.
2. **`tako/unexported-policy`** — not a new concept: `tako.StatusPage`
   has had `unexported-status` since FL11, for the same reason (the
   generated service names it from outside the package).
3. **`Allow` sets `RequiresAuth` in the AppGraph.** "Allow implies
   SignIn" was going to be a doc sentence; making it a fact of the graph
   means codegen emits the 401 gate and every existing rule that reads
   `RequiresAuth` — `cache-signin` above all — sees a guarded route as
   guarded.

**The design decision worth the most.** The policy is evaluated by
`Endpoint.Call`, not by the generated mount. `RequirePolicy(name)`
carries only the NAME, for `Status.Policy`. That gives one enforcement
point for a browser request, an in-package call, a test and a
cross-service call, and it avoids running an app's rule twice per
request when the rule may read the entity store.

A remote hop is the deliberate exception: it does not evaluate the
callee's policy locally, because the rule may read the callee's store
and a caller-side verdict could be confidently wrong in both directions.
The session rides the hop (`X-Tako-Session`) and the callee's own mount
decides.

**Found while building.** A `SignIn` route reached through
`Endpoint.Call` with an anonymous Ctx did not refuse — it reached
`ctx.User()` and **panicked**. Now a 401 error, pinned by
`TestCallOnAGuardedRouteWithNoUserIsA401`.

**A test that lied, caught by mutation.** The first version of
`TestACSRFRefusalDoesNotBorrowThePolicysName` asserted the empty policy
name on a CSRF 403 — and passed with the guard deliberately removed,
because CSRF writes its status directly and never reaches `pageError`.
Rewritten as `TestAnother403OnAGuardedRouteIsNotBlamedOnTheDoor`, whose
first case is a HANDLER's own 403 on a guarded route; that one fails
when the guard is removed:

```
--- FAIL: TestAnother403OnAGuardedRouteIsNotBlamedOnTheDoor
    policy_test.go:140: a handler's own 403 was attributed to the policy:
    "<html>403|policy=Editors|this draft is locked by another editor</html>"
```

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root; all seven example modules green
against `local`:

```
blog ok   gallery ok   hello ok   journal ok
shop ok   shortlink ok   siren ok
```

Analyzer goldens: `testdata/errors/policyshape` (three diagnostics, one
per mistake, exact positions), and journal's AppGraph + summary now
carry the door:

```
GET /moderate → Moderate 🔒 Moderators (app.go:182)
POST /moderate/{id}/retract → Retract 🔒 Moderators (app.go:183)
```

Generated mount, from `.tako/gen/journal/main.go`:

```go
mux.Handle("GET /moderate", runtime.PageHandler(journal.Moderate, nil, runtime.RequireAuth(), runtime.RequirePolicy("Moderators")))
```

Scripted walk `validate/policies.md`, steps 1–2 and 4–7 run. Step 3 also
run **live** against `tako dev` on :8097:

```
--- 1. signed out ---
401
<h2>Sign in first</h2>
Back to the journal
--- 2. signed in as alice (dev bar) ---
303
200
Moderation desk
Signed in as alice@example.test.
```

That walk is also what found journal's missing 401 heading: every other
guarded route in the example is a POST, so until the desk existed nobody
could arrive at a 401 by typing a URL, and the page said "Something went
wrong" about a request that had gone exactly right.

The human walk is batched per the Stage 3 amendment.

### Discovered work

**21. A test still writes `TAKO_BACKEND` to simulate a deploy.** AB4
gave apps a way to READ the environment and no way to SET it under test,
so `journal`'s refusal test does `t.Setenv("TAKO_BACKEND", "gcp")` —
the same private string AB4 removed from app code, now only in tests.
The proposal's gate said exactly this, so it is not a miss; it is the
obvious next inch (a `TestApp` seam, or an exported setter guarded to
tests). Left out of scope.

**22. `Route.Allow` is same-package only.** `resolvePolicy` accepts a
selector expression, but nothing has been built or tested for a policy
declared in another package, and codegen would need that package's
alias. Fine for one door per app; a shared policy across services would
need it.

**23. CLOSED by AB2 (`2845383`) — journal's harness gained two more hand-typed mounts.** Adding the
desk meant re-typing `RequireAuth()` and `RequirePolicy("Moderators")`
into `pages_test.go` to match what codegen emits — which is AB2's
finding, demonstrated once more while AB2 waits. If the harness had
drifted here, every moderation test would have passed against a door
that was not there.

## AB10 — DX proposal: roles, users, and the two registration events (2026-08-09) — AWAITING APPROVAL

AB10 was parked by the abstraction review — "a user store, registration
and roles wait for AB1; one app's requirements are not enough to shape
it". The owner unparked it and made the five shaping decisions on
2026-08-09. This proposal is those decisions turned into surface.

**What is NOT in it**, so the boundary is on the record: flauta's
`config.json` stays flauta's. tako never learns who an editor is. What
it gains is the mechanism — a place for roles, a way for a route to
demand one, an API to grant one, and an event when somebody new arrives.

### The decisions (owner, 2026-08-09)

1. **Roles live in Identity Platform custom claims** in the cloud. Local
   is the same contract over a local store, because there is no
   Identity Platform on a laptop — the choice is about the cloud source
   of truth, not about avoiding a store.
2. **A route demands a role through AB1's policy seam**: `tako.Role` +
   `tako.RequireRole`, feeding `Route{Allow: …}`. No second
   authorization mechanism.
3. **tako owns creation and roles; recovery stays Identity Platform's.**
   Password reset and email verification use its hosted flows. tako
   sends no email, ever.
4. **Both registration events**: `auth.Registered` (tako made the
   account) and `auth.FirstSignIn` (tako met the person).
5. **A role change marks the session stale**; the next request refreshes
   the claims once and rewrites the session. No sign-out.

### The constraint that shaped 4

A true Identity-Platform-side registration hook is **not reachable from
a Cloud-Run-only framework**. `beforeCreate` blocking functions support
**Gen1 Cloud Functions only**, and Firebase Auth create/delete triggers
are 1st-gen only — 2nd gen does not support auth triggers, so there is
no Eventarc path to a Cloud Run service. tako would have to provision a
Node function, against its own standing non-goals.

So the two events are named for what tako can honestly observe. The gap
they do not cover — an account created in the console and never used —
is documented rather than papered over.

---

### The surface

```go
var (
	auth = tako.Auth(tako.AuthConfig{Google: true, Password: true})

	// Roles are declared, so a typo is an analysis error rather than a
	// door that never opens. The string is what lands in the claim.
	Editor    = tako.Role("editor")
	Moderator = tako.Role("moderator")

	// AB1's seam, with a constructor for the common case. Any-of.
	Editors = tako.RequireRole(Editor, Moderator)
)

var AdminHome = tako.Page("GET /admin", adminHome, tako.Route{Allow: Editors})
```

`tako.User` gains the roles it arrived with:

```go
u := ctx.User()
u.Roles              // []string{"editor"}
u.HasRole(Editor)    // true
```

Managing accounts, from Go:

```go
users := auth.Users()   // a handle, like a bucket

u, err := users.Create(ctx, tako.NewUser{
	Email:    "ana@example.com",
	Password: pw,            // optional: omit for a Google-only account
	Name:     "Ana",
	Roles:    []string{Editor.Name()},
})

err = users.Grant(ctx, u.ID, Moderator)
err = users.Revoke(ctx, u.ID, Editor)
err = users.Disable(ctx, u.ID)      // sign-in refused, record kept
err = users.Delete(ctx, u.ID)

u, err  = users.ByEmail(ctx, "ana@example.com")
page, _ := users.List(ctx).Limit(50).Page("")
```

And the two events, exactly like a bucket's:

```go
var (
	OnRegistered  = tako.Subscribe(auth.Registered, seedProfile)
	OnFirstSignIn = tako.Subscribe(auth.FirstSignIn, welcome)
)

func welcome(ctx tako.Ctx, u tako.User) error { … }
```

### How the pieces actually work

**Claims.** Roles ride in one custom claim, `{"roles": ["editor"]}`.
`Grant`/`Revoke` read-modify-write, because Identity Platform's
`setCustomUserClaims` replaces the whole blob and an app may keep claims
of its own there. Two concurrent grants are a lost update, so the
read-modify-write runs under a per-uid `tako.Lock` — the primitive is
already there.

**The 1000-byte cap is real** and it is the framework's job to fail
legibly rather than let Identity Platform reject a write:

```
tako: roles for ana@example.com do not fit Identity Platform's 1000-byte custom-claims
      limit (14 roles, 1043 bytes) — a role is a name, not a payload
```

**Staleness (decision 5), without paying a read per request.** Session
records gain `UID` as an index and a `Stale` flag. `Grant`/`Revoke` query
that user's sessions and set the flag — usually one write, often zero.
The per-request session lookup already happens, so a stale session costs
exactly one admin-API read, once, on the first request after a change;
steady state is unchanged. A user with no live session needs nothing:
their next sign-in mints from fresh claims anyway.

**Local is the same contract.** `tako dev` and `tako test` keep users in
the local entity store with roles on the record. `app.SignIn("alice",
Editor)` is how a test says who somebody is. The conformance suite gets
a `users` case, so local and gcp cannot drift — a role granted must be
visible to the next request on both.

### Cloud errors & permissions

Per the standing rule for anything that touches GCP.

`auth.Users()` needs `roles/identitytoolkit.admin` on the project, and
tako derives it **from usage**, the way a bucket's grant is derived: a
service that only reads (`Get`, `ByEmail`, `List`) gets
`roles/identitytoolkit.viewer`; one that writes (`Create`, `Grant`,
`Revoke`, `Disable`, `Delete`) gets the admin role. A service whose
package never mentions `Users()` gets neither, so "this app can mint
accounts" stays a property of the app that asked.

`docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md` grows one deployer line
(`roles/identitytoolkit.admin` to grant it onward) and one runtime row.

Four failures, four different remediations:

```
403  tako: creating a user needs roles/identitytoolkit.admin on <project> for
     <sa> — tako deploy grants it to services that declare auth.Users(); re-run
     tako deploy if this service started using it since the last one

403  tako: the Identity Platform API is not enabled on <project> — enable
     identitytoolkit.googleapis.com (tako deploy does this; this service is
     running against a project it did not provision)

404  tako: no user with that id in <project>

400  tako: <email> already has an account — Users.Create refuses to take over an
     existing identity; use Users.ByEmail then Grant
```

### Analyzer

```
app.go:22:19: tako.Role takes a string constant — the role name is read at analysis
              time so a route's door can be named in the graph (tako/const-role)
app.go:24:11: tako.RequireRole needs at least one role (tako/empty-role)
app.go:22:5:  role editor must be exported — the generated service names it from
              outside the package; rename it Editor (tako/unexported-role)
```

`tako gen graph` prints the door with its roles, extending AB1's line:

```
GET /admin → AdminHome 🔒 Editors (editor, moderator) (app.go:118)
```

### Slices, each its own gate

1. **AB10a — roles you can enforce.** `tako.Role`, `tako.RequireRole`,
   `User.Roles`/`HasRole`, claims decoded at sign-in, roles on local dev
   identities, `app.SignIn(name, roles…)`. No admin API yet — roles are
   set in the console or the local store. journal's `moderators` slice
   becomes a role. **This is the slice that pays for itself first.**
2. **AB10b — the admin API.** `auth.Users()` and its verbs, over
   identitytoolkit REST and the local store, with the derived grants,
   the conformance case, the lock, and the stale-session refresh.
3. **AB10c — local password sign-in.** `/_tako/api/session` accepts
   email+password locally against the local store when
   `AuthConfig{Password: true}` is declared. **Named as its own slice
   because it is the biggest hidden cost in the whole proposal**:
   without it, `Users.Create(email, password)` creates something a
   laptop cannot sign in as, and the local half of the contract is a
   stub. It is also where password hashing enters tako.
4. **AB10d — the two events.** `auth.Registered`, `auth.FirstSignIn` as
   `EventSource[tako.User]`, the first-sight bookkeeping behind the
   second, and the note that a Google sign-up fires both within a
   second — so a handler bound to both must be idempotent.

### The line this crosses, deliberately

`reference/auth.md` currently says, under "Not yet": *"No roles and no
user store."* AB10 reverses it. Decision 11 is untouched — roles are not
a CMS primitive, and an admin screen for them is still just a site.

## AB10a — shipped (2026-08-09)

Approved by the owner on 2026-08-09: **start with AB10a, keep AB10c in**
(local password sign-in stays in the plan rather than being cut). One
commit, `e635c5a`.

Shipped as proposed. The surface, in full:

```go
var Moderator  = tako.Role("moderator")
var Moderators = tako.RequireRole(Moderator)   // any-of; returns a *PolicyHandle

u.Roles            // []string, off the session record
u.HasRole(Moderator)

app.SignIn("ana", Moderator)   // a test says who somebody is
```

### What the build decided that the proposal left open

**Roles are collected before anything else in the analyzer pass.** A
policy may be declared above the role it names, and `RequireRole`
resolves its arguments at analysis time, so roles get their own loop
ahead of the resource loop — the same "declaration order never matters"
property every other constructor has.

**`RequireRole`'s mismatch got its own rule id, `tako/role-var`.** It
first reported as `policy-var`, whose text is about a policy that is not
a declared var — true but confusing when the thing that is not declared
is a role. Rule ids are UX.

**The refusal names the role**: `this page needs the moderator role`, or
`… the editor or moderator role` for any-of. A role name is not a secret,
and "not authorized" is the message that sends somebody to ask a question
nobody can answer.

**Ticking, not granting, is the local affordance.** The dev sign-in page
renders a checkbox per declared role (`RegisterRoles`, emitted by
codegen). The alternative — every dev session holds every declared role
— was rejected: it makes the refusal path unreachable in dev, which is
the half of authorization worth walking.

### Found while building

**Four handlers rebuilt `tako.User` from a session record, field by
field** (`blob.go`, `http.go`, `page.go`, `status.go`). Adding `Roles`
meant editing four places, and the one nobody edited would have dropped
it — a bug that does not fail, it just quietly refuses somebody at a
door. Collapsed into `sessionRecord.user()`, with the reason in the doc
comment.

**journal's `tako.Environment()` use was retired and replaced in the same
commit.** The `.test`-suffix escape hatch AB1 gave it is exactly what a
role makes unnecessary, so removing it was right — but it was also AB4's
only example demand. Its replacement is better: the refusal page tells a
LOCAL visitor how to grant themselves the role, and says nothing of the
kind deployed. That is what `Environment()`'s own doc comment says it is
for, and `TestTheDevHintIsLocalOnly` pins both halves.

**A stale child from the AB1 walk held the entity-store lock**, so the
first live attempt answered `500 session store error` on every dev
sign-in. Not a tako defect: the earlier `pkill` patterns never matched
those processes. Checked rather than assumed — killing the parent was
confirmed to kill the child, so `guide/local.md`'s "no orphaned binaries
holding the entity-store lock" claim holds.

```
POST /moderate/{id}/retract → Retract 🔒 Moderators (moderator) (app.go:190)
```


## AB10b + AB10c — shipped (2026-08-09)

The owner said "do both", AB10b first because it defines the store
AB10c signs into. Commits `21c6af6` and `bab1a20`.

Shipped as proposed. The REST shapes were checked against Google's
reference before a line was written, because a fake server built from
memory would have enshrined whatever was misremembered:
`accounts:signUp` (create, with `targetProjectId` under a service-account
credential), `projects/{p}/accounts:lookup`, `:update`, `:delete`,
`:batchGet`, and `roles/identitytoolkit.admin` as the IAM role.

### The design that changed while building

**`RequirePolicy` carries a name; `Users.SetRoles` replaces wholesale.**
The backend contract offers no add/remove, because Identity Platform
offers none — `setCustomUserClaims` replaces the entire claims blob. A
contract promising a finer operation would be lying about one of its
backends. Grant and Revoke are read-modify-write ON TOP of it, in one
place, under a lease keyed on the account.

**The grant is matched on the receiver's TYPE.** `users := auth.Users()`
puts a local variable between the declaration and the call, and the edge
scan resolves resource VARS. Matching `*tako.UsersHandle` instead needs
no dataflow analysis and cannot be defeated by renaming the local.

### Two fidelity gaps the build found, both local-vs-cloud

**A dev sign-in minted a session with no account** — which the cloud
cannot do, because Identity Platform holds the account and issues the
token. So `auth.Users().List()` was empty while somebody was
demonstrably signed in, and journal's new admin screen worked deployed
and was **inert on a laptop**. Found by walking it, not by a test. A dev
sign-in now upserts the account, and the ticked roles are the local
grant.

**Email matching had to be case-insensitive on both.** Identity Platform
lower-cases addresses; the local store did not, so a duplicate would
have been refused in the cloud and accepted locally. Pinned as its own
conformance case.

### The guard that made a decision for us

`TestEveryCustomMethodPostIsClassified` (P2's retry-safety guard) refused
to let four new colon-methods through unclassified, and it was right to
ask:

- `:signUp` — **not retried.** A retry after a response tako never saw
  makes a second account under a second id, and the duplicate-address
  check does not catch it because the first write succeeded.
- `:update`, `:delete` — idempotent (set-to-value; deleting twice is
  success).
- `:batchGet` — a POST-shaped read.

### AB10c, and why it is not optional

Without it `Create(email, password)` produces an account a laptop cannot
sign in as. The branch is local-only by construction (`isLocalBackend`),
so password verification never runs in a deployed service — in the cloud
the browser posts credentials to Identity Platform and tako only sees
the resulting token. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 from the standard library, per
the "no new dependency" rule.

Every refusal is the same sentence — wrong password, unknown address,
disabled account. Pinned by a test that compares the two bodies rather
than just their statuses.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root; all seven examples green. Conformance
`-backend=local -run TestUsers` green: create/read, email taken,
case-insensitivity, roles round-trip, the 1000-byte ceiling, disable,
delete, paging.

**The gcp conformance chapter is skipped, deliberately and loudly.**
Identity Platform accounts are project-scoped — there is no namespace to
throw away — so running it would create and delete real accounts in
whatever project is configured. The wire is covered instead by
`pkg/backends/gcp/users_test.go` against a fake identitytoolkit, which
pins the two shapes invisible locally: `customAttributes` is a JSON
string nested in the JSON body, and setting it replaces the whole blob
(the test grants a role to an account carrying `{"tenant":"acme"}` and
asserts the tenant survives).

Live walk on :8099, the whole point of the slice in four lines:

```
bob GET /moderate -> 403
alice POST /people/u_40358fc5babc6fa2/role (on=1) -> 303
bob GET /moderate -> 200      # same session, no re-sign-in
bob GET /moderate -> 403      # after the revoke
```

Derived grants, from the graph rather than from a table someone
maintains:

```
{'from': 'journal.Moderate', 'to': 'auth', 'to_kind': 'auth', 'verb': 'read'}
{'from': 'journal.SetRole',  'to': 'auth', 'to_kind': 'auth', 'verb': 'write'}
```

Scripted walk: `validate/policies.md` steps 12–18. The human walk is
batched per the Stage 3 amendment.

### Discovered work

**27. FIXED (`cf7ee64`). The analyzer did not catch two declared routes
that Go's mux refuses to order.** `POST /moderate/people/{id}` beside `POST
/moderate/{id}/retract` is a startup panic, and it was found by running
the example's tests rather than by analysis — `tako/site-shadow` covers
the site handler, and nothing covers route-vs-route. The app-side fix
was to pick a different shape (`POST /people/{id}/role`), which is
exactly the kind of decision a diagnostic should be making at build
time. Same class as FL5.

**28. shop's harness called `SessionHandler()` with no providers**, so
its tests ran against a shop with no password door while codegen emits
`SessionHandler("email")`. Fixed in AB10c's commit; it is AB2's finding
for the third time, now with a security shape — a harness that forgets a
provider tests an app whose doors differ from the deployed one's.

**29. No `tako users` CLI.** Creating the first account in a deployed
project needs a Go call from inside a service, or the Identity Platform
console. `tako users create --role editor` is the obvious companion to
`tako logs`, and would also give AB10d's `Registered` event a second
producer.

**30. Roles are never garbage-collected from the claims blob.** A role
an app stops declaring stays on every account that holds it, invisible
except through `Users.List`. Harmless today; a `tako.Role` that no
longer exists is a name nothing will ever check.

## AB10d — shipped (2026-08-09), and AB10 closed

Commit `d4a86e2`. The last of the four slices; AB10 is complete.

Shipped as proposed, with the constraint stated in the proposal now
enforced by the shape of the code: both events are things **tako itself
does**, so neither is a guess. There is no Identity-Platform-side
registration event and there cannot be one from Cloud Run — blocking
functions and Firebase Auth triggers are Gen1 Cloud Functions only.

### What the build decided

**One constant, not two.** The source names are topic names shared by
the SDK (which publishes `Registered`) and `pkg/runtime` (which
publishes `FirstSignIn`). The first draft duplicated them with a comment
explaining why that was acceptable; it was not. They live in
`internal/hooks` now — app-invisible, single-source.

**The marker is written before the publish.** `FirstSignIn` needs to
know whether tako has seen an identity, which is one `_tako_seen` record
per person, ever. Writing it first means a crash between the two loses
the announcement rather than repeating it forever. That is the right way
round, and it is a choice rather than an accident: a missed welcome is a
gap somebody notices; a loop that re-announces on every sign-in looks
like a feature until the emails pile up.

**Both publishes are best-effort.** A subscriber must never be able to
fail the act that triggered it. In particular, a `Create` that reported
failure *after* creating the account would invite the caller to retry
and make a second one.

**Provisioning follows the bucket-event pattern** rather than inventing
one: a subscribed event gets a topic, and publish is granted to whoever
can actually publish — route-serving services for `FirstSignIn` (they
serve the session endpoint), account-writing services for `Registered`
(the same edge that earns `identitytoolkit.admin`).

### The examples are the argument

**journal: the first person ever to sign in becomes the moderator.** The
desk that hands out the role is behind the role, so the first one cannot
be appointed from inside the app — this is a real bootstrap problem with
a real answer, and it is four lines. `appointFounder` is idempotent
because an event is delivered at least once.

**shop: creating an account opens a customer record** with 500 credits,
read back through `/api/me`. Nothing in the create path knows the shop
has customers.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root; all seven examples green. Live on
:8102 against a deleted `.tako/data`:

```
alice (first ever, ticking nothing) → GET /moderate -> 200
bob   (second)                      → GET /moderate -> 403
appointing the founding moderator subscriber=OnFirstSignIn email=alice@example.test
```

The founder test was mutation-checked: removing the subscriber
registration from the harness fails it with `the founder was refused:
403`, so it is testing the event and not the door.

Scripted walk: `validate/policies.md` steps 19–21. The human walk is
batched per the Stage 3 amendment.

### Discovered work

**31. ADDRESSED by AB2 (`2845383`) for journal; still true for the other five examples (see 33). Two example harnesses were missing mounts codegen emits** — the
subscriber registration in both, and `GET /api/me` in shop's, which had
never been mounted at all, so nothing had ever driven it. Both found by
writing a test that needed them. AB2's finding for the fourth and fifth
time, and the strongest argument yet for building it.

**32. A test that calls `tako.NewTestApp` twice reads two different
stores.** `NewTestApp` rebinds the package-level backend hooks, so a
second call inside a test that already booted a server silently points
later reads at a fresh empty store. It cost a wrong "the record was
never created" diagnosis here. Worth either a refusal (a second
`NewTestApp` in one test) or a doc line.

## AB2 — shipped (2026-08-09)

Commit `2845383`. The last open item of the abstraction review, and the
one with the most evidence behind it: three separate slices this session
added hand-typed mounts to an example harness, and item 31 in this log
counted it the fifth sighting.

Shipped as proposed, with the wiring the owner chose on 2026-08-09:
`tako test` + `-overlay`, and `tako test` as the documented command for
an app.

### The property, not the copy

`main.go` and the harness are emitted by **one function**
(`writeMounts`). `TestTheHarnessMountsWhatTheMainMounts` then compares
the two generated files route by route AND option by option
(`RequireAuth`, `RequirePolicy`, `CacheFor`) — so the guard asserts a
property rather than policing a duplicate. Contrast the app-side guard
this replaces, which had to **regex `app.go` against `harness_test.go`**
because there was nothing better to compare, and could not see options
at all.

### Three defects it found in itself

All three from running it against the seven examples rather than
reasoning about it:

1. **Two packages in one directory.** The harness declares the app's
   package and sat beside `main.go`, so `go build ./.tako/gen/<svc>` —
   which the image build does — failed with "found packages main and
   hello". Caught by `TestImageDigestIsDeterministic`, not by anything I
   wrote. It gets a `harness/` subdirectory.
2. **A package name is not a path segment.** hello's module is
   `tako-example-hello`, so `path.Base` emitted `package
   tako-example-hello`, which parses as `package tako` and then fails on
   the dash. `pkgAlias` already reads the name off a declaration, which
   is where it is actually written down.
3. **An exclusion filter that had been wrong all along.** `writeMounts`
   skipped worker/subscribe/cron by name, missing `singleton` and `job`.
   Invisible in `main.go` (Generate routes those services elsewhere) and
   fatal in a harness generated for every service — it mounted shop's
   singleton as a JSON endpoint. Now a positive filter: routes only.

### What the harness deliberately leaves out

`runtime.Boot` (NewTestApp booted the backends), the async registrations
(NewTestApp wires every worker and subscriber from the declarations —
double-registering would deliver twice), and the dev bar. journal's
founder test switched from `runtime.WaitIdle` to `app.DrainQueues()`
because of exactly that: the barrier belongs to whoever owns the
dispatcher.

Routes an app does NOT declare are not in there either, by definition.
journal's three runtime-contract routes (a redirect, a permanent
redirect, a handler that fails) mount through `serveWith`, on the same
origin because a session-bound CSRF token is only valid there. An app
should not carry a `/boom` route so that tako can test its 500 page.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root — the framework's own command is
unchanged. All seven examples green under `tako test`. Goldens for the
harness of journal (site + auth + role + policy + cacheable route) and
shop (API-only, no site — the shape that would break if the site block
were assumed).

The message a stale habit meets:

```
tako: app.Handler needs the generated mounts, which `go test` cannot see.
      Run `tako test` (it regenerates first) — or `tako test ./pkg/...` for a subset.
```

Scripted walk: `validate/harness.md`. The human walk is batched per the
Stage 3 amendment.

gallery, shop, shortlink, siren and blog still hand-mounted their

opt-in per app, which is right for shipping it, and leaves five examples
