## AB3a — shipped (2026-08-09), and Stage 13 closed

Commit `5da0324`. The last promoted item of the abstraction review.

`ctx.Client()` returns `{IP, UserAgent}` and nothing else. The IP rule is
the whole of the care:

```
X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.7, 130.211.0.1  →  203.0.113.7
```

Google's frontend APPENDS to the header rather than replacing it, so the
left-most entry is the caller's claim about itself. tako counts from the
right past the one hop it provisions; a list shorter than that did not
come through those hops and is ignored in favour of the socket. Five
cases are pinned, including a forgery split across two headers.

Zero in a worker, cron, job and subscriber. Carried on all four REQUEST
paths — page, JSON, blob, status — because a fact that depended on which
route kind you declared would be worse than no fact.

`Route{Limit: …}` stays unbuilt, now documented in `reference/api.md`
rather than only in this log: it needs a cross-instance counter, and
`tako.Cache` is per-instance in memory even in the cloud.

shortlink's test drives the app through `app.Handler()`, which is **AB2
paying for itself in the same session it shipped** — a header is a
request fact, and `Endpoint.Call` has no request.

### Discovered work — and one of these is serious

**35. FIXED (`cf7ee64`). `tako dev` was broken for any app without auth,
buckets or crons — including `hello`.**

The readiness probe (FL16) GETs `/_tako/dev` and compares a per-run
nonce. That route is only mounted when the generated main builds the
reserved mux, and codegen builds one only when `hasAuth || hasBucket ||
hasCron`. So `hello` and `shortlink` never mount it, the probe reads
404, and `probe` returns `("", nil)` — which `waitReady`'s switch treats
as **someone else's server**:

```
tako: port 8119 is answering, but not with this app — another process has it.
Set PORT (e.g. PORT=8090 tako dev) or free it (`lsof -i :8119`)
```

**Measured, watching the port through a start** (`hello`, PORT=8120):
the listener throughout is **tako's OWN CHILD**, up and serving
`/hello` with 200 — and at t=6s it is gone, because `tako dev` killed
the healthy service it had just started.

*(An earlier version of this entry pasted a probe column taken against
`/_tako/dev`. The readiness path is `/_tako/z/dev`, so that column would
have read 404 whatever the child did and proved nothing. The finding
does not rest on it: the child could not answer the probe on ANY path,
because `answerDevReady` was only reachable through `runtime.Reserved`
and `hello`'s generated main is `runtime.Serve(mux)` — no Reserved. What
proves it is the before and after: `tako dev` on `hello` failed, and
after the fix it prints `ready in 905ms` and serves.)*

That also makes the error actively misleading: it tells you to free the
port, and by the time you run `lsof` the child is dead and the port is
empty — so the advice cannot be followed and the evidence contradicts
the message.

Two separate faults, and both should be fixed together:

1. **The route is conditional and the probe is not.** `/_tako/dev` is
   framework surface and should be mounted by every service that serves
   requests, exactly like the status page is registered.
2. **`probe` collapses "not 200" into "answered with the wrong body".**
   A 404 from a service that has not mounted the route yet, or ever, is
   not evidence of a foreign listener — and `foreign` is sticky, so one
   such answer during startup poisons the whole wait.

It is `hello` — Gate G0's app, the first thing a new user runs. Found by
walking AB3a rather than by any test, because every example that has
been dev-walked recently (journal, flauta) declares auth. **Out of scope
here and worth scheduling first**; it is a one-line codegen change plus
a probe that distinguishes 404 from a nonce mismatch, with a devserver
test per case.

**36. CLOSED by 35's fix — the live walk had to run the built binary
directly** because of it
— `go build ./.tako/gen/shortlink && PORT=8118 ./shortlink`. That is a
fine fallback and it is written into `validate/policies.md` step 23, but
it is a workaround for a tako defect and should be reverted to `tako
dev` once 35 is fixed.

## 35 and 27 — fixed (2026-08-09)

Commit `cf7ee64`. Both were found by walking rather than by testing, and
both are now tested.

### 35 — the dev loop kept killing its own child

Two faults compounding, and only fixing both is a fix:

1. **The readiness answer lived in `runtime.Reserved`**, which codegen
   wraps only around a service declaring auth, a bucket or a cron.
   `hello`'s main is `runtime.Serve(mux)`, so the child could not
   identify itself **on any path**. It is answered by `Serve` now: being
   able to say "I am the child you started" is a property of serving,
   not of what the app declared.
2. **`waitReady` read a 404 as proof of a stranger** — and `probe`
   folded every non-200 into the same empty string, so the three
   distinguishable cases were one. Now: 200 with another nonce is
   another dev loop, reported at once; a 404 colours the timeout message
   and never outranks the child's exit, which is what a real collision
   actually looks like.

The error text changed for the weaker case, because the old one could
not be followed: it said to free the port, and tako had already released
it, so `lsof` came back empty.

**A correction to this log's own evidence.** The transcript filed with
item 35 curled `/_tako/dev`; the route is `/_tako/z/dev`, so that column
would have read 404 whatever the child did. The finding never rested on
it — `answerDevReady` was unreachable without `Reserved`, which
`hello`'s main does not call — and the before/after is the proof:
`tako dev` on `hello` failed, and now prints `ready in 905ms` and
serves. The entry has been corrected rather than quietly improved.

### 27 — the router's refusals are analysis errors

The check **registers the declared patterns on a real
`http.ServeMux`** and turns the panic into a diagnostic, rather than
restating Go's precedence rules. A reimplementation would be a second
rulebook to keep in step with the standard library's, and the two would
disagree exactly once, quietly, years from now.

`muxPattern` moved to `analyzer.MuxPattern` so the string that is
checked is the string that is mounted — checking one and mounting
another is a check of nothing.

The fixture reports the exact pair that panicked while AB10b's
moderation screen was being written, and stays silent on
`GET /admin/new` beside `GET /admin/{slug}` — a literal beats a
wildcard, and refusing that would break the trick every app uses.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root; all seven examples green under `tako
test`. New tests: a bare service answers the probe
(`pkg/runtime/reserved_test.go`), the three probe verdicts and the
child's-exit precedence (`pkg/devserver/devserver_test.go`), and the
analyzer golden `testdata/errors/routeconflict`.

Live: `tako dev` on `hello`, which could not run at all this morning.

```
ready in 905ms — watching (backends: local, in-process)
GET /hello        → 200
GET /_tako/z/dev  → 200  deed38ccec635bdedeb83afcd68ad7b3
```

Scripted walk: `validate/devloop.md`.

### Discovered work

**37. `validate/policies.md` step 23 still runs the built binary
directly**, a workaround for 35 that is no longer needed. Left as-is
because the step also proves the generated service works when run by
hand, which is worth keeping; it should gain a `tako dev` variant.

## AB2 rollout — every example (2026-08-09)

Commit `5400cfc`, closing item 33. gallery, shop, blog and hello join
journal on `app.Handler()`; siren has no HTTP tests and shortlink
already used it. **155 lines of hand-mirrored mounts and binders
deleted.**

### What the mirror was hiding

Two more instances of the drift AB2 was built for, found by converting:

- **gallery's harness never mounted `POST /api/reindex` or
  `GET /api/reindex/runs`** — declared, deployed, driven by no test.
- **shop's never mounted `GET /api/me`**, and called `SessionHandler()`
  with no providers, so its tests ran against a shop with **no password
  door** while the deployed one has one. (Half of that was already noted
  as item 28; the missing route was not.)

### Two defects in AB2 itself

Both invisible until an app with **buckets** and an app with **jobs**
went through the door, which is the argument for rolling a change like
this out rather than shipping it once against one example:

1. **`SignedURLHandler` read `booted`** — the app `runtime.BootLocal`
   sets — so under `app.Handler()` it answered the gcp phase-pointer
   501. Worse, with another test's `BootLocal` earlier in the same run
   it verified against THAT app's signing key and answered `invalid
   signature`. It resolves the signer and bucket store off the wired
   backends now.
2. **`runtime.WaitIdle` was a no-op** when `NewTestApp` booted the app:
   it returned nil immediately, so three tests believed they had a
   barrier and had none. It waits on the wired dispatcher now, and with
   nothing local wired it returns an error naming `app.DrainQueues()`
   rather than quietly succeeding.

The second is the more dangerous shape and the one worth remembering: a
barrier that silently does not wait leaves a test passing most of the
time.

### What stays hand-mounted, deliberately

gallery's two `http.NotFoundHandler()` mounts (a runtime-contract test
that a bucket's signed endpoint and a four-segment wildcard can share a
service on separate muxes), journal's three undeclared routes through
`serveWith`, and gallery's dead-letter suites — which boot their own dir
because they glob it, and therefore register their own async handlers.

### One difference worth stating

`NewTestApp` does not read `.env`; `BootLocal` does. gallery's harness
now calls `app.SetSecret("notifier-key", …)`, which is what the panic
text already told people to do. That is the right default — a test says
what it depends on — but it is a real conversion step for any app whose
handlers read a secret.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root; all seven examples green under `tako
test`. Scripted walk: `validate/harness.md` steps 7–8.

### Discovered work

**38. `runtime.BootLocal` and `tako.NewTestApp` are two boots with
different behaviour**, and an app can now meet both in one package: the
first reads `.env` and sets `runtime.booted`, the second does neither.
Two fixes went in for symptoms of it today (the signer, the barrier).
Worth a look at whether `NewTestApp` should simply set `booted` too, or
whether `booted` should stop existing.

*(Fixed below — there was a third symptom still live: the request
metrics sink.)*

## Audit after the AB2 rollout (2026-08-09)

Asked what was missing, and the answer was four things a passing suite
does not catch — three of them user-facing text, one an ergonomics
regression. Fixed in `f0d1e4a`; recorded because "the tests are green"
was true the whole time.

- **`tako dev` printed the generated test harness** in the line above
  `ready`. A run command should not mention test artifacts.
- **The freshness note said "regenerated: harness was stale"** — it
  derived the service name from the changed file's parent directory,
  and the harness sits one level deeper than the main.
- **Stale comments**: shop kept its old "mirrors the generated main"
  line above the new one; journal's file header still described a
  harness that mirrors codegen "like gallery's http_test.go" — pointing
  at a file that had also just changed.
- **Stale guide text**: blog's chapter said tests register templates
  straight from `site/static` so `go test` needs no Hugo. The site is
  the declared one now, and the command is `tako test`.

### Discovered work

**39. shop's harness reads a gitignored build output.** The generated
harness mounts the declared site, and shop's is `./web/dist` — an
esbuild artifact that `.gitignore` excludes. Verified harmless today
(moved `dist` away and shop's suite still passes, because its tests are
API-only), but it is silent: the first page-rendering test someone adds
to shop will fail on a fresh clone for a reason that has nothing to do
with their test. Either `tako test` should run the site Build the way
`tako dev` does, or the harness should say what it did not find.

*(Fixed below — and it was not latent: blog's page tests already failed
on a fresh clone.)*

## 39 and 38 — the two boots, and the site nobody built (2026-08-10)

Both filed items, both about the same thing from different ends: a
second copy of something the app already has one of. 39 is a site
directory that only some commands produce; 38 is a "which local app is
live" that only some boots set.

### 39 — the site under test is the site that ships

**It was not latent.** The item said shop's risk was theoretical
because its tests are API-only. blog's are not:

```
$ cd examples/blog && mv site/public /tmp/blog-public-backup && tako test
tako test · blog
  analyzing   1 service, 2 endpoints, 1 site
  generating  .tako/gen/blog/main.go
  harness     1 package(s) — app.Handler() serves the real mounts
  go test -overlay=…/blog/.tako/gen/overlay.json ./...
ERROR page error req=ea89cd err="the site has no templates/ directory —
  site.Render needs web/templates/layout.html plus one file per page"
--- FAIL: TestIslandRoundTrip (0.01s)
    comments_test.go:70: fragment = 500, csrf input present = false
--- FAIL: TestCSRFAndPathJudgments (0.01s)
FAIL	blog	0.343s
```

So the repo had an example whose suite passed only because the working
copy had been built at some point. That is the "green the whole time"
failure the last audit was about, one layer down.

**Shipped: `tako test` runs declared site builds**, exactly as `tako
dev` and `tako deploy` do. The tested app is the app that ships, which
is AB2's whole premise; a harness that mounts a directory no test
command produces was AB2 half-applied.

```
$ cd examples/blog && rm -rf site/public && tako test -count=1
tako test · blog
  analyzing   1 service, 2 endpoints, 1 site
  ⛅ site      cd site && hugo --minify → site/public (7 files)
  generating  .tako/gen/blog/main.go
  harness     1 package(s) — app.Handler() serves the real mounts
ok  	blog	0.295s

$ cd examples/shop && rm -rf web/dist && tako test -count=1
  ⛅ site      cd web && npx --yes esbuild … → web/dist (2 files)
ok  	shop	1.464s
```

**The guard, because this is a four-call-sites problem.** `runDeploy`,
`runBuild`, `session.cycle` and now `runTest` each have to remember —
and `tako test` is proof that "each one remembers" does not hold.
`cmd/tako/site_build_test.go` reads all four and fails if one stops
calling `build.Sites`. Mutation-checked by deleting the call:

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryCommandThatAssemblesTheAppBuildsItsSites
    site_build_test.go:40: runTest (main.go) never calls build.Sites —
    an app whose site is generated serves an empty one there, and a
    fresh clone has no site at all
```

**The error text that sent people to the wrong place.** The message
above names `web/templates/layout.html`. blog's site is `site/public`;
there is no `web/` anywhere in it. Now it says `templates/layout.html
inside the declared site directory` — the FS reaching
`RegisterSiteTemplates` is an embed in the deployed service, so there
is no real path to print, and a made-up one is worse than none.

### 38 — one live app, not two

`runtime.booted` was set only by `BootLocal`, and read as though it
meant "the local app that is running". `tako.NewTestApp` boots through
the same `internal/boot` and sets nothing there, so under the harness
that variable is either nil or points at a DIFFERENT app — and it was
preferred over the wired backends when both existed.

Three defects came from it. Two were found in the AB2 rollout (the
signer, the barrier) and fixed one at a time, at their call sites. The
third was still live and is the reason to fix the cause instead:

**Every request through `app.Handler()` recorded into a nil metrics
sink.** `SetRequestMetrics` was a second copy of `hooks.Metrics` that
each boot path had to remember to make. The slice originally shipped
with the call missing everywhere — fixed by adding it twice, once per
boot path, plus a test that read the source to check both. Then
`NewTestApp` arrived as a third boot, knew nothing about it, and the
harness served into nil again. Same defect, same cause, one slice
later; the source-reading test could not see it, because it only knew
about the two boots that existed when it was written.

**Shipped:**

- The duplicate is gone. `recordRequest` reads `hooks.Metrics` — one
  wiring, read where it is used, so there is no call for a fourth boot
  path to forget. `SetRequestMetrics` is removed from `pkg/runtime`'s
  surface (runtime lock updated; codegen never emitted it).
- `booted` → `owned`, documented as what it actually is: the app THIS
  package opened, kept so a second `BootLocal` can close the first. Not
  "the app that is running".
- `WaitIdle` and `SetQueueRate` resolve through one `localQueue()` —
  the wired dispatcher, and only that.
- The source-reading test is replaced by two that BOOT: `BootLocal` and
  `tako.NewTestApp`, each followed by a real request through the
  middleware, asserted against the wired backend's own `OnMetric`. A
  test that injects its own dependency can never notice a missing
  injection; these cannot be passed by accident by a boot path that
  does not exist yet. `BootGCP` cannot be booted, so its wiring is
  still read from source — now for `hooks.Metrics = `, the assignment
  that actually matters.

Mutation-checked by restoring the old shape (a package var filled at
`BootLocal` time):

```
--- FAIL: TestATestAppBootRecordsRequests
    boot_metrics_test.go:45: requests never reached the wired sink —
    the per-endpoint alerts over it are dead
    boot_metrics_test.go:45: request_ms never reached the wired sink —
```

`TestALocalBootRecordsRequests` stayed green under that mutation, which
is exactly the asymmetry that let the defect live.

### What did NOT change, deliberately

- **`NewTestApp` still does not read `.env`.** A test says what it
  depends on (`app.SetSecret`). That difference is a feature and is
  documented as one.
- **`hooks.CronSkipped` is still local-boot only.** It is a console
  line for `tako dev`; silence in a test is not a fidelity gap.
- **Rate limits still do not apply under `NewTestApp`.** `SetQueueRate`
  is emitted only into generated mains, never the harness, and tests
  exercise the retry contract rather than production pacing.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples green under `tako
test`, including blog and shop with their site outputs deleted first.
Scripted walk: `validate/harness.md` steps 9–10, both added here and
run.

## SC1 — DX proposal: `tako users`, the account you cannot make without writing code (2026-08-10) — AWAITING APPROVAL

First of a scaffolding series the owner opened on 2026-08-10 (SC2 `tako
setup`, SC3 `tako new`, SC4 `tako secrets`, SC5 `BootGCPWith` are named
but not proposed). SC1 goes first because it is the only one that closes
a **local annoyance and a cloud hole with one build**.

### The evidence

- **Local.** `docs/guide/local.md` tells you, in prose, to make an
  account with `auth.Users().Create` — so a one-off `main.go`, a test,
  or a dev-only branch on `tako.Environment()`. The dev bar offers two
  hardcoded names (`session.go:740`), which is enough until the app
  declares `Password: true` or a policy that needs a role.
- **Cloud.** There is no bootstrap path at all. Deploy an app whose
  admin door is `Route{Allow: Editors}` and the first editor can only
  be created by code you write, deploy, run once, and delete.
- **The surface already shipped.** AB10 built `auth.Users()` —
  Create/Get/ByEmail/List/Grant/Revoke/Disable/Enable/Delete — over a
  contract (`backends.Users`) that both backends implement and the
  conformance suite already governs. This is a door onto it, not a
  feature under it.

### The boundary — why this is not the admin scaffold (decision 11)

The implementation plan records that "no feature without an example
demanding it" once killed an admin scaffold, and decision 11 bars
admin/CMS primitives. Both hold here:

- **The app gains nothing.** No new exported SDK symbol, no template, no
  route, no generated code. `tako.UsersHandle` is unchanged.
- **The operator gains a door** onto a surface that already exists, the
  way `tako dlq` is a door onto queues rather than a queue feature.

If this proposal ever needs to add a symbol to the root package to
work, that is the signal it has crossed the line — and it does not (see
D3).

---

### The surface

```
tako users list   [--role R]
tako users show   <email|id>
tako users create <email> [--name N] [--password] [--role R]...
tako users grant  <email|id> <role>
tako users revoke <email|id> <role>
tako users disable|enable <email|id>
tako users delete <email|id>
```

**Local** — the common case, the one in the dev loop:

```
$ tako users create ana@example.com --name Ana --role editor
tako users · local · .tako/data
  created  usr_01J8ZK4M  ana@example.com  Ana  [editor]
  no password set — this account signs in with Google; --password sets one
```

```
$ tako users list
tako users · local · .tako/data
  ID            EMAIL              NAME   ROLES              STATE
  usr_01J8ZK4M  ana@example.com    Ana    editor
  usr_01J8ZK7Q  bruno@example.com  Bruno  editor, moderator  disabled
  2 accounts
```

```
$ tako users grant ana@example.com moderator
tako users · local · .tako/data
  granted  moderator to ana@example.com  [editor, moderator]
  1 live session marked stale — it picks the role up on its next request
```

That last line is the point of the whole design. A role change is
invisible machinery — the roles a request sees come off the session,
minted before the change — and the transcript says both that it
happened and *when it lands*, instead of leaving the operator to
wonder why the admin page is still 403.

```
$ tako users disable bruno@example.com
tako users · local · .tako/data
  disabled  bruno@example.com — sign-in refused, record kept
  2 sessions ended
```

**Cloud** — the same command, the target on line one:

```
$ tako users create ops@acme.com --password --role admin --project acme-prod-4821
tako users · cloud · acme-prod-4821 / prod
  password: ········
  created  Xk3nQ82mVd  ops@acme.com  [admin]
  auth.Registered published — welcomeMail will run
```

**The ladder** (`tako --help`: friction scales with irreversibility).
Deleting a local account is disposable — `.tako/data` is the reset
story, and the guide says so. Deleting a cloud account is a person who
cannot sign in again:

```
$ tako users delete bruno@example.com --project acme-prod-4821
tako users · cloud · acme-prod-4821 / prod
  bruno@example.com  Bruno  [editor, moderator]
  this is permanent: the account is gone, and anything your app keyed on
  its id is orphaned. tako users disable keeps the record.
  type the email to confirm: bruno@example.com
  deleted  Xk3nQ82mVd  2 sessions ended
```

---

### The three decisions this needs

**D1 — the cloud target is never inferred.** No `--project` on the
command line means local. Not `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, not `gcloud
config`. `--env` without `--project` is refused:

```
tako: --env names a cloud environment but no project was given
      add --project <id>, or drop --env to work on .tako/data
```

**This deviates from the shared rule** the usage text states — "Cloud
commands resolve --project (else GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, else gcloud
config) … identically" — and that text must gain the exception or
become false. The reason for the exception: every other cloud command
reads, or converges the project toward what the code already says.
This one writes a person. A `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` left in a shell
turns `tako users create` into a real account in a real project, and a
dev fixture named `test@test.test` in prod is not something a later
deploy corrects. `env.go` already argues this for `--env` on destroy:
a silent reinterpretation is unforgivable on the paths where it is.

**D2 — a role that the app does not declare is refused.**

```
$ tako users grant ana@example.com moderatr
tako: "moderatr" is not a role this app declares
      declared: editor, moderator (tako.Role)
      did you mean moderator?
```

`AppGraph.Roles` already exists — the analyzer collects it so the dev
sign-in page can offer roles to tick. Granting an undeclared role is
not an error the store can catch: it writes a claim that every policy
ignores, so the operator sees success and the user still cannot get in.
**No `--force`.** An escape hatch on a check whose entire value is
catching a typo defeats the check.

**D3 — the CLI calls the SDK, never the store.**

```go
// wire the hooks for the chosen target, then:
ctx := runtime.NewCtx(context.Background())
err := (&tako.UsersHandle{}).Grant(ctx, id, tako.Role(name))
```

Both pieces are already exported (`runtime.NewCtx`, and `UsersHandle`
is an empty struct that reads the wired hooks). Nothing new is needed.

This is item 38's lesson, one day old. "Write the account, then mark
its sessions stale, under a lease keyed on the account" is
orchestration that lives in `users.go` today; a second copy in the CLI
is a duplicate every future change must be copied into, and the copy
that gets missed is a role that never lands or a disabled user still
signed in for a week. Reusing the path means the lease, the stale
marking, the session ending and the `auth.Registered` publish all come
for free, and stay correct by construction.

**One consequence, stated rather than discovered.** The publish is real
in the cloud and absent locally: `hooks.Topic` is unwired in a CLI that
is not the app, so `publishAuthEvent` no-ops. So `tako users create`
fires the app's registration subscriber against a project and does not
on a laptop. The graph knows whether there is a subscriber to miss, so
the line is printed only when there is one:

```
  auth.Registered not published — this is the CLI, not the app; run
  tako dev if you need welcomeMail to see this account
```

---

### Cloud errors & permissions

**A finding this proposal surfaces.** `docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md`
puts `identitytoolkit.viewer`/`identitytoolkit.admin` in the Layer 2
table (runtime, derived per service) and nowhere in Layer 1. So an
operator holding the full documented deployer bundle runs `tako users
create --project` and gets a 403. **Proposed: add
`roles/identitytoolkit.admin` to the Layer 1 bundle**, on the honest
justification that a principal who can `tako deploy` can already deploy
code that mints accounts — the grant adds no power, it removes a
detour. That is a permissions-model change and it is named here rather
than patched at the call site, per the working rules.

Four failures, four different problems, four different remediations:

```
tako: identitytoolkit.googleapis.com is disabled on acme-prod-4821 — this
      app's sign-in has never been deployed there. Run tako deploy (it
      initializes Identity Platform), or enable the API alone:
        gcloud services enable identitytoolkit.googleapis.com --project acme-prod-4821
```
```
tako: you lack identitytoolkit.admin on acme-prod-4821 — grant it once:
        gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding acme-prod-4821 \
          --member user:$(gcloud config get account) --role roles/identitytoolkit.admin
```
```
tako: Identity Platform is not initialized on acme-prod-4821 — tako deploy
      initializes it when the app declares tako.Auth. Deploy once, then re-run.
```
```
tako: not authenticated to Google Cloud — run:
        gcloud auth application-default login
```

Also required and already in the bundle: `roles/datastore.owner`
(sessions live in Datastore, so stale-marking and ending need it) and
`serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer` (FL19 — tako bills its calls to the
target project).

**Preflight order.** Everything the graph can answer runs before any
credential is touched: no `tako.Auth` declared, an undeclared role, a
malformed email. A typo costs no round trip and no 403.

```
tako: this app declares no tako.Auth — accounts exist because an app has a
      sign-in door. Add tako.Auth(...) and the accounts follow.
```

---

### Non-goals

- **No password reset, no email verification.** AB10 decision 3:
  Identity Platform's hosted flows own recovery, and tako sends no email.
- **No `tako sessions`.** `disable` ends them, which is the operational
  need; a command for listing them waits for an example that wants it.
- **No bulk import/export, no CSV.** One account at a time is the
  bootstrap story; a fixture set is a test's job.
- **No account creation during `tako deploy`.** A deploy converges code;
  a person is not derived from code.
- **No `--force` on D2**, and no way to address a project tako has not
  provisioned (v0 non-goal: shared multi-tenant projects).

### Test plan (test-first)

1. **Golden transcripts and every error text** in `cmd/tako` — exact
   strings, the way analyzer errors are tested. Error text is product UX.
2. **Conformance, first.** The `Users` contract has per-method cases;
   this adds cases for the *compound* acts the CLI depends on — a grant
   marks live sessions stale, a disable ends them — at the contract
   level, so `local` and `gcp` cannot answer differently.
3. **The D3 guard, mechanical**: `cmd/tako/users.go` must not import
   `pkg/backends`. If the CLI ever reaches past the SDK to the store,
   that is the failure, and it fails here rather than as a role that
   quietly never landed.
4. **`validate/users.md`** — the scripted walk, including one cloud run
   against a real project, transcript pasted into this log.

### The one question I could not decide

**D1's deviation.** The alternative is to keep the shared resolution
rule intact and pay for it with a typed confirmation on every cloud
write, not just delete. That is more consistent and more annoying. I
recommend D1 as written — the inconsistency is one sentence in the
usage text, and it buys "this command cannot address prod by accident."

### Gate

Stopping here. No code written; nothing in this proposal exists yet.

---

## SC1 — shipped (2026-08-10)

Owner approved D1 on 2026-08-10 ("D1 approved, go ahead and implement
it"); D2 and D3 were recommendations rather than open questions and
shipped as proposed.

`cmd/tako/users.go` (the command), `cmd/tako/usersboot.go` (the wiring),
`cmd/tako/users_test.go`, `validate/users.md`. No new exported SDK
symbol — the point of D3, and the thing that keeps this clear of
decision 11.

### The three decisions, as built

**D1 — the target is never inferred.** `--project` on the command line
or nothing. `--env` alone is refused with the reason, and `tako --help`
and `reference/cli.md` both carry the exception rather than leaving a
false "every cloud command resolves identically".

**D2 — an undeclared role is refused**, with the declared set and a
did-you-mean bounded at two edits (a hint naming something unrelated is
worse than no hint). No `--force`.

**D3 — the command calls the SDK and never the store.** `runtime.NewCtx`
+ `&tako.UsersHandle{}`, both already exported; nothing new was needed.

### What the walk actually proved

The end-to-end run is in `validate/users.md` §5, and it is the one that
mattered: bob signs in to journal (403 on `/moderate`, behind
`RequireRole(Moderator)`), a `tako users grant` from the terminal, and
**bob's original session cookie gets 200** — no re-sign-in. That is the
SDK's stale-marking reaching a live session through the CLI, which is
the whole argument for D3 stated as a transcript.

§6 is the other half: an account created by `tako users create
--password` signs in through shop's real door, and the uid in the
sign-in response is the id the CLI printed.

### Mutation proofs

Each guard was broken and watched to fail:

| Mutation | Guard that caught it |
|---|---|
| restore the ordinary `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` fallback | `TestNoProjectMeansLocalEvenWithAProjectInTheEnvironment` — "a dev fixture would land in production" |
| import `internal/hooks` and call `hooks.Users.SetRoles` | `TestTheUsersCommandNeverReachesPastTheSDK` |
| wire the accounts but not the entity store | `TestWiringTheAccountsAlsoWiresWhatSessionsNeed` — "a role change would never reach a live session, and nothing would say so" |

The third is the one worth keeping: it is the exact shape where the
command works, prints success, and silently leaves every signed-in
browser on the old role.

### Deviations from the approved proposal

1. **No session counts.** The proposal's transcript said "1 live session
   marked stale" and "2 sessions ended". `Grant`/`Disable` return only
   an error, and adding a count would re-shape an exported SDK symbol as
   a side effect of another task. The lines keep the part that carries
   the meaning — WHEN the change lands, and that nobody is signed out —
   and drop the arithmetic.
2. **No STATE column in `list`.** `tako.User` carries no `Disabled`
   field (`userFromRecord` does not copy it), so the SDK cannot report
   it and reaching past the SDK for it would break D3. Filed below.
3. **`golang.org/x/term` added** as a direct dependency, for reading a
   password with echo off. Piped input still works (`printf 'pw' |
   tako users create … --password`), so nothing here needs a TTY.

### What SC1 found, and did not fix

- **`tako dev` holds `.tako/data`.** bbolt takes an exclusive lock, so
  `tako users` cannot run beside a dev server — the single most natural
  workflow ("dev is up, I need a user"). The command now says the
  likely thing (`tako dev` holds it) instead of the store's guess about
  an orphaned process, but the limitation is real and filed.
- **A false alarm, chased down rather than assumed.** The first walk had
  alice holding `moderator` with no role ticked, which looked like the
  dev sign-in silently granting everything — contradicting its own doc
  comment. It is journal's own
  `OnFirstSignIn = tako.Subscribe(auth.FirstSignIn, appointFounder)`.
  Nothing is broken; noted because the reproduction is in the log.

### Discovered work (not done — see the standing list)

- **40. `tako.User` cannot report a disabled account.** `Disable` works
  and `list` cannot show its effect. An SDK change, so its own task.
- **41. `tako users` cannot run while `tako dev` does.** A read-only
  bolt open would cover `list`/`show`; the writes need a seam into the
  running process. Its own task.
- **42. The dev bar offers alice and bob only.** With `tako users` able
  to make accounts, the bar could offer the accounts that exist.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples
green under `tako test`. Scripted walk: `validate/users.md`, every step
run, transcripts pasted there rather than paraphrased.

---

## SC2 — DX proposal: `tako setup`, the block the doc admits it should be (2026-08-10) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Second of the scaffolding series. SC1 shipped 2026-08-10.

### The evidence, and the correction it forces

I proposed SC2 as "turn the documented block into a command", implying
tako cannot tell you what is missing. **That was wrong, and the code is
better than I credited.** `gcp.Preflight` (preflight.go:71) already:

- computes the APIs and permissions THIS app's graph needs (`Needs`),
  not a generic list;
- checks each API's enabled state, and every permission through
  `testIamPermissions`;
- checks that declared secrets exist, that a Datastore database exists,
  that each custom domain is verified, that the region supports
  mappings;
- prints an exact, copy-pasteable remediation for every gap;
- and `Classify` gives 401, 403-API-disabled, 403-permission,
  403-org-policy and 404-project five different texts.

So detection is done, and done well. What does not exist is **doing
any of it**. `docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md` says of its own setup
block: *"later `tako deploy` will print exactly this when preflight
finds gaps; until then it's the documented block."* Half of that
shipped — the printing. Nobody applies it.

The gap is therefore narrower and sharper than I said: a first-time
user copies eleven `gcloud services enable` arguments and fourteen
`add-iam-policy-binding` lines out of a markdown table by hand, and
gets them wrong one at a time, each mistake costing a full preflight
round trip.

### What SC2 is

`tako setup --project <id>` — **apply the setup, converge, and be
honest about the remainder.** It plans, prompts, enables, grants,
creates the Datastore database, and then prints exactly what tako
cannot do, with the commands or console links for each.

It is stateless and idempotent, like everything else here: re-running
skips what is already true and says so. There is no state file and no
"setup completed" marker.

---

### The surface

```
tako setup [--project <id>] [--env prod] [--member <principal>]
           [--plan] [--minimal] [--yes]
```

**The normal run**, from an app directory:

```
$ tako setup --project acme-prod-4821
tako setup · acme-prod-4821
  granting to  user:memo@example.com
  app          shop · 6 services, entities, queues, a cron, 1 secret

  APIs — 4 to enable, 7 already on
    + artifactregistry.googleapis.com    push images
    + cloudscheduler.googleapis.com      crons
    + cloudtasks.googleapis.com          rate-limited and delayed queues
    + identitytoolkit.googleapis.com     sign-in

  Roles for user:memo@example.com — 5 to grant, 9 already held
    + roles/run.admin                    create and update services
    + roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin      one identity per service
    + roles/pubsub.admin                 topics and subscriptions
    + roles/cloudscheduler.admin         crons
    + roles/identitytoolkit.admin        tako users — NOT needed to deploy

  Datastore
    + a datastore-mode database in us-central1
      the location is permanent: a database cannot be moved later

  apply? [y/N] y
  ✓ enabled  4 APIs
  ✓ granted  5 roles
  ✓ created  the Datastore database

Still yours — tako cannot do these:
  · the Google sign-in provider: Google exposes no public API for
    creating external OAuth clients
      https://console.firebase.google.com/project/acme-prod-4821/authentication/providers
      → Google → Enable (pick a support email) → Save
  · a value for the secret shop declares
      printf '<value>' | gcloud secrets create prod-stripe-key --data-file=- --project acme-prod-4821

Next: tako deploy --project acme-prod-4821
```

**Re-running** says the useful thing rather than nothing:

```
$ tako setup --project acme-prod-4821
tako setup · acme-prod-4821
  granting to  user:memo@example.com
  nothing to do — 11 APIs on, 14 roles held, the database exists

Still yours — tako cannot do these:
  · the Google sign-in provider …
```

**The failure that matters most.** Granting yourself the permission to
grant is the one thing nobody can bootstrap, so setup must be excellent
at handing the job over:

```
$ tako setup --project acme-prod-4821
tako setup · acme-prod-4821
  granting to  user:intern@example.com
tako: you cannot change IAM on acme-prod-4821 — setup needs
      resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy, which comes with
      roles/owner or roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin. Granting
      yourself the permission to grant is the one step nobody can
      bootstrap, so it is somebody else's to run.

      Send them this — it is the whole of it:

        gcloud services enable artifactregistry.googleapis.com \
          cloudscheduler.googleapis.com cloudtasks.googleapis.com \
          identitytoolkit.googleapis.com --project acme-prod-4821

        for R in run.admin iam.serviceAccountAdmin pubsub.admin \
                 cloudscheduler.admin identitytoolkit.admin; do
          gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding acme-prod-4821 \
            --member user:intern@example.com --role roles/$R
        done

      Then re-run tako setup to finish (it will skip what is done).
```

**CI**, granting to a service account rather than to you:

```
tako setup --project acme-prod-4821 \
  --member serviceAccount:deploy@acme-prod-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com --yes
```

`--plan` stops after the plan, exactly like `tako deploy --plan`.

---

### The four decisions this needs

**D1 — the full Layer 1 bundle by default, not the graph's subset.**
`--minimal` grants only what this app's graph needs.

The permissions doc's own reasoning: *"Each C-task's preflight checks
only the subset that task touches; the full bundle exists so a user can
grant once and never think about it again."* Granting the subset makes
`tako setup` something you re-run in the middle of a feature — you add
your first `tako.Cron` and the next deploy fails on a missing role.
Layer 2's derived least privilege is about the RUNTIME, where the
principal is a machine and the blast radius is a service; Layer 1 is a
human on a dedicated project.

`identitytoolkit.admin` is annotated in the plan as not needed to
deploy, because it is the one role a CI principal can decline.

**D2 — standard target resolution, NOT SC1's exception.** `--project`
→ `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` → gcloud config, like every other cloud
command.

Stated because I just shipped the opposite one week's work ago and the
asymmetry needs a reason rather than a mood. SC1 writes a person into a
project and no later run corrects it. This one converges project
configuration: every effect is additive, revocable, and re-derivable,
the plan names the project in the first line, and there is a y/N before
anything happens. Consistency wins where the danger does not.

**D3 — apply what it can, print what it cannot, always.** Two kinds of
"cannot": no permission (hand it over, above), and genuinely impossible
(the Google provider, domain ownership, DNS, secret VALUES). Both end
in a block someone can act on. Setup never half-applies silently and
never claims to have finished something it skipped.

**D4 — setup creates the Datastore database.** It is the one create
here whose consequence outlives the command: a Firestore/Datastore
database's location cannot be changed afterward. So the plan names the
location and says permanent, and `--yes` covers it — creation, not
destruction, is rung 2 of the ladder. **This is the one I am least
sure about** and it is called out again below.

---

### Cloud errors & permissions

**What setup itself needs**, beyond what it grants:

| Permission | Why |
|---|---|
| `serviceusage.services.enable` | turn APIs on (`roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin`, or owner) |
| `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` | grant the bundle (`roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin`, or owner) |
| `datastore.databases.create` | the database (`roles/datastore.owner`, already in the bundle) |

In practice: **the person who created the project**. That is the honest
persona, and the partial-power path above is what everyone else gets.

Failure texts, each distinct because each has a different remedy:

```
tako: you cannot enable APIs on acme-prod-4821 — setup needs
      serviceusage.services.enable (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin,
      or roles/owner). [hand-over block]
```
```
tako: project "acme-prod-482" not found (or you have no access) — check the id
```
```
tako: enabling artifactregistry.googleapis.com is blocked by your
      organization's policy — tako will not try to work around it
      (see docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md): <the policy's own message>
```
```
tako: acme-prod-4821 has no billing account — Cloud Run, Artifact Registry
      and Datastore all refuse without one. Link one in the console, then
      re-run: https://console.cloud.google.com/billing/linkedaccount?project=acme-prod-4821
```
```
tako: cannot authenticate to Google Cloud — run:
        gcloud auth application-default login
```

`Classify` already produces four of these shapes; setup reuses it
rather than growing a second classifier. **Billing is new** — it is
the commonest first-project failure and currently surfaces as an
opaque 403 from whichever API is touched first.

**Ordering.** APIs before roles before the database: a grant against a
project whose API is off fails confusingly, and the database needs
Datastore enabled. Setup stops at the first failure rather than
pressing on, because the later steps' errors would be consequences of
the earlier one.

---

### Non-goals

- **Creating the project.** Billing accounts, org membership and quota
  are the user's relationship with Google, not tako's.
- **Org policy.** Doctrine, and unchanged: tako reports, never
  circumvents.
- **Service-account KEYS.** ADC only. Setup will not mint a downloadable
  credential, for CI or anyone.
- **Secret values.** SC4's territory, and the value is the user's data.
- **Domains, DNS, the Google provider.** Impossible or genuinely
  interactive; setup names them and stops.
- **`tako setup --revoke`.** Taking roles off a human is not tako's
  call, and the confirmation ladder has no rung that makes it one.
- **A "setup completed" marker.** Stateless reconciliation, decision 4.

### Test plan (test-first)

1. **The bundle is tested against the doc.** A guard parses the Layer 1
   table in `docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md` and asserts it matches the
   bundle in code. The table has been the source of truth for a year;
   the moment code owns it, one of the two starts lying.
2. **Fake-server tests** over `pkg/provision/gcp`'s existing
   `fake_test.go` harness: plan output golden, apply issues exactly the
   expected calls, and **a re-run issues none** (idempotence is the
   property, not a nice-to-have).
3. **Every refusal above**, exact text, including the hand-over block —
   it is the output a blocked user reads most carefully.
4. **`--plan` mutates nothing**: the fake server fails the test if any
   non-GET arrives.
5. **`validate/setup.md`**, run against a REAL fresh project, transcript
   pasted into this log. This one cannot be validated any other way: a
   fake server cannot tell me the block is right.

### Both questions, ruled (owner, 2026-08-10)

**D1 → the tighter permissions, always.** Setup grants only what this
app's graph needs; there is no full-bundle mode and no `--minimal`
flag, because the subset IS the behaviour. My recommendation was the
opposite and the owner overruled it.

The consequence is accepted rather than hidden: **setup is a command
you re-run as the app grows.** So it has to be pleasant to re-run — it
already is, being idempotent and reporting "nothing to do" — and the
deploy's preflight, which finds the gap that prompts the re-run, should
name `tako setup` in its remediation rather than printing raw gcloud
lines. That is a change to preflight's gap text and is part of SC2.

It also lands on the right side of tako's own doctrine: every runtime
grant is derived from the graph, and the deployer's now is too. The
Layer 1 table in `docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md` becomes documentation
of the maximum rather than a block to paste.

**D4 → not part of setup. Its own command, with the region typed.**

```
tako datastore create --region us-central1 --project acme-prod-4821
```

`--region` is REQUIRED here — no default, no inheriting `TAKO_REGION`,
no falling back to us-central1 — because a Datastore database's
location cannot be changed afterward and every other region default in
this CLI exists to save typing on a decision that is reversible. This
one is not.

`tako setup` therefore never creates a database. It reports the missing
one and names the command:

```
Still yours — tako cannot do these:
  · this app declares entities and acme-prod-4821 has no Datastore database
      tako datastore create --region <region> --project acme-prod-4821
      (the location is permanent — pick the region your services run in)
```

Preflight's existing gap text (`preflight.go:163`, currently a raw
`gcloud firestore databases create` line) changes to name the tako
command for the same reason.

### Gate

Stopping here. No code written. SC2 is now fully specified — say the
word and it gets built.

---

## FL20 — DX proposal: `entity:"index"` decides what is indexed (2026-08-10) — AWAITING APPROVAL

From flauta's friction log, 2026-08-09: *"every scalar field is indexed
in Datastore, and Datastore caps an indexed string at 1500 bytes"* —
the entry they marked as the one **no amount of app-side care can work
around**. Every other open entry in that log has a workaround.

Owner direction, 2026-08-10: *"indexes need to be explicit."*

### What is actually wrong

Not "tako chose to index everything." The tag exists, is read, and does
something — just not the thing its name promises. Three facts:

**1. The tag is read into a set** (`entity.go:141`):

```go
case "index":
    s.indexed[f.Name] = jsonName(f)
```

**2. That set has exactly one consumer in the whole repo**
(`entity.go:344`), and it is the QUERY layer:

```go
jsonField, ok := s.indexed[field]
if !ok {
    return "", fmt.Errorf("tako: entity %q: %s is not an indexed field", q.h.name, field)
}
```

**3. The write path cannot see it**, because the contract carries only
bytes (`pkg/backends/entity.go`):

```go
Put(ctx context.Context, kind, id string, doc []byte) error
```

So the GCP store re-derives properties by unmarshalling the JSON and
mirroring every scalar it finds (`pkg/backends/gcp/entity.go`,
`entity()`), with `excludeFromIndexes` set on the document blob and on
nothing else.

**`entity:"index"` is a query permission, not a storage instruction.**
An untagged `Body string` is still mirrored as an indexed Datastore
property, and Datastore rejects an indexed string over 1500 bytes — so
an app fails to write a field it never asked to index, with an error
about an index it never declared. That is why it cannot be worked
around: the app has already said the right thing.

### The constraint that shapes the fix

The two failure directions are not symmetric, and this decides the
design:

- **Over-indexing** (today) fails the WRITE, loudly, at the API.
- **Under-indexing** fails the READ, **silently**. A Datastore filter
  on an excluded property does not error — the entity is simply not in
  that property's index, so the query returns nothing. A page of posts
  quietly becomes empty.

So the fix must not trade a loud bug for a silent one. Anything that
lets a call site forget to pass its indexed set is worse than what we
have now.

**The framework's own kinds are the sharp edge here.**
`pkg/runtime/session.go` writes `sessionKind` through
`hooks.Entity.Put` in three places, and `eachSession` queries sessions
**by uid** — that query is what sign-out, revocation and role
stale-marking are built on. Exclude `uid` by accident and revocation
silently stops revoking. That is a security property, failing quietly,
and it is the reason the design below refuses to make the set optional.

### The surface — nothing changes for the user

```go
type Post struct {
    ID     string `entity:"id"`
    Author string `entity:"index"`   // queryable, and therefore indexed
    Slug   string `entity:"index"`
    Title  string                    // stored, never queried, never indexed
    Body   string                    // 40 KB of markdown — fine now
}
```

That is already what the doc comments say the tag means. FL20 makes it
true. The user-visible change is that the second and third fields stop
being indexed, so `Body` can hold a document.

**A tagged field that is too long gets a message about the thing the
app actually declared**, instead of Datastore's:

```
tako: entity "posts": Title is declared entity:"index" and this value is
      1,842 bytes — Datastore caps an INDEXED string at 1500. Drop the
      tag if you do not query on Title; keep it and store the long text
      in another field.
```

### The contract change

```go
// pkg/backends/entity.go
Put(ctx context.Context, kind, id string, doc []byte, indexed []string) error
```

and the same fifth argument on `EntityTxOps.Put`. `indexed` names the
document's queryable fields, by their JSON names. `local` ignores it
(bbolt indexes nothing and scans); `gcp` sets
`excludeFromIndexes: true` on every mirrored property not in the list.

**Where the set comes from — one place per kind, never a call site's
choice:**

- **App entities**: `EntityHandle[T].loadSchema()`, which already
  computes it and caches it per handle. One site (`entity.go:57`),
  fed structurally. There is no way for an app to get this wrong.
- **The runtime's own kinds** (`sessionKind`, `seenKind`): a `var`
  beside each record type, so the four call sites in `session.go` name
  a constant rather than a literal.

### The alternative I did not pick

A schema table emitted by codegen into the generated main and
registered at boot — which fits "static analysis + codegen, never
reflection" better, and the analyzer already collects the fields.

It fails on the constraint above. A bare test, or any path that boots
backends without a generated main, would have an EMPTY table — and an
empty table means "index nothing", which means every query silently
returns nothing. A design whose failure mode is a silent empty read in
exactly the environment where people write assertions is the wrong
design, however well it matches the doctrine.

The reflection cost stays where it already is: once per handle, in
`loadSchema`, which is init-shaped work and not on the request path.

### Conformance cases (written first, as the rule requires)

1. **A long untagged field round-trips.** Put a 2 KB untagged string,
   get it back. This is flauta's blocker, and it fails against `gcp`
   today.
2. **A tagged field is still queryable after a write.** `Where` on it
   returns the row — the under-indexing regression, pinned in the
   direction that fails silently.
3. **A tagged field over 1500 bytes is refused with tako's text**, not
   Datastore's.
4. **Sessions survive.** A runtime-level case: mint a session, mark it
   stale by uid, and assert `eachSession` found it. Not a conformance
   case (sessions are runtime, not a backend contract) but it belongs
   in the same slice, because it is the one that fails quietly.

Cases 1–3 go in `pkg/backends/conformance`, so `local` and `gcp` are
held to them together. Per "conformance is law", they are written and
red before the gcp change.

### Migration, and what does not change

- **No data migration.** Datastore re-indexes an entity when it is
  written, so existing documents keep their current indexes until they
  are next put. Over-indexed old data is harmless — and a document that
  would now be legal could never have been written before, so there is
  nothing stranded.
- **Composite index derivation is unaffected.** The deploy derives
  composites from query call sites (`Resource.Composites`), and a field
  can only be queried if it is tagged — so every composite names fields
  that remain indexed.
- **`local` behaviour does not change at all.** It never indexed
  anything; it scans. Which is exactly why this bug could not be caught
  locally, and why case 1 is a conformance case rather than a unit test.

### Non-goals

- **No `entity:"exclude"` tag.** Untagged already means unindexed once
  this lands; a second tag for the default is surface with no job.
- **No automatic long-field detection.** tako will not silently drop a
  tag because a value got long — that would make a query start
  returning nothing based on data.
- **Not touching the 1500-byte limit itself.** It is Datastore's, it is
  not negotiable, and the fix is to stop indexing things nobody asked
  to index.
- **No change to how queries validate fields.** `indexedField` already
  refuses an untagged field, which is what makes the tag set a safe
  source of truth for the write path.

### Cost, stated plainly

This changes an interface in `pkg/backends`, which is the one place the
repo treats as a contract. Both backends, the conformance suite, the
runtime's session store and the local user store all move together. It
is the largest surface change since AB10, and it is worth it because
the alternative is an app that cannot store a paragraph.

### Gate

Stopping here. No code written.

---

## FL20 — shipped (2026-08-10)

Approved 2026-08-10 ("Go"). `pkg/backends/entity.go` (contract),
`local/entity.go`, `gcp/entity.go`, `conformance/entity.go`,
`entity.go` (SDK), `pkg/runtime/session.go`,
`pkg/backends/gcp/entity_index_test.go`, `validate/entity-index.md`.

**No example changed, and no app has to.** The tags were already right;
they simply did nothing on the way in.

### What shipped

`Put`, `Update` and `Tx` carry the queryable set. `EntityTxOps.Put` did
NOT change — a transaction is scoped to one kind, so the set belongs on
`Tx` and the per-write call has nothing left to get wrong. That was not
in the proposal and is strictly better than what it described.

The set reaches the store from one place per kind:

- app entities — `EntityHandle.indexedFields()`, off the cached schema.
  An app never passes one, so it cannot pass the wrong one.
- `_tako_session` — `sessionIndexed`, and see below.
- `_tako_seen` — empty, deliberately, with a comment saying it was
  chosen rather than forgotten.

### The session constant, which is the part worth reading

The proposal called sessions "the sharp edge" and planned a test.
Building it showed a test would not have worked: `eachSession` looks
sessions up by uid, revocation and stale-marking are that query, and a
wrong declaration there fails **silently on gcp only** — `local` scans,
so it answers the query whatever was declared. Every existing session
test would have stayed green while revocation quietly stopped revoking.

So it is structural instead. `sessionUIDField` is one constant, used by
the query and by the declared index, and the two cannot disagree
because there is only one of them. Two names that must agree, one of
which fails only in production, is the exact shape FL20 exists to
remove — it would have been odd to fix it in the contract and reproduce
it in the framework's own code.

### local now enforces a limit it does not need

`checkIndexed` refuses an indexed value past 1500 bytes on the LOCAL
backend, which indexes nothing and scans. It buys local nothing and
buys the developer the only thing that matters: a 2 KB indexed title
fails on the laptop where it was written rather than on the first
deploy. The message is one shared `backends.IndexedTooLong`, so the two
backends cannot drift in wording — the same reasoning as
`ErrPageNeedsOrder`.

### Mutation proofs

The two directions fail differently, and both were broken and watched:

| Mutation | Caught by |
|---|---|
| index every mirrored scalar (the pre-FL20 behaviour) | `TestOnlyDeclaredFieldsGoUpIndexed` — "a 5 KB body is refused for an index nobody asked for"; `TestAnEntityWithNoDeclaredFieldsIndexesNothing` |
| exclude everything (index nothing) | `TestOnlyDeclaredFieldsGoUpIndexed` — "went up EXCLUDED — a filter on it would match nothing, and Datastore reports no error for that"; `TestAnIndexedValuePastTheCapIsRefusedBeforeItIsSent` |

The second mutation is the one that mattered. Over-indexing fails the
write loudly; under-indexing fails the read silently. A fix that traded
one for the other would have looked like progress and passed a suite
that only tested the first.

### Where the proof had to live

Conformance states the contract but proves it only against a live
project, and against `local` all three new cases pass **before and
after** the fix. So the binding proof is
`pkg/backends/gcp/entity_index_test.go`, asserting the properties
handed to Datastore — the one place the defect ever existed.

### What this fixes, concretely

`examples/journal`'s `Post` tags two of six fields. Before this,
`owner`, `title`, `body` and `id` all went up indexed — so a deployed
journal could not have stored a post longer than about 250 words, and
the error would have named an index nobody wrote. Every local test
passed.

### Not covered

The live path. These cases prove what tako sends; only `-backend=gcp`
conformance against a real project proves Datastore accepts it. That
check is outstanding and is named as such in `validate/entity-index.md`.

### Discovered work

- **43. The analyzer's derived index set and the struct tags are two
  sources.** `Resource.Indexes` comes from `Where`/`OrderBy` call sites
  and drives composite-index creation; the write path now uses the tag
  set. They cannot currently disagree (`indexedField` refuses an
  untagged field), so this is not a bug — but nothing enforces that
  invariant, and it is the kind that stops being true quietly.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples
green under `tako test`, unchanged. Scripted walk:
`validate/entity-index.md`, every step run.

---

## SC2 — shipped, with one gate outstanding (2026-08-10)

Approved 2026-08-10 ("Carry on then"), after both questions were ruled
on. `pkg/provision/gcp/setup.go`, `setup_test.go`, `setupdoc_test.go`,
`cmd/tako/setup.go`, `preflight.go` (Requirements extracted, gap texts
retargeted), `gcp.go` (two hosts, one verb classification),
`docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md`, `validate/setup.md`.

**Read the outstanding gate first** (below). Everything here runs
against a fake project; none of it has touched a real one.

### Built as ruled

**Tighter permissions, always.** `Requirements(needs)` returns the APIs
and permission→role pairs THIS graph needs, and setup grants exactly
those. No full bundle, no `--minimal`. An app with no queues is never
granted `pubsub.admin`, and a test says so.

The consequence, accepted: setup is re-run as the app grows. So
preflight's gap text now names it — `enable it with the rest: tako
setup --project p` rather than a raw gcloud line — and a test pins that,
because a gap that told the user to paste a binding would route them
around the command that exists to do it.

**The database is its own command**, `tako datastore create --region
<r>`, with `--region` required and refused BEFORE the project is
resolved: the refusal needs nothing from the cloud, and meeting "no
project set" first would teach the wrong lesson.

### One table, two readers

`Requirements` was extracted from `Preflight` rather than written
beside it. Two derivations would eventually disagree, and the failure
would be setup granting a set preflight still called incomplete — a
user told to run the command they had just run.

### What the doc guard found

`TestEveryRoleSetupCanGrantIsInThePermissionsDoc` failed on its first
run and turned up three real defects in a table that has been the
documented setup for months:

1. **`artifactregistry.writer` was not enough.** The deploy CREATES the
   repository; only `.admin` grants `repositories.create`. A deployer
   granted exactly what the table said failed on their first deploy.
2. **`resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin` was missing entirely**, though
   preflight has required `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` all
   along — every derived runtime grant is a policy write.
3. **`serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin`** was needed the moment setup
   started enabling APIs.

The first two mean the documented one-time setup has been quietly
incomplete for anyone who followed it literally. Corrected, and now
held by a test: every role tako can grant must appear in the table. The
table may list more — it is the "grant once and stop thinking" maximum
while setup grants a graph's subset — but never less.

### The CI case, which is easy to get silently wrong

`testIamPermissions` answers for the CALLER. Using it to decide what a
`--member serviceAccount:…` already holds would report every role as
held (the human running setup holds them), grant the service account
nothing, and print success — leaving CI unable to deploy with no
message anywhere. So `PlanSetup` takes `self`, and reads the policy
directly for anyone else.

### Existing guards that caught this work

Worth recording, because they are the repo's own immune system:

- `TestEveryCustomMethodPostIsClassified` rejected `:batchEnable` until
  it was classified. It is idempotent-mutating: enabling an enabled
  service is a no-op, and it is the call a flaky first setup most wants
  retried, since everything after it fails citing a disabled API.
- The doc guard above, on its first run.

### THE GATE, mostly closed (2026-08-10)

Owner supplied `tako-test-01` the same day. Full transcripts in
`validate/setup.md` §6; what the live run proved:

- **The tighter set, in real data.** One project, one principal, and a
  different answer per graph: hello 4 APIs/6 roles, blog 5/7, shortlink
  7/9, gallery 10/11.
- **A real gap, seen only by the graph that needs it.**
  `cloudscheduler` was disabled (no jobs existed, and the command under
  test puts it back). gallery, which declares a cron, planned it;
  hello, in the same project at the same moment, said `nothing to do`.
- **Apply and idempotence.** `✓ enabled 1 API(s): cloudscheduler`,
  confirmed with `gcloud services list --enabled`, and an immediate
  re-run reporting `nothing to do`. `services:batchEnable` behaves as
  assumed and its idempotent-mutating classification holds.
- **`DatastoreExists` is right** (gallery's remainder correctly said
  nothing about a database), and creating one anyway produced the
  intended conflict message.
- **The CI path** — the one that could have failed silently. A
  throwaway service account planned as `6 to grant, 0 already held`
  against a project where the caller holds everything. Had this used
  `testIamPermissions` it would have said "6 already held, nothing to
  do" and granted nothing. Deleted afterward.

It also turned up a cosmetic defect no fake would have: a doubled blank
line before `--plan: nothing was changed`. Fixed.

**The IAM write, authorized and run.** `✓ granted 6 role(s)`, verified
against `gcloud projects get-iam-policy` before and after: all six
landed on the probe, and `changes to anything NOT the probe: none`
across 13 existing bindings. That last line is the one that mattered —
an IAM policy is a document written whole, so the read-modify-write
either preserves every other principal or quietly removes people.
`TestApplyingKeepsBindingsItDidNotComeFor` asserts it against a fake;
this proves it against a real policy. Re-running granted nothing.

**And the ruling's consequence, live.** The same principal planned
against gallery rather than hello: `5 to grant, 6 already held` —
datastore.indexAdmin, cloudscheduler.admin, pubsub.admin and the two
secretmanager roles. "Re-run as the app grows" doing precisely what the
tighter set intended, incrementally, against a real policy.

Cleanup: six bindings removed, the service account deleted, the policy
diffed back to identical with where it started (13 bindings, `policy
restored: True`). `tako-test-01` is as it was found.

### A brand-new project found two defects (tako-test-04, 2026-08-10)

The owner asked for a fresh project. It was the highest-yield hour of
the whole slice.

**1. `tako setup` could not prepare a project — and `tako deploy` would
have failed too.** A new GCP project has `serviceusage` on and
`cloudresourcemanager` OFF. Every IAM read goes through the latter, so
setup asked about permissions and died citing a disabled API — the
command whose whole job is fixing that. Worse, `cloudresourcemanager`
was missing from `preflightAPIs` entirely, so a first deploy would have
failed at the `ProjectNumber` lookup and at every derived runtime grant.
Nobody had noticed because every project we had ever tested was already
warm.

Fixed: it is a required API, and `PlanSetup` reports
`PermissionsUnknown` instead of failing when IAM cannot be read. The
apply enables, waits for propagation (which is what `WaitForAPIs` was
written for — item 44 answered), then re-plans and grants inside the
same approved run.

**2. A billing failure was dressed as a permissions hand-over.** With
no billing account, `batchEnable` returns a 400 naming services the user
never mentioned. `handOver` matched any error mentioning "enable APIs",
so setup printed the full "somebody else must grant you permission"
block — whose commands fail identically. It sent the reader to a
colleague for a permission they already had, about a problem that
colleague could not fix either.

Fixed on both sides: billing gets its own text in `Classify` (triggered
by the real API error, since the pre-check cannot fire — `cloudbilling`
is itself disabled on a new project, the same chicken-and-egg), and
`handOver` now requires `you lack permission to`.

Regression tests for all of it:
`TestABrandNewProjectPlansTheAPIThatMakesIAMReadable`,
`TestNoBillingAccountSaysSo`,
`TestTheHandOverBlockIsOnlyForAPermissionDenial`.

**The lesson worth keeping:** every earlier validation ran against a
project that was already set up, so the one state `tako setup` exists to
handle was the one state never tested. A fake server modelled the
project we had, not the project a user starts with.

**Still unproven**, and honestly so:

- **The hand-over block in the wild**, which needs a principal WITHOUT
  `setIamPolicy`; the owner's account is not one. Its text and its
  discrimination are unit-tested.
- **The from-zero apply past the billing wall.** tako-test-04 had no
  billing account; the owner chose to delete the project rather than
  link one (2026-08-10). Everything up to that wall is proven live, and
  the sequence past it is covered by the fake. Redoing it live needs a
  billed project, and would be confirmation rather than discovery — the
  defects that path found are fixed and tested.
- **Item 44 is closed by the fix above**: the fresh-project path enables
  cloudresourcemanager and then immediately needs it for an IAM read,
  which is exactly the propagation window. `WaitForAPIs` is called there
  and is no longer dead code.

### Discovered work

- **44. `tako setup` does not wait for API enablement to propagate.**
  `waitForAPIs` exists and is not called: batchEnable returns before
  the change is visible, and a grant issued into that window can fail
  citing the API. Unproven either way without a live project, so it is
  filed rather than guessed at.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples
green under `tako test`. Scripted walk: `validate/setup.md`, steps 1–5
and 7 run; step 6 explicitly not.
