## SC4 — DX proposal: `tako secrets`, the value nobody can put anywhere (2026-08-10) — AWAITING APPROVAL

Fourth of the scaffolding series. SC1 and SC2 shipped 2026-08-10; SC3
(`tako new`) waits on the v0.1.0 tag, so SC4 goes next.

### The evidence

SC2's own output is the argument. `tako setup` ends by telling you what
it cannot do, and one of those lines is:

```
Still yours — tako cannot do these:
  · the secret notifier-key has no value — that is your data, not tako's
      printf '<value>' | gcloud secrets create notifier-key --data-file=- --project tako-test-01
```

Preflight has printed a version of that line for months. The value IS
the user's data — that part is right and does not change — but "tako
cannot create it" and "tako cannot help you put it anywhere" are
different claims, and only the first is true.

Locally it is worse, because there is no line at all:

- `.env` is hand-written, and its format is documented in a doc comment.
- Nothing lists what an app declares. You learn the name when boot
  refuses: `secret "notifier-key" is not set — add it to .env`.
- One at a time. Three declared secrets is three boot failures.

### The surface

```
tako secrets                       what this app declares, and which have a value
tako secrets set <name>            value from stdin, or prompted with echo off
tako secrets rm <name>             local only — see D5
```

**Local**, the dev-loop case:

```
$ tako secrets
tako secrets · local · .env
  NAME           VALUE     DECLARED AT
  notifier-key   set       app.go:41
  stripe-key     MISSING   app.go:42
  2 declared, 1 without a value — tako dev will refuse to boot
```

```
$ tako secrets set stripe-key
  value: ········
  ✓ wrote stripe-key to .env
```

**Cloud**:

```
$ tako secrets --project acme-prod-4821
tako secrets · cloud · acme-prod-4821 / prod
  NAME           VALUE     PHYSICAL              DECLARED AT
  notifier-key   set       prod-notifier-key     app.go:41
  stripe-key     MISSING   prod-stripe-key       app.go:42
  2 declared, 1 without a value — those services will refuse to boot
```

```
$ printf '%s' "$KEY" | tako secrets set stripe-key --project acme-prod-4821
  ✓ created prod-stripe-key and added version 1
```

The physical column earns its place: the name in Secret Manager is
env-prefixed (`gcpb.SecretName`), so `prod-stripe-key` and
`staging-stripe-key` are different secrets from one declaration, and
an operator looking at the console needs to know which row is theirs.

### The decisions

**D1 — a value is never printed. Ever.** `tako secrets` shows `set` or
`MISSING`, never a value, and there is no `--show`, no `get`. A
secret manager you can `cat` teaches people to paste secrets into
terminals that are logged, shared and screen-shared. If you need the
value you have the console and an audit trail; tako will not be the
convenient way around that.

**D2 — a value never arrives as a flag.** No `--value`. It comes from
stdin (`printf '%s' "$KEY" | tako secrets set …`) or an echo-off
prompt, reusing SC1's `askTerminal`. `--value hunter2` lands in shell
history, in `ps`, and in any CI log that echoes its commands.

**D3 — the project is explicit, exactly as `tako users`.** No
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, no gcloud config.

This is now a rule rather than a special case, and it is worth naming
because SC2 went the other way on purpose:

> **Commands that write your DATA type the project. Commands that
> converge INFRASTRUCTURE infer it.**

`tako users` and `tako secrets` write things no later run re-derives —
a person, a value — so an inherited project is how a dev fixture or a
test key lands in production. `tako setup`, `deploy`, `prune` converge
what the code already says, and re-running fixes a wrong guess.

**D4 — `.env` must be gitignored, and tako checks.** `tako secrets set`
refuses to write a file `git check-ignore` does not claim:

```
tako: .env is not gitignored, and this writes a secret into it
      add it first — one line, once:
        echo '.env' >> .gitignore
      (examples/gallery commits a .env on purpose: a dummy value so the
       demo runs. That is a demo's choice, not a default.)
```

The convention exists today only as a comment inside
`examples/gallery/.env`. A comment is not a guard, and the failure it
prevents is the worst one in this whole series.

**D5 — `rm` deletes in the cloud too, and fully** (owner, 2026-08-10;
my recommendation to leave it out was overruled).

That makes it the most destructive command in the series: deleting a
Secret Manager secret destroys the secret AND every version, permanently
— there is no undelete. So it sits on the ladder's bottom rung: typed
confirmation, always, and **`--yes` never applies**, exactly like
`tako destroy` and `prune --data`.

Locally it stays a convenience — `.env` is a file the user owns, and the
guide already says deleting `.tako` is the reset story — so it removes
the line and moves on.

The cloud transcript shows what is about to be lost before asking:

```
$ tako secrets rm stripe-key --project acme-prod-4821
tako secrets · cloud · acme-prod-4821 / prod
  prod-stripe-key   3 versions, created 2026-04-02, updated 2026-08-01
  this destroys the secret and all 3 versions, permanently — Secret
  Manager has no undelete, and the versions ARE the audit trail.
  type the secret's name to confirm: stripe-key
  ✓ destroyed prod-stripe-key and 3 versions
```

**Declared and orphaned are different, and the message says which.**
The safe case is the one the ruling exists for — a value created in the
wrong project or under a wrong name, or left behind after a declaration
was removed:

```
  stripe-key is not declared by this app — an orphan, which is the safe
  case for this command.
```

The dangerous case gets its own sentence, because the consequence is
specific and immediate:

```
  stripe-key IS declared, at app.go:42. Every service that resolves it
  refuses to BOOT without a value — this does not degrade, it stops the
  next deploy and the next cold start.
```

It still proceeds after the typed name. Refusing would block the exact
cleanup the ruling asked for, and an operator who has read that sentence
and typed the name has made a decision, not a mistake.

**Individual versions are still out of scope.** Disabling or destroying
one version of a live secret is rotation, which has an ordering and a
rollback story tako has no opinion about. The whole-secret delete is a
different act — "this should not exist" — and that is the one being
added.

### Cloud errors & permissions

Needed: `roles/secretmanager.admin` to create a secret and add a
version. Already in the Layer 1 table AND derived by `Requirements`
when the graph declares any secret — so `tako setup` grants it, which
is the whole point of the two commands landing in sequence.

```
tako: you lack secretmanager.admin on acme-prod-4821 — grant it with the rest:
        tako setup --project acme-prod-4821
```
```
tako: secretmanager.googleapis.com is disabled on acme-prod-4821 — enable it
      with the rest: tako setup --project acme-prod-4821
```
```
tako: this app declares no secrets — tako.Secret("name") is what puts one here
```
```
tako: "stripe-ke" is not a secret this app declares
      declared: notifier-key, stripe-key (tako.Secret)
      did you mean stripe-key?
```

That last one is SC1's role check, in the same shape and for the same
reason: writing a value under a name nothing reads is a silent no-op.

### Non-goals

- **No reading values back** (D1), and therefore no `tako secrets get`.
- **No rotation, expiry or per-version policy.** Adding a version is the
  whole write surface, and `rm` removes a secret entirely (D5);
  disabling or destroying ONE version of a live secret is rotation, and
  belongs in the console.
- **No `.env` for tests.** `NewTestApp` deliberately does not read it —
  a test says what it depends on via `app.SetSecret`. That difference
  is documented as a feature and stays one.
- **No secret values in the AppGraph, ever**, and no caching to disk.
- **No `--env` shortcut for copying a value between environments.**
  "Promote staging's key to prod" is a decision, not a convenience.

### Test plan (test-first)

1. **A guard that no value can reach stdout.** The strongest available
   version: `tako secrets` and `tako secrets set` run against a store
   holding a known sentinel value, and the test fails if the sentinel
   appears anywhere in their output. That is the one property D1 is.
2. **The gitignore refusal**, in a real temp git repo — `.env` ignored
   and not, both asserted.
3. **Golden transcripts and every error text**, as SC1.
4. **Local round-trip**: set, then `tako dev`'s boot resolves it (the
   real `local.LoadEnvFile` path, not a mock), and an existing `.env`
   keeps its comments and its other lines.
5. **`validate/secrets.md`**, including a live run against
   `tako-test-01`, which already has `secretmanager` enabled and a
   `notifier-key` gap that gallery declares — so the cloud half has a
   real target on day one.

### Ruled

**D5 → the cloud `rm` is in, as a full delete** (owner, 2026-08-10),
overruling my recommendation. Designed above: typed confirmation,
`--yes` never applies, the version count and dates shown before the
prompt, and a different sentence for a declared secret than for an
orphan.

The test plan gains two cases for it:

6. **`--yes` does not answer this prompt.** The ladder's rule is that
   the bottom rung has no flag, and the way that breaks is somebody
   adding `--yes` handling for consistency with the rung above.
7. **A wrong typed name deletes nothing**, asserted against a fake that
   fails the test if any DELETE arrives.

### Gate

Stopping here. No code written. SC4 is now fully specified.

## SC4 — shipped (2026-08-10)

Approved 2026-08-10 ("Build it"), with D5 ruled the other way from my
recommendation the same day. `pkg/provision/gcp/secrets.go`,
`pkg/backends/local/envfile.go` (writer), `cmd/tako/secrets.go`,
`cmd/tako/secrets_test.go`, `validate/secrets.md`, plus the SC2 fix
below.

### The two properties, and how they are held

**No value is printed.** `TestNoCommandEverPrintsAValue` seeds a
sentinel, runs every subcommand, and fails if it appears in output OR in
an error. Written as "can a value reach the output by any path" rather
than "does list have a value column", because the way this stops being
true is a column added for debugging. Nothing in
`pkg/provision/gcp/secrets.go` calls `:access`, so there is no code path
from a stored value to a terminal.

**No value arrives as a flag.** stdin or an echo-off prompt, reusing
SC1's `askTerminal`.

### The rule, now stated rather than implied

`tako users` was an exception; `tako secrets` makes it a rule, and
`tako --help` and `reference/cli.md` both carry it:

> Commands that CONVERGE INFRASTRUCTURE may infer a project, because
> re-running fixes a wrong guess. Commands that WRITE YOUR DATA may not,
> because nothing re-derives a person or a secret.

### The gitignore guard

`tako secrets set` refuses a `.env` that `git check-ignore` does not
claim. The convention existed only as a comment inside
`examples/gallery/.env` — and that file is exactly what the guard fired
on during validation, which is why its message names the case.

### What SC4 found in SC2, one day old

`setup`'s remainder listed every declared secret as valueless without
checking, so against `tako-test-01` it told an operator to create
`notifier-key` — which existed, with a version in it. It checks now, and
names `tako secrets set` instead of a raw gcloud line. A command that
reports a gap that is not there is worse than one that reports nothing:
the second time it is right, nobody believes it.

### Live validation (tako-test-01)

Full transcripts in `validate/secrets.md` §6. Proven against the real
project: list with version counts, `set` adding a version (1 → 2,
re-read to confirm), the typed-name refusal deleting NOTHING (confirmed
with `gcloud secrets describe`), and the real delete (confirmed
`NOT_FOUND` after). The orphan-vs-declared message was exercised on an
orphan, which is the safe case the ruling exists for.

### Corrections to the proposal

- The proposal's transcript showed `prod-stripe-key` as the physical
  name in prod. Wrong: `Prefixed` leaves the DEFAULT env unprefixed, so
  in prod the physical name is the declared name. The command shows the
  real one, which is the argument for showing it at all.
- I nearly shipped a second `SecretName` in `pkg/provision/gcp`, which
  is the exact drift this codebase spent the week removing. Deleted; the
  CLI uses `pkg/backends/gcp`'s, the one a deployed service resolves
  with.

### Existing guards that caught this work

`TestEveryCustomMethodPostIsClassified` rejected `:addVersion` until it
was classified. Non-idempotent: a retry after a response tako never saw
leaves two versions holding one value — harmless to read, and a phantom
entry in an audit trail somebody later has to explain.

### Discovered work

- **45. `tako secrets` makes one API call per declared secret.** Fine at
  gallery's one; an app with a dozen pays a dozen round trips on `list`.
  Secret Manager has a list endpoint that would answer in one.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples
green under `tako test`. Scripted walk: `validate/secrets.md`, every
step run, including the live half.

---

## SC5 + SC3 — design and build, self-directed (2026-08-10)

Owner: *"Do them both, design and implementation non stop, if multiple
options exist, ask yourself, come with a proposal and follow it."* So
the decisions below are mine, recorded before the code rather than
after, and the reasoning is here to be overruled later.

### SC5 — `runtime.BootGCPWith`

**The ask** (flauta friction, 2026-08-09): they needed a CLI that writes
into a deployed store. `runtime.BootGCP()` takes no arguments and reads
`TAKO_PROJECT`/`TAKO_APP`/`TAKO_ENV`/`TAKO_SERVICE`, so their tool set
those variables in-process and then called it. Their words: *"the target
of a CLI run is an argument, not an ambient fact, and a process that
mutates its own environment to configure a library is a shape worth not
spreading."*

**Decision — export the function, not a new options type.**
`gcpb.Options` is already exported and is already what `BootGCP` builds.
Adding a second struct to avoid naming `pkg/backends/gcp` would be a
type whose only job is to be copied into another type.

```go
func BootGCPWith(opts gcp.Options) error   // explicit target
func BootGCP() error                        // reads the env, calls the above
```

**Decision — the two paths get different refusals**, because they are
different bugs. A missing `TAKO_PROJECT` in a generated main means the
deploy failed to inject it (a tako bug, and it says so). A missing
`Options.Project` in a hand-written tool means the caller left it out.
One message cannot be right for both.

**Decision — `Env` is required, not defaulted to prod.** Env is the
Datastore namespace and the name prefix. A tool that silently addresses
prod because a field was empty is the exact hazard the SC1/SC4 project
rule exists for. `BootGCP` still gets it from the environment, where the
deploy always sets it.

### SC3 — `tako new`

**The gap**: the guide's entry point is "the six examples". There is no
documented path from `go install tako` to an app of your own beyond
three shell commands in the README — fine for an API, and wrong for a
site, where the missing pieces (`web/templates/layout.html`, a page
template, the site declaration) fail with `the site has no templates/
directory`.

**Decision — two kinds, `api` and `site`.** Not `worker`: a worker is a
`tako.Queue` and a handler inside a package that already exists, so
scaffolding one produces a project that does nothing until you add an
endpoint anyway. The value is in the file *pairs* a site needs, not in
generating a line of Go anybody can type.

**Decision — the scaffold pins the version of tako that generated it**,
read from `debug.ReadBuildInfo()`. A CLI and an SDK that disagree is a
support question nobody can answer from the transcript; this way the
go.mod says which binary made it.

**Decision — and when that version is `(devel)`, say so and offer
`--replace`.** A tako built from a checkout has no published version to
pin. Rather than write a go.mod that cannot resolve, `tako new` writes
the require, runs `go mod tidy`, and on failure prints both ways
forward. `--replace <path>` writes the replace directive for a local
checkout, which is what makes the command usable today, before v0.1.0
is tagged.

**Decision — the module path defaults to the directory name**,
`--module` overrides. `go mod init hello` is what the README already
tells people to type; matching it means the scaffold is not a third
convention.

**Decision — `.gitignore` is generated, with `.env` in it.** SC4 refuses
to write a secret into a `.env` git would commit. A `tako new` that did
not create that line would be shipping the failure SC4 exists to
prevent, one project at a time.

**Non-goals.** No template repository, no `--from <url>`, no interactive
wizard, no framework-version upgrade command. `tako new` writes the
smallest thing that runs and gets out of the way.

### SC5 + SC3 — shipped (2026-08-10)

Both built without a gate, as instructed. Transcripts in
`validate/new.md`.

**SC5** — `runtime.BootGCPWith(gcp.Options)`. `BootGCP` now reads the
env and calls it; both reach one shared `bootGCP`. The API lock gained
exactly one symbol, regenerated deliberately.

The refusals are the design: `BootGCPWith` names the missing field and
does NOT say "this is a tako bug" — that sentence belongs to the
generated-main path, where an empty `TAKO_PROJECT` really is the
deploy's failure, and telling a hand-written caller their own omission
is tako's fault sends them to file an issue. `Env` is required rather
than defaulted, because it is the Datastore namespace.

`TestTheCloudBootWiresTheMetricsBackend` now reads the shared body
rather than either entry point — item 38's lesson applied before it
cost anything this time.

**SC3** — `tako new <name> [--kind api|site] [--module] [--replace]`.

### Two things the build changed about the design

Both are the same lesson, and it is the one worth keeping: **a
scaffold's bar is "the next command works", and it is easy to be one
step short of it.**

1. **`go mod tidy` cannot see the generated main.** It skips
   dot-directories, and generated code lives in `.tako/gen`. The first
   working version resolved the app's own imports, reported success, and
   `tako dev` died with six `missing go.sum entry` lines naming
   goldmark, bluemonday and x/net — packages the user has never heard
   of. Fixed by fetching `pkg/runtime` by name. Guarded, because the
   failure is invisible until somebody runs the app.

2. **A `go build` binary reports a pseudo-version, not `(devel)`.** The
   design branched on `(devel)`; Go actually stamps
   `v0.0.0-20260811030652-…+dirty` from VCS state, which is equally
   unfetchable. `released()` now recognises only a real tag.

Neither was visible from the design. Both were found by running the
thing the command produces, which is the only test that means anything
for a scaffold.

### Discovered work

- **46. `tako new` needs `--replace` until v0.1.0 is tagged.** Not a
  defect — the refusal says exactly why and prints the command with the
  flag — but the plain `tako new <name>` path is unexercised, and it is
  the one every user will take. Worth re-running §1 of `validate/new.md`
  the day the tag lands.

### Gate (agent-side)

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` green at the root. All seven examples
green under `tako test`. Both scaffolded kinds built, booted and served:
`{"message":"Hello, ada!"}` and a rendered page.

## CR — the full-repo code review, and its fixes (2026-08-11)

A review over all of tako (~40k lines of non-test Go, 17 packages),
looking for simplifications, organization, security, inconsistency and
semantic divergence. Fourteen findings, all fixed, each with a test that
fails without the fix. Four commits: 1de878d, 5c398b5, 5be680c, 28734b8.

**Security (all confirmed by reproduction before the fix)**

- **CR1** Reflected XSS on the DEPLOYED sign-in page: `?next=` went into
  a JS string literal via `%q`, which escapes what breaks a Go literal
  and not `</script>`. Plus an open redirect (`//evil.example` passes
  `HasPrefix(next, "/")`) in three places, and a second XSS on the dev
  page where the same value went into an attribute unescaped — forty
  lines from a call site that escapes it. One `safeNext` origin rule,
  per-sink escaping, and an enforcing `script-src` CSP with a
  per-response nonce on tako's own pages.
- **CR2** `Route{Private: true}` on a deployed public route issued NO
  IAM call: `allowPublic` only ever added `allUsers`. The service stayed
  open, and since `isPublic` feeds `liveHash` the plan reported it as
  changed on every deploy without converging. It was also a blind
  `setIamPolicy` carrying one binding, which replaces the policy —
  destroying the invoker grants and any human's binding every deploy,
  against the read-modify-write rule `grants.go` states. Now reconciles
  both ways, with the etag, writing nothing when already correct.
- **CR3** `/_tako/push` authenticated nothing, though its doc promised
  Phase F would. Now verifies the Google-signed OIDC token both
  deliverers already carry, sharing the cron route's check; the deploy
  injects `TAKO_PUSH_AUDIENCE`/`TAKO_PUSH_INVOKER`. Fails closed in the
  cloud, skipped locally.
- **CR5** A local signed GET served uploaded bytes with the uploader's
  content type, no `nosniff`, from the app's own origin — local was the
  more dangerous of the two backends, since GCS serves from elsewhere.

**Correctness**

- **CR4** `BlobHandler` minted a fresh request id (breaking trace
  chains) and skipped `callContext` (no deadline, no session for its own
  Calls). A mis-typed remote transport silently ran the callee's handler
  in the caller's process against the caller's backends; now an error.
- **CR6** Nothing validated the CHARACTERS of a declared name, while
  `CheckNames` claimed they were guaranteed. New `tako/resource-name`,
  scoped to bucket/queue/topic and Cloud Tasks' charset — not to
  Counter/Histogram/Secret, where underscores and capitals are legal.
- **CR7** Env isolation is a prefix with no separator, so it is not
  injective: topic `orders` in `--env staging` and topic
  `staging-orders` in prod are one topic. Refused at deploy time.
  **Discovered work:** the structural fix is a separator a name cannot
  contain, which renames every physical resource in every deployed app.
- **CR8** `entity:"index"` on a `json:"-"` field indexed a key no
  document carries — the silent empty read FL20 exists to remove.
- **CR10/CR11** setup named the wrong secret when one name was a suffix
  of another; a DISABLED version read as "set".

**Consistency** — CR9 (piped secrets truncated at the first line),
CR12 (a shared refusal naming the wrong command), CR13 (`--data`
accepted by promote/rollback, flags after it ignored), CR14 (`secrets
rm` unreachable for the orphan case it exists for), plus `destroy`
saying which data it leaves behind, six simplifications, and `tako new`
documented in the pages `tako docs` serves.

**Validation** — `go vet` clean, root suite green, all seven examples
green under `tako test`, a scaffolded site app booted and served, and
the sign-in guard checked live against journal:

```
$ curl -s 'localhost:8124/_tako/signin?next=/"><script>alert(1)</script>'
name="next" value="/&#34;&gt;&lt;script&gt;alert(1)&lt;/script&gt;"
$ curl -s 'localhost:8124/_tako/signin?next=//evil.example'
name="next" value="/"
$ curl -si 'localhost:8124/_tako/signin' | grep -i content-security
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
```

**Not done, deliberately** — the app-wide CSP is still
`Report-Only` with no reporting endpoint, so it neither blocks nor
reports. Making it enforcing would break user templates carrying inline
script or style; that is a product decision with a migration story and
needs its own DX proposal. Recorded as discovered work.

## CR7b — DX proposal: env separation that is parseable, not just checked (2026-08-11) — AWAITING APPROVAL

### A correction to the recommendation that produced this task

I proposed this as "the fix, before the tag, because after v0.1.0 it is a
migration". Working the algebra to write the proposal weakened the
premise, so it goes first.

The shipped CR7 check (`checkCollisions`) refuses two DECLARED names that
become one physical name in some environment. I described that as partial.
It is not:

> Two declarations `a` and `b` collide iff `e1-a == e2-b` for some pair of
> environments. Take `|a| < |b|`. Both are suffixes of the same string, so
> `a` is a suffix of `b`; the character before it is the separator, so `b`
> ends with `-a`. Both are declared, so the shipped scan — which tests
> every declared name against every other declared name's `-`-suffix —
> already refuses it. The prod case (`a == e2-b`) is the same statement
> with `e1` empty.

So for declared-versus-declared, under the one-app-one-project doctrine
(`RepoName`'s comment, `desired.go:56`), **the shipped check is complete**.
What it does not cover is narrower than I implied:

1. **Declared versus DERIVED, across environments.** A bucket `photos`
   publishes on `photos-uploaded` in prod. An app deployed `--env photos`
   declaring a topic `uploaded` produces the same name. Requires an
   environment named after a bucket.
2. **Declared versus a SERVICE-derived name.** `<service>-dead`,
   `<name>-sa`, `<queue>-tako`. A declared queue named
   `gallery-makethumb-dead` collides with that worker's dead-letter topic.

Both are reachable and neither is likely. So this is no longer "fix the
hole"; it is a judgment about whether env separation should be
**parseable** rather than merely **checked**, and it is worth deciding
before a tag only because the rename is free today and is not free after.

### What the user sees

**Physical names gain a double hyphen, in non-prod environments only.**

```
                      today            proposed
prod    topic orders  orders           orders          (unchanged)
staging topic orders  staging-orders   staging--orders
pr-42   bucket photos p-app-pr-42-photos  p-app-pr-42--photos
staging service api   staging-api      staging--api
staging secret key    staging-key      staging--key
```

**Prod does not move.** `Prefixed` returns the base name unchanged for
`DefaultEnv`, so every name in a production deployment — flauta's
included — is byte-identical before and after. The blast radius is
preview and staging environments, which are the ones built to be torn
down.

**Two declaration rules tighten**, and they are what makes the separator
safe rather than merely different: a `--` in either half would make the
split ambiguous again.

```
app.go:12:19: tako.Topic name "order--placed" cannot contain "--" — a double
              hyphen separates the environment from the name (staging--orders),
              so a name carrying one could not be told from an environment
              (tako/resource-name)

$ tako deploy --env pr--42
--env "pr--42" cannot contain "--"

    a double hyphen separates the environment from the resource name
    (staging--orders), so an environment carrying one could not be told
    from the name beside it. Try --env pr-42.
```

Neither costs anything today: no example, and no environment anyone has
deployed, uses `--`.

**Operators get something they did not have.** `staging-orders` does not
say whether the environment is `staging` or the topic is called that.
`staging--orders` does, in the console, in `gcloud` output, and in a
billing export — none of which have the graph to ask.

### The migration, and the one thing it must not do automatically

Renaming means the old resources become orphans. `tako prune` already
deletes labelled stateless orphans (topics, subscriptions, services,
indexes, SAs) and holds data behind `--data`, so the machinery exists.
What it must not do is pretend a rename moves anything:

- **Buckets** — the objects do not move. A renamed bucket is a new, empty
  bucket, and the old one keeps the data until somebody says otherwise.
- **Secrets** — the VALUE does not move, and tako has never created one.
  A renamed secret has no version, so every service resolving it refuses
  to boot. This is the sharp edge of the whole change.
- **Queues and topics** — messages in flight at the moment of the deploy
  are in the old topic and are not redelivered from the new one.

So the proposed story is **rebuild, not migrate**, and only for non-prod:

```
$ tako deploy --env staging
tako deploy · my-project (staging)

  ⚠ environment separation changed in v0.1.0

    Names in this environment now separate the env with "--":
      staging-orders   →  staging--orders     topic
      staging-api      →  staging--api        run service
      staging-key      →  staging--key        secret
      …14 more

    This deploy CREATES the new ones. It does not move anything into
    them: a bucket's objects, a secret's value and any message in
    flight stay where they are.

    Non-prod environments are meant to be rebuilt, and that is the
    supported path:
      tako destroy --env staging     (types the app name; deletes data)
      tako deploy  --env staging
      tako secrets set <name> --project my-project --env staging

    prod is unaffected — its names never carried a prefix.

  continue and create the new names? [y/N]
```

The prompt is rung two of the ladder: recoverable, y/N, `--yes`
pre-answers it in CI. It is not rung three, because this deploy destroys
nothing — the old resources are still there, and removing them is
`prune`'s or `destroy`'s act with their own confirmations.

### Options

| | What | Cost | Buys |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | `--` separator, prod unchanged (**proposed**) | every non-prod name; two new declaration rules; one release note | parseable names; both residual collision classes gone |
| **B** | `--` everywhere, including prod | every name in every deployment, flauta's included | one rule with no special case |
| **C** | Extend the shipped check to derived names; no rename | ~40 lines, no migration, no release note | the two residual classes refused, names unchanged |
| **D** | Nothing further | zero | — |

**B** is rejected: it renames production to remove a special case that is
already documented and tested, and `DefaultEnv`-goes-unprefixed is what
SC4's secret naming is built on.

**D** is defensible now that the declared-versus-declared case is proved
complete, and would be my answer if a tag were not imminent.

### My recommendation, and it is not the one I gave you

**C now, A only if you want parseable names.**

The argument I made an hour ago — "fix the hole before it becomes a
migration" — does not survive the algebra above: the hole in the
realistic case is already closed. What A actually buys is that an
operator can read an environment out of a resource name, which is a real
but ordinary benefit, and it costs every non-prod name plus a release
note on the first tag tako has ever had.

C closes both residual classes for about forty lines and no migration at
all. It leaves names unparseable, which is a papercut nobody has reported
in a repo whose rule is *no feature without an example demanding it.*

If parseable names are worth a rename to you, A is the moment — the cost
is genuinely zero today and genuinely not zero after the tag. I would
rather you make that call knowing the collision argument no longer
carries it.

### Scope, either way

- No change to Datastore: env isolation there is the namespace, not a
  prefix, and namespaces do not concatenate.
- No `tako migrate`. Decision 12, and one app has ever needed this.
- `SAName`'s 6–30 char IAM window and `CheckNames`' 63-char bucket cap
  both already exist and both already guard; the separator adds one byte.

### Gate

Goldens for the two analyzer rules; `pkg/provision` name tests; a
conformance run; one full deploy/destroy cycle on `tako-test-01` under
`--env staging` proving the new names and that prod's are untouched;
transcripts in this log.

**Stopping here for approval — nothing is implemented.**

### CR7b — verdict: leave it (owner, 2026-08-11)

Option **D**. No rename, and not the forty-line extension either: the
declared-versus-declared case is proved closed by the shipped check, and
the two residual classes are not worth code in a repo whose rule is *no
feature without an example demanding it.* Recorded rather than fixed —
if an app ever meets one, the proposal above is written and the argument
does not need re-deriving.

- **47. Env separation is checked, not parseable, and two derived-name
  collision classes stay open.** `Prefixed` is `env + "-" + base`. The
  shipped `checkCollisions` refuses every collision between two DECLARED
  names (proof in CR7b). Still reachable, and unrefused: a declared name
  colliding across environments with a name tako DERIVES —
  `<bucket>-uploaded`, `<service>-dead`, `<name>-sa`, `<queue>-tako`.
  Both need an environment named after one of the app's own resources.
  Also, `staging-orders` does not say whether the env is `staging`, which
  costs an operator reading the console or a billing export. The fix is
  CR7b option A (a `--` separator, prod unaffected) and it gets more
  expensive after v0.1.0, when a rename stops being free. Owner declined
  2026-08-11, knowingly.

## Z6 — v0.1.0 tagged and pushed (2026-08-11)

`origin` is `github.com/gsandoval/tako`; main fast-forwarded 54 commits
(`7a40353..199e43a`) and **v0.1.0** is an annotated tag on `199e43a`.

### The fresh-project cycle, and the one thing it could not prove

The gate asks for a cycle against the PUBLISHED module path. The
repository is **private**, so `proxy.golang.org` and `sum.golang.org`
cannot see the tag, and a stranger's `tako new` fails on verification
before it reaches git:

```
$ tako new z6new
tako: could not resolve github.com/gsandoval/tako v0.1.0 — check your network or
      go mod tidy said:
      go: downloading github.com/gsandoval/tako v0.1.0
        verifying module: reading https://sum.golang.org/lookup/…@v0.1.0: 404 Not Found
        fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com'
```

Owner's ruling (2026-08-11): **stay private, validate the private path**
— which proves the tag is well-formed without publishing anything. With
`GOPRIVATE` set (bypassing both the proxy and the checksum database), the
whole cycle runs:

```
$ GOPRIVATE='github.com/gsandoval/*' tako new z6priv
tako new · z6priv
  + z6priv/.gitignore
  + z6priv/go.mod
  + z6priv/z6priv.go

  tako v0.1.0

Next:
  cd z6priv && tako dev

$ cat z6priv/go.mod
require github.com/gsandoval/tako v0.1.0        ← a tag, not a pseudo-version

$ curl localhost:8126/hello      {"message":"Hello from Tako!"}
$ curl localhost:8126/greet/ada  {"message":"Hello, ada!"}
$ curl -o/dev/null -w '%{http_code}' localhost:8126/greet/nobody   404

$ GOPRIVATE='github.com/gsandoval/*' tako new z6site --kind site
$ curl localhost:8127/ | grep h1
  <h1>Hello from Tako!</h1>
```

Both kinds scaffold, resolve against the tag, generate, build, boot and
serve — no `--replace` anywhere.

**Item 46 is closed on the half that was tako's.** The binary now stamps
`v0.1.0` (`released()` accepts it, the pseudo-version path is not taken)
and the scaffold pins it. What remains is not a tako defect: a module in
a private repository needs `GOPRIVATE` and repository access, whoever
publishes it.

- **48. `tako new`'s resolution failure blames the network for a PRIVATE
  module.** `unresolvedTako`'s non-dev branch says "check your network or
  GOPROXY", which is right for a public module that would not fetch and
  wrong for the state this repo is in: the 404 is `sum.golang.org` saying
  it has never heard of a private path, and the fix is `GOPRIVATE`, not a
  retry. Worth a third branch if tako stays private past the first
  outside user; moot the day the repository goes public.

### Z6 status

**Tagged and validated as far as private allows.** The public
fresh-project cycle — the gate's literal wording — remains unrun, and
will stay unrun until the repository is public. That is a visibility
decision, not an engineering one.
