## CR2 + CR3 — live validation on tako-test-01 (2026-08-11)

The two CR fixes with cloud surface had only fake-API and unit coverage.
This is the live walk. `examples/shortlink` (one public service, three
Pub/Sub-driven workers), deployed, exercised, flipped, re-deployed,
destroyed.

### CR3 — the push endpoint authenticates, and real deliveries still arrive

The deploy injects the pair the worker verifies against:

```
$ gcloud run services describe shortlink-countclick --format='…env…'
{'name': 'TAKO_PUSH_INVOKER',  'value': 'shortlink-countclick-sa@tako-test-01.iam.gserviceaccount.com'}
{'name': 'TAKO_PUSH_AUDIENCE', 'value': 'https://shortlink-countclick-119764066724.us-central1.run.app'}
```

and the subscription Google delivers with carries exactly those:

```
$ gcloud pubsub subscriptions describe shortlink-countclick
endpoint: https://shortlink-countclick-119764066724.us-central1.run.app/_tako/api/push
oidc:
  audience:            https://shortlink-countclick-119764066724.us-central1.run.app
  serviceAccountEmail: shortlink-countclick-sa@tako-test-01.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

Five resolves, five clicks, counted exactly once each through real
Pub/Sub push with the new check in the path:

```
$ curl .../api/links/cr3      → hits 5      (3 + 2 resolves, no double count)
$ gcloud run services logs read shortlink-countclick
  21:44:29 POST 204 …/_tako/api/push
  21:44:30 POST 204 …/_tako/api/push
```

**The scare, and what it actually was.** The first deliveries after a
fresh deploy answered 403, and the pipeline looked broken:

```
  21:42:19 POST 403 …/_tako/api/push   ×3
  21:42:32 POST 403 …/_tako/api/push   ×2
```

Not the new check — Cloud Run's front door, before the container. The
worker's `run.invoker` grant had been written seconds earlier and had
not propagated; Pub/Sub retried with backoff and every message acked
once it had (`204` from 21:43:05 on, and hits reached exactly 5). The
same propagation pacing C4's walk recorded. Verified by reading the live
policy, which held the binding throughout.

**It cost twenty minutes to establish that, which is a finding of its
own:** `verifyPushCaller` writes its refusal to the RESPONSE and nothing
to the log, so a rejected delivery is invisible to `tako logs` — the
operator sees a 403 in the request log and cannot tell tako's refusal
from the platform's. Recorded as **49**.

### CR2 — private actually closes, and the rest of the policy survives

Before: the service public, plus a foreign binding deliberately added by
hand — the half the old blind `setIamPolicy` destroyed on every deploy.

```
$ gcloud run services get-iam-policy shortlink
- members: [allUsers]                  role: roles/run.invoker
- members: [user:darchitect@gmail.com] role: roles/run.viewer     ← foreign
```

`Route{Private: true}` on shortlink's three routes, then `tako deploy`:

```
$ gcloud run services get-iam-policy shortlink
- members: [user:darchitect@gmail.com] role: roles/run.viewer     ← survived
                                                                  ← allUsers GONE
```

Both halves, against a real policy: the binding this used to be unable
to remove is removed, and the binding it used to remove without being
asked is untouched.

The ingress really closes — under 40 seconds for the revocation to
propagate:

```
$ curl -o/dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://shortlink-…-uc.a.run.app/api/links
200      (immediately after the deploy — authz still cached)
403      (t+20s)
```

And it CONVERGES, which is the symptom that used to persist forever:

```
$ tako deploy --project tako-test-01 --yes
      skip    run service shortlink
    0 creates, 0 updates, 45 skips, 0 orphans
```

### Teardown

`tako destroy` (typed app name) removed all four services, six topics,
subscriptions, queues, indexes, four SAs, the repo, 8 entities and the
framework bucket. `gcloud run services list`, `pubsub topics list` and
the tako SAs are all empty; only the project's own pre-existing
identities remain. `examples/shortlink/app.go` restored, tree clean, its
suite green.

- **49. A refused delivery is invisible in the logs.** `verifyPushCaller`
  and `CronDispatch` both answer the caller and log nothing, so an
  operator watching `tako logs` sees only the platform's request line and
  cannot tell "tako rejected this token" from "Cloud Run rejected this
  caller" — which are different problems with different fixes (a stale
  audience after a URL change versus a missing grant). Both should log
  the refusal at WARN with the reason. Found by spending twenty minutes
  on exactly that ambiguity during CR2/CR3's own validation.

### Verdict

**CR2 and CR3 hold in the cloud.** Agent-side validation complete; the
human row for the CR series is still unwritten.

## FL21 — templates are a tree (2026-08-11)

Asked for directly by the app that filed it, after the entry changed weight
twice.

### The gap

`RegisterSiteTemplates` read `templates/` with `fs.ReadDir` and skipped every
entry where `e.IsDir()`. A template in a subdirectory was never registered, and
`site.Render` named it back at you as not found.

Filed against tako on 2026-08-09 by an app with seventeen templates in one
folder — the admin's and the public site's — told apart by a filename prefix,
which is a convention rather than a boundary. It was **workaround-fine** then:
nothing was blocked and nothing was at risk.

It gained a second consumer the same day and a third on 2026-08-11. The app
now serves more than one site, a site bundle would naturally own
`sites/<name>/templates/`, and it cannot — so the entry stopped being about
tidiness and became the ceiling on how different a second site can look. Then
template editing in the admin became committed scope, and **a site that cannot
own a template cannot be given one to edit**.

### The fix, and the part a WalkDir alone would not have done

`fs.WalkDir` in place of `fs.ReadDir`, keyed by path relative to `templates/`.

The subtlety is that **`ParseFS` names a template after its base name**, so
walking a tree and parsing with `ParseFS` would have made `admin/nav.html` and
`site/nav.html` one template with the second silently winning — a worse failure
than the one being fixed, because it renders. So each template is parsed by
name instead:

```go
layout.New(rel).Parse(src)          // partials, into the shared base
t.New(rel).Parse(src)               // pages, into their own clone
```

The two-tier rule is untouched: a file defining `content` is a page and gets
its own clone, everything else is a partial parsed into the shared base. That
split was always path-agnostic. Only the **top-level** `layout.html` is the
shell; one deeper in the tree is an ordinary template with an ordinary name, so
a bundle can carry its own without becoming the root for everybody.

`site.Fragment` executes a template by its own name, so the name a partial is
defined under and the name it is looked up by have to be the same string —
which is why partials are keyed by path too, not just pages.

### Compatibility

**No exported symbol changed** (`docs/surface_test.go` unchanged), and no flat
site is renamed: for a template at the top level, path-relative-to-`templates/`
IS its base name.

Proven rather than argued — the 17-template app that filed the friction runs
its whole suite, golden HTML files included, against this build with no change
to a single template name or render call.

### Validation

```
pkg/runtime            6 new tests, 4 of which fail before the change
go test ./...          18 packages ok
go vet ./...           clean
the consumer's suite   ok (106s), golden files byte-identical
```

The four that fail first are the ones that matter: a page in a subdirectory, a
base-name collision, a nested partial used both by path and as a fragment, and
a nested `layout.html`. The two that pass before the change do so honestly —
the flat-site test is the compatibility claim, and the parse-error test passes
because "not found" also happens to name the path.

### Verdict

**Shipped.** Agent-side validation complete; the human row is unwritten, and
the consumer's own move — `git mv` its templates into two directories and turn
its prefix test into a path test — is that app's task, not this one.

## Items 49 and 43 — the two the last walk left behind (2026-08-12)

Both were discovered work, both filed by the walks that found them rather
than planned, and both turned out to be one sentence wide and worth more
than that.

## 49 — a refused trigger said nothing

`verifyPushCaller` and `CronDispatch` answered the caller and logged
nothing. The caller is Pub/Sub or Cloud Scheduler, which reads no
message and asks no questions, so the refusal reached nobody: `tako
logs` showed the platform's request line and that was the whole record.

**Why that costs an operator real time:** tako's 403 and Cloud Run's 403
are the same three digits from outside the container, and they are
different problems with different fixes — a stale audience after a
service URL change versus a missing `run.invoker` grant. This item was
filed from the inside of that ambiguity: twenty minutes of CR3's own
live validation went to establishing that fresh 403s were the platform's
front door and not the new check.

### What each refusal carries now

```
WARN tako refused this delivery handler=countClick status=403
  reason="delivery rejected: token audience is not this service"
  expected_audience=https://shortlink-countclick-119764066724.us-central1.run.app
  expected_invoker=shortlink-countclick-sa@tako-test-01.iam.gserviceaccount.com

WARN tako refused this cron trigger cron=nightly status=401
  reason="cron triggers carry an OIDC bearer token"
  expected_audience=... expected_invoker=...
```

Three deliberate choices:

- **WARNING, not ERROR.** A refused delivery is not the service failing;
  it is the service working. But it must be findable by severity next to
  the platform's own lines, which INFO would not be.
- **The expectations travel in the log**, not only in the response body,
  because comparing them against the deliverer's own `oidcToken` config
  IS the remediation. Neither is a secret: a service URL and an SA email,
  both readable from the deploy by anyone who can read the logs.
- **`reason.Error()`, not the error.** A JSON handler marshals a bare
  `errors.errorString` as `{}`, so logging the error value itself would
  have shipped a line with the reason silently missing — in the cloud
  only, where the JSON handler is installed and nobody is watching a
  terminal.

`logRefusal` is one function for both routes, for the same reason
`verifyGoogleToken` is one function for both routes: a second copy is
how one of them ends up quieter than the other. Cron grew a
`verifyCronCaller` mirroring `verifyPushCaller` so the two routes have
one shape.

The unknown-cron 404 is narrated too — it means the schedule outlived
the handler, and it is the one refusal below whose test cannot be
written: reaching it requires a token Google signed, so it is covered by
inspection only. Said plainly rather than left to look covered.

**Statuses and check order are untouched** and now noted as item 50:
push answers 500 for a missing identity and cron answers 403, and cron
checks the token before the identity while push checks the identity
first. Both are pre-existing, neither is wrong, and changing a status
inside a logging fix is how a logging fix breaks a retry policy.

## 43 — two readings of one struct tag

Filed as "not a bug, but nothing enforces it": the analyzer derives
composite indexes from the tags via `go/types`, the SDK writes documents
from the same tags via `reflect`, and nothing held the two readings
together.

**Examined, it was already a bug — twice.**

| tag | analyzer said | runtime said | encoding/json says |
|---|---|---|---|
| `json:"-,"` | property `-` | property `Owner` | **`-`** |
| `json:"a\"b"` | property `a"b` | property `a"b` | **`Owner`** |
| `json:"-"` + `entity:"index"` | indexed, property `Owner` | refused | not stored at all |

The first two are the silent failure FL20 exists to remove, arrived at
by disagreement instead of contradiction: an index provisioned on one
property name while the document carries another matches nothing, and
Datastore answers an empty result without erroring. The third is a
divergence my own CR/FL20 work introduced — the SDK started refusing
`entity:"index"` + `json:"-"` and the analyzer kept accepting it, so the
failure moved from analysis time (a file and a line) to first store use
in a deployed service, with composite indexes already provisioned on a
property no document has.

### The fix: one reading, and encoding/json as the oracle

`internal/entitytag` — `Kind`, `Name`, `Omitted`, taking the raw tag
string, which is what both callers already hold. Not a shared type
(there cannot be one across `go/types` and `reflect`), a shared **rule**.

The test is the part worth keeping. It does not re-read the spec; it
builds a struct via `reflect.StructOf` carrying the tag under test,
marshals it, and asserts `Name` reports **the key that actually came
out**:

```go
{`json:"-,"`,     "NOT the skip: a field named literally -"},
{`json:"a\"b"`,   "a quote is not legal: encoding/json ignores the whole name"},
{`json:"a b"`,    "a space is legal in a json name, surprisingly"},
```

A rule derived from reading the documentation would have agreed with
itself and still been wrong. The value is deliberately non-zero, because
with a zero one `omitempty` drops the field and every tag carrying it
reads as a skip — the first version of this test failed that way and was
telling the truth about the oracle, not about the rule.

`validName` mirrors `encoding/json`'s `isValidTag` character set,
including the space it allows and the quote it does not.

And the analyzer now refuses the contradiction the SDK refuses:

```
app.go:15:2: field Secret is tagged entity:"index" but json:"-" keeps it out of the stored document — an index on a field nothing writes matches nothing, silently; drop one of the two tags (tako/entity-index)
```

New rule id `entity-index`, documented in `docs/reference/errors.md` and
`docs/reference/entity.md`. **This is a new refusal an existing app
could hit** — flagged as such for the human rather than folded in
quietly; the text mirrors the SDK's already-approved one almost word for
word.

### Validation

```
internal/entitytag     3 tests; the old runtime rule fails 2 cases, the old analyzer rule fails 1
pkg/runtime            5 new tests, all 5 fail before item 49's change
root package           1 new test (json:"-," indexed as "-")
pkg/analyzer           1 new golden fixture, entityindextag
go test ./...          19 packages ok
go vet ./...           clean
gofmt -l               clean (3 committed test files had drifted; reformatted)
tako test              blog gallery hello journal shop shortlink siren — all ok,
                       against a CLI rebuilt with the new analyzer
```

The golden carries exactly one error for a fixture with two odd tags,
which is the point: `json:"-,"` beside it is accepted and indexed under
`-`, so the corner is handled rather than blanket-refused.

Mutation proofs, both directions: reinstating `name == "-"` (the old
runtime rule) fails the oracle on `json:"-,"` and `json:"-,omitempty"`;
dropping `validName` (the old analyzer rule) fails it on `json:"a\"b"`.

### Also done, in passing

- Dead `fields` counter in `analyzer.go` (incremented, then `_ = fields`).
- `tagValue` in `resources.go`, unused once `entitytag.Kind` replaced it.

### Discovered work

- **50. Push and cron refuse in two shapes.** A missing identity is 500
  on the push route and 403 on the cron route, and cron checks the
  bearer token before the identity while push checks the identity first.
  Neither is wrong; they should agree, and the honest status for tako's
  own missing configuration is 500 on both.

### Verdict

**Shipped.** Agent-side validation complete. The human rows for the CR
series, Z6, FL21 and these two are all still unwritten.

## DOC1 — documentation accuracy, held down by tests (2026-08-12)

Asked for directly: "focus on documentation accuracy and quality, it has
to be extremely good."

The docs already had real machinery — every page renders, every internal
link resolves, every exported symbol has a page, every `tako.X` the prose
names exists, every struct field it names exists. So the useful question
was not "are the docs good" but **which claims nothing could check**.
Three turned out to be false.

### 1. errors.md called itself the index and was missing a third of the rules

The page opens with "This page is the index" of every analysis error.
**Eighteen rule ids were in no table on it** — every role and policy rule
(`role-var`, `unexported-role`, `empty-role`, `policy-var`,
`unexported-policy`, `policy-private`, `const-role`), every alert rule
(`alert-condition`, `alert-subject`, `channel-binding`, `window`,
`quantile`, `status-class`, `scoped-label`), plus `resource-name`,
`route-conflict` and `reserved-prefix`.

These are not exotic. A door with no key (`empty-role`) and a private
route with a policy (`policy-private`) both describe an app that
compiles, deploys and refuses everybody; `route-conflict` is a startup
panic. A reader met all eighteen for the first time in their terminal.

Four new sections, seventeen rules, every text quoted verbatim from the
golden corpus. The eighteenth is below.

### 2. "The text is golden-tested" was true of 78 of 86 quoted lines

Six of the texts the page quoted had no fixture behind them, so they had
been transcribed by hand — and two had drifted into something no tako
build has ever printed:

```
- service X cannot be both latency (Web) and batch (Sweep) …
- service X cannot carry both traffic (timeout 45s) from Web and traffic (http2) from Api …
+ service mixedprofile cannot be both latency (Web) and batch (Sweep) …
+ service mixedtraffic-work cannot carry both traffic (http/2 end to end) from Work and traffic (timeout 45s) from mixedtraffic.Svc …
```

`X` was never a service name, and `http2` is not how the formatter
renders that setting — it prints "http/2 end to end".

**Six new fixtures** rather than six edits, because the fix for an
untested error text is a test: `pagebinding`, `jobbinding`, `jobnobody`,
`cronconfig`, `statuspage`, `mixedprofile`, `mixedtraffic`. Writing them
surfaced a structural fact worth recording: `Analyze` returns early if
the declaration phase produced any error, so whole-graph rules
(`job-binding`'s unbound job, `mixed-*`) can only be reached by a fixture
whose declarations are otherwise clean. That is why `jobnobody` exists
beside `jobbinding` instead of inside it.

Two quoted lines legitimately have no golden and now say so in the test:
the `unknown field Footprint` line is a Go type error (a fixture for it
could not load — which is the point that passage makes), and the
site-shadow line is a warning, pinned in `pkg/analyzer/shadow_test.go`.

### 3. `tako setup` and `tako datastore create` were documented nowhere

Not in `reference/cli.md`, not in the guide, not in any reference page —
`grep -rn "tako setup" docs/guide docs/reference` came back empty. Both
are prerequisites for a first deploy: setup enables the APIs and grants
the roles the graph needs, and `datastore create` makes the database
**whose location is permanent**. The documented path to a deploy skipped
them both, and `guide/cloud.md`'s "One-time project setup" section
described the automated parts while naming neither command.

Fixed in three places: cli.md's mutating table plus a section on each,
cloud.md's setup section (both commands, why datastore is separate), and
one line in `01-hello.md`, which had told a reader to run `tako deploy`
with nothing before it.

### The tests that keep all three true

`pkg/docserver/rules_test.go`, `pkg/docserver/clidoc_test.go` — with the
existing doc-accuracy tests, because that is where this kind of test
lives.

- **Every rule id ↔ errors.md, both directions.** Ids come from
  `Rule: "…"` literals in the analyzer plus every id the golden corpus
  emitted; the second half is what catches `alert-subject`, whose id
  reaches `Error.Rule` through a variable. Stated limit: a brand-new rule
  with neither a literal nor a fixture slips both — which is a rule with
  no test, already refused by the project's test-first rule.
- **Every message errors.md quotes came out of the corpus**, byte for
  byte, or is named in `notInTheCorpus` with its reason. 84 of 86 match;
  the two exceptions are the two above.
- **Every command the CLI dispatches appears in cli.md.**

Mutation-proofed, all three: deleting the `scoped-label` row, changing
`Status("503")` to `Status("500")` in a quoted line, and renaming
`tako setup` in the reference each fail with the message that names the
problem.

### Two code fixes the audit forced

- **One `alert-condition` message, not two.** Two reachable sites
  answered the same mistake ("that is not a reading I can read") with two
  different menus, and the shorter one was four options short — it told a
  reader `tako.Requests`, `tako.RequestMs`, `tako.ServicePercentile` and
  `tako.ServiceInstances` did not exist, depending on how they got it
  wrong. Now one `notAReadingMsg`, and the fixture covers both paths.
- **`tako/invalid-option` deleted.** It survived on `tako.Lock`, whose
  signature is `Lock(name string)` — so `call.Args[1:]` is empty for
  every input that compiles. Unreachable, unfixturable for the same
  reason, and errors.md had already described the rule as gone. The
  signature was doing the work; the rule was decoration.
- **`tako --help` had two commands' lines crossed**: `tako logs`'s
  description sat under `tako metrics`, leaving metrics undescribed and
  logs' summary attached to the wrong verb. cli.md had it right, which is
  how it was found.

### Also verified and left alone

The numeric claims scattered through the reference are all true: the
lease TTL (30s, `backends.LeaseTTL`), the histogram bounds (18 buckets
doubling from 1 → 262144), Cloud Tasks' 500/s rate ceiling, the cron
attempt deadline default (180s), `tako logs` having no `--severity`
flag, `tako.Cache` taking no options, three named profiles. Every
reference page is in the reference index, and every "Not yet" section
still describes a real limit. The guide's snippets match the examples
they cite — one identifier in chapter 2 (`published`) is journal's,
borrowed ahead of chapter 4, and now says so.

### Delivery security, which CR3 had made stale

`queue.md` still said the push endpoint was safe because the service is
private — "curl gets 403 at Google's front door" — which is exactly the
reasoning CR3 replaced. It now describes both doors and says which one
matters: "the service happens to be private" is a fact computed in
another package and one graph change away from being false. `topic.md`
gained the same pointer, and `observability.md` documents the refusal
line from item 49 as a Cloud Logging record, next to the JSON example
already there.

### Validation

```
go test ./...          19 packages ok
go vet ./...           clean
gofmt -l               clean
tako test              blog gallery hello journal shop shortlink siren — all ok,
                       against a CLI rebuilt with the new analyzer
new fixtures           7 (each generated with -update, then read)
new tests              3, all mutation-proofed in both directions
```

### Verdict

**Shipped.** Agent-side validation complete. What a test cannot reach is
still the human's: whether the new sections read as well as the ones they
sit beside.

## FL22 — `tako users` bills its own API calls (DX proposal)

Friction filed 2026-08-11 by flauta, verdict **promote-to-tako-task**: the
command the runbook names for making the first editor does not work for
the credentials an operator has.

```
$ tako users list --project tako-test-03
tako: this service may not list accounts on tako-test-03 — auth.Users() derives
      roles/identitytoolkit.admin at deploy time, so re-run tako deploy if this
      service started using it since the last one (The identitytoolkit.googleapis.com
      API requires a quota project, which is not set by default.)
```

Two things are wrong there and they are separate bugs.

### 1. The call is unbilled, and FL19 already fixed this once

`gcloud auth application-default login` mints a credential with no quota
project, so Google bills the call to the project behind gcloud's own
shared OAuth client. identitytoolkit refuses outright rather than
rate-limiting. The fix is the header FL19 added — and FL19 added it to
`pkg/provision/gcp/gcp.go:274`, which `tako deploy` uses. **`tako users`
goes through a different client**, `pkg/backends/gcp/client.go`'s `do`,
which sets `Content-Type` and nothing else. Same defect, second copy;
the copy an operator is told to run.

`gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project` does not help,
because the credential file's `quota_project_id` only matters if
something sends it as `x-goog-user-project`. Nothing did.

### 2. The 403 is misdiagnosed as a missing role

`UserStore.explain` (`users.go:267`) maps every 403 to "you lack
`identitytoolkit.admin`", and `usersCmd.cloudErr` says the same. flauta
granted the role; it changed nothing, because the refusal is about
billing attribution. A message that names the wrong fix costs more than
no message.

### The proposal

**Send the header only for user credentials.** `New` learns the
credential type once, via `google.FindDefaultCredentials`, and records a
quota project only when the credential JSON is `"type":
"authorized_user"`:

```go
// quotaProject is the project API calls are billed to, and it is set
// ONLY for user credentials. On Cloud Run the credential comes from the
// metadata server and bills correctly already — and a deployed service
// must not start sending a header that costs serviceusage.services.use,
// a permission its derived least-privilege SA deliberately does not
// have. The header would turn every runtime call into a 403.
quotaProject string
```

That asymmetry is why this is not simply FL19's line pasted into a
second file: `pkg/provision/gcp` is CLI-only, while
`pkg/backends/gcp` is shared by the CLI **and** every deployed service.
Unconditional here would break the runtime.

**After:**

```
$ tako users list --project tako-test-03
EMAIL                      ROLES     DISABLED  CREATED
editor@1dos3porti.com      editor    no        2026-08-11
```

**And the 403s tell the truth.** Two new branches ahead of the generic
one, in `UserStore.explain` and mirrored by `cloudErr`:

```
tako: cannot bill identitytoolkit calls to tako-test-03 — grant:
        gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding tako-test-03 \
          --member user:$(gcloud config get account) \
          --role roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer
```

```
tako: identitytoolkit.googleapis.com needs a billing project on tako-test-03 and this
      credential carries none — tako sends one for user credentials from
      `gcloud auth application-default login`. On a service-account key file, use
      ADC instead, or set GOOGLE_CLOUD_QUOTA_PROJECT.
```

The first text is deliberately the one `pkg/provision/gcp/gcp.go:399`
already prints for the same denial, word for word: one refusal, one
remediation, whichever command met it.

### Cloud errors & permissions

- `serviceusage.services.use` on the target is what the header costs.
  It is already in the documented deployer bundle as
  `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer`
  (`docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md:69`, added by FL19), so a deployer who
  followed the setup doc has it, and `tako setup` grants it. An operator
  who only ever runs `tako users` may not — hence the first branch above.
- 401 (unauthenticated), `SERVICE_DISABLED`, `CONFIGURATION_NOT_FOUND`
  and a genuine `identitytoolkit.admin` 403 keep their current texts and
  their current order; the new branches go ahead of the generic 403 only.
- Nothing changes for a deployed service: metadata credentials carry no
  JSON, so `quotaProject` stays empty and no header is sent.

### Scope

`pkg/backends/gcp/client.go` (`New`, `do`), `pkg/backends/gcp/users.go`
(`explain`), `cmd/tako/usersboot.go` (`cloudErr`),
`docs/reference/cli.md` and `docs/tako-cloud-permissions.md`.

**Non-goals**: `tako secrets --project`, which already goes through
`provision/gcp.NewClient` and has the header; any change to the runtime
path; any new flag. `GOOGLE_CLOUD_QUOTA_PROJECT` is named in an error
text only — reading it is a separate ask if anyone wants it.

### Tests

A fake identitytoolkit server asserting the header is present for a
user credential and **absent** for a metadata/SA one (the regression
that would break every deployed service), plus a `cloudErr` table for
the two new branches and the four existing ones. The header assertion
fails before the change; the absence assertion passes before and after,
which is the point of writing it.

### Gate

Fake-server tests are the automated tier. The live tier is
`tako users list --project <p>` under a real `gcloud auth
application-default login` — the exact command flauta could not run.

**Status: approved 2026-08-14 ("Approved, build it") — shipped, see below.**

### FL22 — shipped, and validated against the project that filed it

Built as proposed, nothing added.

**The header.** `New` now uses `google.FindDefaultCredentials` and keeps
`quotaProject`, set by `quotaProjectOf` only for a credential whose JSON
says `"type": "authorized_user"`. `do` sends `X-Goog-User-Project` when
it is set. Twelve lines and a long comment, because the comment is the
part that keeps someone from "simplifying" it into FL19's unconditional
version and taking every deployed service down.

**The diagnosis.** Two branches ahead of the generic 403, in the store's
`explain` and in the CLI's `cloudErr`: one for a
`serviceusage.services.use` denial (the grant, worded exactly as
`pkg/provision/gcp/gcp.go:399` already words it) and one for a call with
no billing project at all. Neither is a role problem, and both used to
be answered with a role.

**Live, from `examples/journal`, against flauta's own staging project,
with the operator's real `gcloud auth application-default login`
credential (`type: authorized_user`):**

```
### BEFORE — tako at 9eb87dc, built in a worktree at HEAD
$ tako users list --project tako-test-03
tako users · cloud · tako-test-03 / prod
tako: tako: this service may not list accounts on tako-test-03 — auth.Users() derives
roles/identitytoolkit.admin at deploy time, so re-run tako deploy if this service started
using it since the last one (Your application is authenticating by using local Application
Default Credentials. The identitytoolkit.googleapis.com API requires a quota project, which
is not set by default. …)

### AFTER — FL22
$ tako users list --project tako-test-03
tako users · cloud · tako-test-03 / prod
  ID                            EMAIL            NAME  ROLES
  ckxEf7zgJyMkEsvCaqZ9pTlXL253  e2e@flauta.test
  1 account
```

The BEFORE reproduces flauta's report word for word, including the
misdiagnosis. The AFTER lists the account flauta's own e2e suite made.
Worth noting for the credential file: it already carried
`quota_project_id: tako-test-03`, and that is precisely what did not
help — the value only matters if something sends it as a header.

**Validation**

```
pkg/backends/gcp      4 new tests (header present, header ABSENT, credential
                      types, the classification ladder)
cmd/tako              2 new rows on the refusal table, beside the four that
                      must keep working
go test ./...         19 packages ok · go vet, gofmt clean
tako test             all seven examples ok
live                  the transcript above, tako-test-03
```

Mutation-proofed three ways: dropping the header fails the billing test;
sending it unconditionally fails the deployed-service test with "the
header costs serviceusage.services.use…"; moving the billing branches
after the generic 403 fails the classification test.

### Discovered work

- **51. A store error reaches the operator prefixed twice.** The BEFORE
  transcript reads `tako: tako: this service may not…`: the store's
  `explain` prefixes, and the CLI prefixes again for anything its own
  ladder does not rewrite. Cosmetic, pre-existing, and visible in every
  unclassified cloud failure.

### Verdict

**Shipped and live-validated.** The friction entry is flauta's to close
in its own log — a tako session never writes there.

## FL23 — a template set that can be replaced (DX proposal)

Friction filed 2026-08-12, sharpened 2026-08-13, verdict **worth asking
for** and the only entry in flauta's log with **no app-side workaround
worth taking**. It blocks M8's last slice: an editor saving a template
from the admin UI.

### What exists

`RegisterSiteTemplates` parses the set at startup into
`var siteTemplates map[string]*template.Template`, and `renderSite`
reads it. **No mutex, no atomic, no re-registration path.** The function
is exported and idempotent in shape, so calling it again *looks*
supported; doing it while a request renders is a concurrent map read and
write, and Go's runtime kills the process for that. Verified at
`af82c3c`.

Four package-level vars are really one value — `siteTemplates`,
`siteParseErrors`, `siteSetupError`, `siteHasLayout` — and a swap that
moved them one at a time could hand a render new templates with old
parse errors.

### The surface

One method on the declared site:

```go
// LoadTemplates parses fsys as a complete candidate template set and
// installs it. All or nothing: if any template fails to parse, the live
// set is untouched and the error names every file that failed.
func (s *SiteHandle) LoadTemplates(ctx Ctx, fsys fs.FS) error

// TemplateErrors reports which templates in a refused set failed, and
// why. Keyed by path relative to templates/ — the name the editor sees.
type TemplateErrors struct {
	Failed map[string]string
}
```

`Failed` holds strings rather than `error` values on purpose: the admin
UI's job is to hand them back to whoever typed the mistake, which means
rendering them and often serializing them.

**The app's half, in the order that matters:**

```go
func saveTemplate(ctx tako.Ctx, req SaveReq) (tako.HTML, error) {
	// A candidate SET, not a file: templates reference each other, so
	// one validated file can still produce a set that will not render.
	next := templatesWith(current, req.Path, req.Source)

	if err := site.LoadTemplates(ctx, next); err != nil {
		var bad *tako.TemplateErrors
		if errors.As(err, &bad) {
			return site.Fragment(ctx, "admin/template-errors.html", bad.Failed)
		}
		return tako.HTML{}, err
	}
	// Only now is it worth storing: a set that would not load is not a
	// draft, it is a broken site nobody has served yet.
	return site.Fragment(ctx, "admin/saved.html", nil), posts.Put(ctx, req.Path, req.Source)
}
```

Validate-then-persist is the shape the all-or-nothing rule exists to
make possible, which is why the snippet leads with it.

### How it works

The four vars become one immutable struct behind an `atomic.Pointer`:

```go
type templateSet struct {
	byName    map[string]*template.Template
	parseErr  map[string]error
	setupErr  error
	hasLayout bool
}
var siteSet atomic.Pointer[templateSet]
```

`renderNamed` loads the pointer **once** and renders from that value, so
an in-flight render finishes against the set it started with — flauta's
second requirement, which falls out of the design rather than needing
machinery. `RegisterSiteTemplates` keeps its signature and becomes the
boot-time caller of the same parse, so there is one parser and not two.

### Against the six rules

1. **Declared noun** — no new global; a method on the site already
   declared. 2. **One constructor shape** — no new constructor.
3. **One method shape** — `(Ctx, …) error`; `Ctx` first because the rule
says so and because the swap is worth logging with the request that
caused it. 6. **No primitive owns a general concept** — scoped to the
handle, not a `tako.Templates` namespace.

Rule 4 (**one verb vocabulary**) is the one it strains: `Load` is a new
verb beside `Render`/`Fragment`/`Markdown`, and the store verbs
(`Get`/`Put`/`Delete`) do not fit something with no key. `LoadTemplates`
reads as what it does. **Flagged rather than settled** — if you prefer
`SetTemplates` or `ReplaceTemplates`, now is the moment, because it is
an exported symbol and renaming it later is its own task.

### The thing to rule on: a swap is per-INSTANCE

Cloud Run autoscales, and this replaces the set **in one process**. An
editor saving a template changes the instance that served their request;
every other live instance keeps rendering the old set until it restarts.
With min-instances 1 and a quiet site that is invisible. Under any real
concurrency it is an editor seeing their change flicker in and out
depending on which instance answers.

Tako has no mechanism for "tell every instance" and building one is a
subsystem, not this task. Three honest options:

- **A. Ship it per-instance, document the limit.** The app loads its
  stored set at boot, so a restart converges, and the window is one
  deploy or one scale event. Recommended: it unblocks M8, and the
  alternative to a per-instance swap today is no swap at all.
- **B. Hold until there is a coherence story** (a lease-driven reload, a
  topic every instance subscribes to). Correct, and it is a milestone,
  not a slice.
- **C. Ship A, and make the limit structural** — a note in the reference
  plus a `SiteConfig` field that pins the site's service to
  `MaxInstances: 1` while template editing is on. Cheap, honest, and it
  makes the tradeoff the app's decision rather than a footnote.

I recommend **A**, with C's documentation but not C's field: pinning
instances from a template feature couples two unrelated things, and an
app that wants max=1 can already say so.

### Scope

`pkg/runtime/page.go` (the set struct, the atomic, one parser),
`site.go` (`LoadTemplates`, `TemplateErrors`), `docs/reference/site.md`,
`docs/api/surface.txt` via the lock.

**Non-goals**: persistence (tako never stores a swapped set — the app
owns its storage and reloads at boot); per-file swaps; a watcher; a
separate validate-only call, since a failed `LoadTemplates` already
validates without changing anything; any change to `tako dev`'s reload.

### Tests

- **The crash that exists today**: concurrent renders + a re-register
  under `-race`. Fails now, passes after.
- All-or-nothing: a candidate with one broken template is refused whole,
  and the live set still renders the page that was already working.
- `TemplateErrors.Failed` is keyed by path, with every failure present —
  not just the first.
- An in-flight render finishes against its own set (swap mid-render).
- The boot path is unchanged: existing site tests stay green untouched.

### Gate

Automated tier is the `-race` test. Scripted tier: `tako dev` on the
journal example, edit a template through a test handler, watch a
subsequent request render the new one and a broken candidate leave the
old one serving.

**Status: superseded by the amendment below; approved 2026-08-14 with ruling A.**

### FL23 — amended before it was built: the gate above is on the wrong property

The proposal gates publication on **parsing**, and parsing is not the
property that matters. Go resolves `{{ template "site/card.html" }}` at
EXECUTE time, not parse time — measured, not assumed:

```
parse error:   <nil>
execute error: html/template:page.html:1:22: no such template "site/card.html"
```

So a candidate set that lost a partial parses perfectly and fails on the
first page that uses it. `LoadTemplates` would have waved it through and
the site would have 500'd — through the gate built to prevent exactly
that. The point came from flauta's own read of the same file, and it is
correct.

**The shape that follows**, adopted over the one above: a candidate must
be *renderable* before it is published, which means it has to exist as a
value the app can render against.

```go
func (s *SiteHandle) PrepareTemplates(ctx Ctx, fsys fs.FS) (*TemplateSet, error)
func (set *TemplateSet) Render(ctx Ctx, name string, data any) (HTML, error)
func (s *SiteHandle) UseTemplates(ctx Ctx, set *TemplateSet) error
```

flauta renders its thirteen public surfaces against the candidate and
publishes only if all thirteen come back. Three notes on the diff from
flauta's version of this sketch:

- **`Ctx` first on all three** (rule 3), where the sketch omitted it on
  `PrepareTemplates`, and `UseTemplates` returns `error` where the sketch
  returned nothing — which also gives it somewhere to refuse a nil or
  foreign set instead of panicking inside a later render.
- This is **better on rule 4** than `LoadTemplates` was: `TemplateSet.Render`
  is the verb the site already has, with the signature it already has, so
  the feature adds no new vocabulary.
- `TemplateSet.Render` incidentally gives markup-from-a-candidate without
  opening a general `HTML`-from-bytes constructor.

Unchanged from the proposal: the atomic swap, the single load per render,
`RegisterSiteTemplates` keeping its signature as prepare-then-use, the
`-race` test, and every non-goal.

**Ruling A (owner, 2026-08-14): ship it per-instance and document the
limit.** A publish replaces the set in the process that served the
request; other instances keep theirs until they restart. The app loads
its stored set at boot, so a restart converges.

**One hazard the split introduces**, worth stating where the feature is
described rather than discovering it in production: prepare-then-use is
not atomic as a pair. Two editors saving at once can have B publish and
then A publish a set prepared before B's edit, silently reverting it.
Last-writer-wins is correct for `Use` alone; serializing save is the
app's business, and it is cheap there.

### FL23 — shipped (2026-08-14)

Built to the amended shape, ruling A.

**The registry is one value.** `siteSet` holds the templates, the
per-template parse errors, the setup error and `hasLayout`;
`parseSiteTemplates` builds it entirely in locals and returns it, and
`currentSet atomic.Pointer[siteSet]` is the only published state. Every
render loads the pointer once. `RegisterSiteTemplates` keeps its
signature and is now the boot-time caller of the same parser, so a
deployed service's first set is built exactly the way a replacement is.

The torn read is gone with it: `renderNamed` used to read
`siteParseErrors` and then `siteTemplates`, so a set landing between
those two lines could report a parse error from the set before it.

**Three calls**, `Ctx` first on all three, per the amendment:
`SiteHandle.PrepareTemplates`, `TemplateSet.Render`,
`SiteHandle.UseTemplates`, plus `TemplateErrors{Failed map[string]string}`.
The SDK lock and `docs/api/surface.txt` carry exactly those six lines and
nothing else.

**Live, through `tako dev` and generated code**, on a scratch app (no
example touched — a page that prepares from a directory, renders the
candidate, and publishes only if it rendered):

```
### 1. before
<h1>ORIGINAL</h1> card v1
### 2. publish alt/ (good candidate)
<h1>REPLACED</h1> card v2
### 3. after — a fresh request
<h1>REPLACED</h1> card v2
### 4. publish broken/ — parses fine, card.html deleted
candidate refused: template home.html: html/template:home.html:1:51: no such template "card.html"
### 5. the live site after the refusal
<h1>REPLACED</h1> card v2
```

Step 4 is the whole argument for the three-part shape in one line: that
candidate **parses**, and only rendering it finds the missing partial.
The single-call design in the original proposal would have published it.
(The walk also met the CSRF gate on the POST and had to carry `_csrf` —
which is the framework working.)

**Tests** — `pkg/runtime/templateswap_test.go`, 7 cases: the race
(8 readers, 200 publishes, under `-race`), publish-replaces-what-renders,
all-or-nothing naming every failure, the parses-but-cannot-render case,
an in-flight render keeping its own set, a foreign set refused, and one
that goes through the SDK surface rather than the runtime's internals —
because a correct implementation behind an unwired hook is a feature
nobody can call.

**The before state is not a failing test, it is a dead process.** Run in
a worktree at `af82c3c`:

```
fatal error: concurrent map read and map write
github.com/gsandoval/tako/pkg/runtime.renderNamed(…) page.go:229
github.com/gsandoval/tako/pkg/runtime.renderSite(…) page.go:213
```

**Validation**

```
go test ./...          19 packages ok · vet, gofmt clean
go test ./pkg/runtime -race   ok
tako test              all seven examples ok
docs                   site.md's new section; symbolPage maps the two new types
```

The scratch app needed `go get …/pkg/runtime` before `tako dev` would
resolve — which is not a gap: `tako new` already does exactly that
(`cmd/tako/new.go:135`), and hand-writing the go.mod skipped it.

### Verdict

**Shipped and validated.** Flauta's entry is theirs to close. The
per-instance limit and the prepare/use race are documented in
`site.md` where the feature is described, not in a footnote.

## FL24 — CronMissed derives a lookback Cloud Monitoring refuses (DX proposal)

Friction filed 2026-08-11, workaround-fine but **worth asking for**: the
one cron whose silent failure is invisible — *"a backup that quietly
stops running looks exactly like a backup that is running"* — could not
be alerted on. The deploy died at the last resource:

```
tako: create alert policy BackupMissed: create the alert policy:
custom.googleapis.com metrics are not supported in PromQL alerts with
lookback windows longer than 1d1h. (HTTP 400 from monitoring.googleapis.com)
```

### It is worse than the report

`CronMissed` derives its lookback as twice the schedule, from
`cronPeriod` (`pkg/provision/alerts.go:565`):

```go
if d, err := time.ParseDuration(strings.TrimPrefix(h.Schedule, "every ")); err == nil {
	return d
}
return 24 * time.Hour
```

That parses `every 6h`. It does not parse a **cron expression**, and
`tako.Cron` accepts those — so `*/5 * * * *` falls through to the 24h
fallback and gets a **48h lookback**. Measured, by walking the parsed
schedule twice from a fixed instant:

| schedule | true period | `cronPeriod` today | derived lookback |
|---|---|---|---|
| `every 6h` | 6h | 6h | 12h ✓ |
| `*/5 * * * *` | **5m** | 24h | **48h ✗ refused** |
| `0 3 * * *` | **24h** | 24h | **48h ✗ refused** |
| `0 0 * * 0` | **168h** | 24h | **48h ✗ refused** |

So it is not "daily or slower" — **every cron declared with a cron
expression** is undeployable with `CronMissed`, including a
five-minutely one, where the derived alert would also have taken two
days to notice a stopped job.

And tako already knew the number: `maxRetestLookback = 25 * time.Hour`
(`promql.go:78`), used to decide whether a *retest* window is allowed
and never applied to the lookback itself.

### The proposal

**1. Derive the period from the schedule, not from a prefix.**
`schedule.Parse` already exists and `Next` is exact for every form tako
accepts; two calls give the period (5m, 24h, 168h in the table above).
The 24h fallback stays for a schedule that will not parse, which the
analyzer refuses anyway.

**2. Cap the derived lookback at Cloud Monitoring's ceiling.**

```go
lookback = min(2*cronPeriod(g, a.SubjectVar), maxCustomLookback)  // 25h
```

Capping tako's OWN derivation is not the thing tako refuses to do
elsewhere — `Delivery` says "tako will not quietly clamp yours" about a
value the user wrote. This is the default, and it stays visible: `tako
alerts` and the deploy plan both print the lookback, so a daily cron
reads `no data for 25h0m0s` rather than a number that fails at apply.

For every cron up to daily the cap still leaves slack: a 24h cron gets
25h, which is one missed run plus an hour — the window flauta ended up
choosing by hand.

**3. Refuse, at analysis time, what cannot be expressed.** A cron slower
than daily has no legal window: 25h is the ceiling, and anything under
its own period fires between healthy runs.

```
app.go:31:24: tako.CronMissed watches a cron that runs every 168h0m0s, and absence over
that long cannot be expressed — Cloud Monitoring refuses a lookback past 25h on a custom
metric, and any window it accepts is shorter than this cron's own interval, so the alert
would fire between healthy runs. Run the cron at least daily and watch that, or check
freshness inside a daily cron that can fail (tako/window)
```

**4. Refuse an explicit `Window{For: …}` past 25h on an absence.** Today
the analyzer checks `For` only for threshold conditions
(`alerts.go:757` is gated on `spec.Op != "absent"`), which is exactly
how an unbounded absence window reaches a deploy:

```
a Window's For on an absence cannot exceed 25h — Cloud Monitoring refuses a longer
lookback on a custom metric; got 172800s (tako/window)
```

**5. Fix two documentation claims, which disagree with the code and with
each other.** `alert.go:613` says a daily cron "gets… 26 hours"; the
code computes 48; `alerts.md:116` says 48. After this change the true
rule is "twice the schedule, capped at 25h", and all three say that.

### Scope

`pkg/provision/alerts.go` (`cronPeriod`, the cap), `pkg/provision/promql.go`
(the constant serves both uses), `pkg/analyzer/alerts.go` (two refusals),
`alert.go` doc comment, `docs/reference/alerts.md`, plus a golden fixture
for each new refusal.

**Non-goals**: any other reading's lookback (only `cron_missed` derives
one); a non-PromQL alert path for long absences; a `CronStale`-style
freshness primitive — if long-interval absence deserves first-class
support it is its own feature, and no example demands it.

### Tests

- The period table above, as a unit test over `cronPeriod`: `every 6h`,
  `*/5 * * * *`, `0 3 * * *`, `0 0 * * 0`.
- A daily cron's rendered PromQL carries `[90000s]` and not `[172800s]`
  — the deploy-refusing number, pinned so it cannot come back.
- Golden fixtures for both refusals (weekly `CronMissed`, and an
  explicit 48h `For` on an absence).
- The existing alerts goldens must move only where intended: a
  cron-expression cron's lookback changes because it was wrong.

### Gate

Automated only. The live tier would be a deploy of an alert policy that
Google accepts, which is worth doing on the next cloud walk rather than
standing up a project for one policy — the failure this fixes is an
HTTP 400 at apply, and the unit test pins the exact number Google
rejected.

**Status: approved 2026-08-14 ("Approved, build it") — shipped, see below.**

### FL24 — shipped (2026-08-14)

Built as proposed, plus one divergence the work uncovered.

**The period is read from the parsed schedule**, two `Next` calls from a
fixed instant, so every form tako accepts gives its true interval. The
old prefix-trim answered 24h for all of them:

```
every 6h        6h    (was 6h)
*/5 * * * *     5m    (was 24h → a 48h lookback on a five-minutely cron)
0 3 * * *       24h   (was 24h)
0 0 * * 0       168h  (was 24h)
```

**The derived lookback is capped** at `maxCustomLookback` — the 25h
constant that already existed in `promql.go` for the retest decision and
had never been applied to the lookback itself. A daily cron now renders
`[90000s]`, not the `[172800s]` in flauta's HTTP 400.

**Two refusals**, both at analysis time, with fixtures:

```
app.go:13:28: tako.CronMissed watches a cron that runs every 168h, and absence over that long
cannot be expressed — Cloud Monitoring refuses a lookback past 25h on a custom metric, and any
window it accepts is shorter than this cron's own interval, so the alert would fire between
healthy runs. Run the cron at least daily and watch that, or check freshness inside a daily
cron that can fail (tako/window)

app.go:16:23: a Window's For on an absence cannot exceed 25h — Cloud Monitoring refuses a
longer lookback on a custom metric; got 172800s (tako/window)
```

The second is the check that already existed for thresholds and was
gated on `spec.Op != "absent"` — the gate is what let an absence window
through to a deploy.

### The divergence the work uncovered

The incident documentation derived the lookback **again**, in
`alertdoc.go`, from its own `2 * cronPeriod`. Capping only the query
would have shipped a policy asking about 25h beside the page it opens
telling the responder 48h. Both now call one `cronMissedLookback`:

```
query:  …}[90000s])
page:   **No run of cron `Cleanup` has reached `gallery` in the last 25h.**
```

That is the third time this shape has turned up in a fortnight —
`verifyGoogleToken`, `entitytag`, and now this — and each time the second
copy was the one that was wrong.

### Documentation, which had three claims and no two agreeing

`alert.go` said a daily cron gets "26 hours", the code computed 48, and
`alerts.md` said 48. All three now say twice the schedule capped at 25h,
and both docs state why a slower-than-daily cron is refused.

### Validation

```
pkg/provision   3 new tests (the period table, the capped daily lookback,
                a cron expression's real period); 3 existing expectations
                moved, each one an assertion on the number that failed
go test ./...   19 packages ok · vet, gofmt clean
tako test       all seven examples ok
fixtures        cronmissedlong, absencewindow
```

The three moved expectations are worth naming, since a test changing with
the code it tests deserves an argument: `alerts_test.go` asserted
`[172800s]` for a daily cron, `alert_plan_test.go` asserted the same in
the plan, and `alertdoc_test.go` asserted "in the last 48h". All three
encoded the deploy-refusing number as correct.

### Discovered work

- **52. An absence condition is described as "sustained".** `tako alerts`
  prints `evaluated every 1m0s, sustained 5m0s` for a `CronMissed` with
  an explicit window, but on an absence `For` is the lookback, not a
  sustain — "no data for 5m0s" is what it means. Wording only, in
  `describe.go`.

### Gate

Automated. The live tier — a policy Google accepts on a daily cron —
belongs to the next cloud walk; the unit tests pin the exact number that
drew the 400.

### Verdict

**Shipped.** flauta's entry is theirs to close, and their workaround (a
daily backup with an explicit 25h window) needs no undoing: it is what
the derived default now produces on its own.
